topics.title: Discover attack surfaces
topics.blocks: 1; revisit after new routes or hosts
topics.access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
topics.intro: Discovery establishes reachable behavior from a particular source. Keep host discovery, TCP coverage, UDP coverage and application identity separate; each produces different evidence.
topics.start: Start with an assigned address/list and your actual source interface; no open service is assumed.

workflow.label: Confirm the source interface, route and host-discovery limitations
Separate initial TCP selection, full TCP coverage and UDP investigation
Establish application evidence on discovered listeners, including nonstandard ports
Save the endpoint queue and revisit it after a new identity or route

topics.title: Extract opportunities from services
topics.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
topics.intro: A service can disclose names, files, rights or execution. Test authentication, read, write and execution separately. A write becomes an execution path only when a useful consumer and trigger exist.
topics.start: Start with application evidence from discovery; anonymous access, valid credentials and useful rights are separate questions.

workflow.label: Use the matching protocol client and establish which identity the service accepts
Investigate names, account clues and configuration with the available service context
For databases inspect the current identity and grants before file or execution hypotheses
Retrieve relevant artifacts, classify credentials, and re-enumerate with any new accepted identity

topics.title: Map useful web behavior
topics.access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
topics.intro: Build the request and role map before selecting a weakness. Distinguish scheme, virtual host, route, method, parameter, object and identity; the same path can expose different behavior in another context.
topics.start: Start with a reachable URL. A suspicious parameter, hidden administration path or accepted account is not assumed.

workflow.label: Record scheme, hostname, redirects and session state
Browse real functions and capture their requests; inspect source/scripts and exposed artifacts
Use missing-path/host controls before content or virtual-host discovery
Map methods, input locations, object ownership and roles before selecting a weakness

topics.title: Turn application weaknesses into access
topics.access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison
topics.intro: Prove the primitive first: file read, interpreted inclusion, write, query influence, authorization change or browser/server execution. Then validate the additional condition required to turn that primitive into useful access.
topics.start: Start from a valid request produced by web mapping. Preserve account, cookies, method and normal input before changing one property.

workflow.label: Locate file-related functions and distinguish reads, interpreted includes and writes
Compare controlled commands or SQL predicates only in a known request context
Use authorized role/object comparisons to identify missing server-side checks
Prove the primitive, then inspect the additional execution/credential/consumer condition

topics.title: Recover and use authentication material
topics.access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
topics.intro: Treat passwords, keys, stored verifiers, challenge responses and tickets as different capabilities. Recovering a password, authenticating and obtaining useful authorization are separate transitions.
topics.start: Start with an artifact produced by an actual read, query, session or collection source; the artifact type and username may still be unknown.

workflow.label: Record source and account scope, then inspect the artifact's structure
Separate an immediately usable password/key from material needing recovery
Use type-specific handling for stored verifiers, captured responses and tickets
After acceptance, test the specific service right and return to authenticated enumeration

topics.title: Select and adapt public exploits
topics.access: An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source
topics.intro: Match the exploit's assumptions before editing it. Separate dependency, transaction, payload, connection and result failures; make the smallest evidence-backed change.
topics.start: Start with product/build/configuration evidence; a matching exploit or vulnerable version is not assumed.

workflow.label: Compare advisory and PoC prerequisites with the actual component and enabled features
Review code and establish its interpreter/dependencies before interpreting failures
Inspect process architecture and runtime before native compilation/adaptation
Reconstruct the real request when a web PoC's login, path or parser assumptions differ

topics.title: Establish sessions and move files
topics.access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path
topics.intro: Delivery, execution, connection and a usable session are separate states. Select a connection direction and compatible interpreter before generating payloads; transfers must preserve bytes and destination permissions.
topics.start: Start with a claimed effect, command primitive or accepted remote identity; a usable shell and return path remain unproved.

workflow.label: Verify destination, execution identity and the actual output channel
Inspect interpreters and both connection directions before choosing reverse, bind or native access
Match artifact/handler and terminal requirements to the selected consumer
Select a transfer route by available client, authentication and direction, then verify bytes

topics.title: Escalate privileges on Linux
topics.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
topics.intro: For each candidate prove controlled object → effective permission → privileged consumer → execution identity → trigger → effect. Enumeration tools suggest candidates; they do not establish that chain.
topics.start: Start with a low-privileged Linux command channel. No sudo rule, writable privileged script or usable SUID binary is assumed.

workflow.label: Establish effective IDs/groups, mounts, processes and exact sudo rules
Follow readable application/history/process artifacts into typed credentials
Inspect sudo/SUID/capabilities and prove effective object/parent permissions
Identify each job/service's real identity, consumed path and trigger; only then examine resolution abuse
Investigate daemon/mount/software candidates against their exact conditions

topics.title: Escalate privileges on Windows
topics.access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups
topics.intro: An administrator-group membership, enabled token privilege, writable object and effective privileged execution are different claims. Establish the precise right, consumer identity and available trigger before choosing a route.
topics.start: Start with a Windows foothold. Administrator-group membership, a high-integrity token and a working privileged trigger are separate facts.

workflow.label: Inspect whoami /all and host/process state before choosing a privilege route
Inventory real services/tasks and inspect exact object and parent ACLs
Separate writable service configuration, replaceable binaries, unquoted prefixes and dependency loads
Follow application/history/saved-credential artifacts and exact token privileges
Match software/driver/build evidence only after validating simpler permission routes

topics.title: Map Active Directory attack paths
topics.access: A known domain identity or a directory endpoint that permits the selected anonymous query
topics.intro: Build identity, object-right, host-access and session maps. A graph relationship is a candidate until its effective permission, destination and current state are checked.
topics.start: Start with a known domain identity or a directory query context; useful group, object-right and session edges are not assumed.

workflow.label: Resolve identity, realm, DC, DNS, clock and route first
Enumerate objects, group nesting and relevant shares with a supported client
Associate SPNs and effective ACEs with actual accounts and object types
Check host-specific rights and session freshness, then validate graph paths edge by edge

families.title: Effective rights, host access and path ranking

topics.title: Gain a more useful domain identity
topics.access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right
topics.intro: Choose a credential source or object transition by its prerequisites. Track the exact account, credential type and compatible service after every transition. Conditional AD CS/delegation/GPO branches require their own complete enabling chain.
topics.start: Start from a mapped object/right, an available ticket, or a host whose current privilege may expose a credential source.

workflow.label: Inspect existing tickets and host privilege/protection before invasive collection
Choose matched local credential sources and classify what each produces
Discover the actual account flag or SPN before choosing a roast path
Resolve the exact ACE and object before password, group, DACL or replication transitions
Expand certificate, delegation or GPO paths only when their specific configuration evidence exists

families.title: Conditional policy, delegation and certificate paths

topics.title: Move to another host
topics.access: Identified authentication material, destination service reachability and a candidate authorized identity
topics.intro: Select credential type → accepted authentication → reachable service → service authorization → execution effect. Hash/ticket use is an authentication dimension; SMB, tasks, WMI, WinRM and RDP are different access mechanisms.
topics.start: Start with material tied to a known identity and a destination candidate; neither valid authentication nor remote execution rights are assumed.

workflow.label: Check the destination from the actual source, including dynamic RPC and names
Classify password, NT hash, long-term key or service-scoped ticket
Match effective service/task/WMI authorization to its separate output path
Check endpoint or remote-interactive rights for WinRM/RDP and verify the resulting token

topics.title: Reach internal services
topics.access: A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path
topics.intro: A tunnel moves traffic; it does not grant destination authorization. Draw listener location, connection initiator, remote destination, DNS resolution and return path separately.
topics.start: Start from the pivot's current shell/process or accepted SSH access; another reachable subnet and an operational tunnel are not assumed.

workflow.label: Inspect pivot interfaces, routes, local listeners and destination reachability
Draw listener location and connection initiator before fixed or SSH forwarding
Choose proxy versus routed access according to the real client/protocol requirements
Validate names, KDC access and the separately required delivery/callback route
For additional hops test each leg before chaining the final application

families.title: SSH listener direction and proxy access
Names, return paths and multiple hops

topics.title: Resolve payload execution obstacles
topics.access: A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect
topics.intro: Locate the first failed boundary: delivery → trigger → parser → format/runtime → execution policy/control → connection → session. Change the condition supported by evidence instead of replacing every payload component.
topics.start: Start with the saved delivery/trigger/parser/runtime/connection chain and the last state actually proved.

workflow.label: For client-side paths establish the consumer and required interaction before callbacks
Inspect bytes, format, architecture, parser and runtime at the first failed boundary
Differentiate PowerShell language/policy and endpoint-control evidence
Match the exact handler and session lifecycle, then inspect actual packet direction

topics.title: Complete attacks and retain reproducible evidence
topics.access: An assigned objective, scope and accumulated host/identity/route evidence
topics.intro: Operate the attack as changing state. Keep coverage questions separate from vulnerability hypotheses, select tests that resolve an uncertainty, re-enumerate after transitions and preserve enough evidence to reproduce each step.
topics.start: Start with assigned scope/objectives and saved observations; no complete path or report-ready evidence is assumed.

workflow.label: Record hosts, identities, material, routes and unresolved questions
Connect only methods whose receiving prerequisites have evidence
Return to the last working state when tests stop producing new evidence
Capture each transition and validate rendered report/archive artifacts

methods.title: Validate the source path and discover hosts
methods.clue: No response, a new subnet, or uncertainty about the interface and route
methods.conditions: Correct VPN/interface and explicit scope; discovery probes must be compatible with the path
methods.access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
methods.result: A source-qualified reachable-host list and a defensible discovery limitation
methods.mechanics: Discovery probes identify responders; silence can be caused by filtering. A known assigned host can still require a port scan that skips discovery.
methods.checks:
```bash
ip addr
ip route get TARGET
nmap -sn SUBNET -oA host-discovery
```
methods.example: Observation: a known host is absent from the ping sweep. Test: confirm the route and scan its selected application port with discovery skipped. Illustrative output: TCP/443 is open. Interpretation: discovery missed a live service; retain the host and enumerate HTTPS.
methods.verify: Record source address/interface, route and the exact responding endpoint; a missing ping response does not prove a host is down.
methods.failure: No route or wrong VPN interface is an environment failure. If only discovery is blocked, use the known-host TCP method; a SOCKS path requires a compatible connect-based client.

recognition.where: From the assessment host inspect the assigned interface and the route to the exact target before interpreting silence.
recognition.commands:
```bash
ip addr
ip route get TARGET
nmap -sn SUBNET -oA host-discovery
```
recognition.sample:
TARGET via VPN_GATEWAY dev tun0 src SOURCE_IP
Nmap scan report for HOSTNAME (TARGET)
Host is up
recognition.spot: The route names the intended interface/source; a responder is evidence from that source, not a global reachability claim.
recognition.confirm: Check scope, target state and whether host-discovery probes are permitted by this path.
recognition.enabled: The assigned route is correct and the selected application responds: proceed to service coverage.
recognition.ruledout: The route points outside the assigned VPN: repair that route before evaluating the target.
recognition.unknown: No discovery response but a plausible route exists: the host may filter probes; test a justified selected port.

methods.procedure:
> **Purpose:** Confirm the source path and discover explicitly assigned hosts before spending time on port coverage. ##### 1. Check the path From the target's working folder: ```bash mkdir -p scans ip -br addr ip route get TARGET ``` > **Read:** selected interface/source address. A route lookup does not prove reachability.
Variants — discover one host, a host list or a subnet ##### Host discovery **One host:** ```bash nmap -sn -n -oA scans/host TARGET ``` **Assigned list:** put IPs in `targets.txt`, one per line. ```bash nmap -sn -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/hosts ``` **Explicitly assigned subnet:** ```bash nmap -sn -n -oA scans/subnet SUBNET ``` No response does not establish that a host is offline. A list of assigned hosts does not imply the surrounding subnet is in scope.

methods.title: Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans
methods.clue: An assigned host needs an initial service queue or full TCP coverage
methods.conditions: SYN scanning needs raw-packet privileges; connect scanning needs OS TCP connections; specify selected versus full port coverage
methods.access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
methods.result: A saved TCP port-state inventory with explicit coverage
methods.mechanics: SYN and connect scans infer reachability differently but both cover only their selected ports. A common-port scan is a prioritization pass, not full TCP coverage.
methods.checks:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sT --top-ports 1000 TARGET -oA tcp-initial
nmap -Pn -sT -p- TARGET -oA tcp-full
```
methods.example: Observation: the initial scan exposes SSH and HTTP. Test: finish full TCP selection. Illustrative output: an additional management service appears on a high port. Interpretation: add it to the queue before committing to a web-only path.
methods.verify: Retain the selected port set, source context, completion/errors and raw output; follow open ports with focused application evidence.
methods.failure: Filtered is not closed. Through SOCKS use supported TCP-connect behavior and skip unsupported raw discovery/UDP; if results conflict, compare from the actual source.

recognition.where: After path validation, compare a first TCP pass with explicit full-port coverage; record skipped discovery or privilege limitations.
recognition.commands:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sT --top-ports 1000 TARGET -oA tcp-initial
nmap -Pn -sT -p- TARGET -oA tcp-full
```
recognition.sample:
Initial selection: 22/tcp open ssh; 80/tcp open http
Full selection also: 18080/tcp open unknown
recognition.spot: The high listener exists outside the first selection; its application label remains provisional.
recognition.confirm: Confirm scan completion, source, errors and application behavior on each interesting port.
recognition.enabled: A focused connection and application response confirm the listener: queue its service.
recognition.ruledout: The earlier result cannot be reproduced after a completed focused check: retire that stale listener hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: Filtered ports or interrupted scans leave coverage/reachability unresolved; save the limit and choose a focused check.

methods.procedure:
> **Purpose:** Get quick leads, complete TCP coverage, and adapt scan type, discovery handling, timing and output to the access path. ##### 2. Get initial TCP results ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -oA scans/tcp-initial TARGET ``` > **Coverage:** 1,000 common TCP ports. Review `scans/tcp-initial.nmap` in a text editor.
Variants — host list, connect scan or selected ports ##### Initial view: 1,000 common ports **Assigned host list, SYN scan:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-initial-list ``` **One host, connect scan without raw-packet privileges:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -oA scans/tcp-connect TARGET ``` Default coverage is the common-port selection, not ports 1-1000. ##### Selected ports or a range **One host:** replace PORTS with, for example, `25,43` or `1-1024`. ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-selected TARGET ``` **Find relevant services across assigned hosts:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-service-sweep ``` A focused service sweep is not a full port map.
##### 3. Complete TCP coverage ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all TARGET ``` > **Coverage:** TCP 1-65535. Investigate useful initial results while this runs.
Variants — connect scan, blocked discovery, timing and progress ##### All TCP ports: 1-65535 **Connect scan:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-connect TARGET ``` Inspect additional endpoints before narrowing the investigation. TCP coverage says nothing about UDP. ##### Discovery skips a running target **Recheck relevant ports with response reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn --reason -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-recheck TARGET ``` **Proceed with full TCP coverage despite failed discovery:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-no-discovery TARGET ``` `-Pn` assumes online status; inspect actual responses. It does not fix routing. Use `-sT` without sudo if ordinary TCP connections are needed. ##### Timing and progress **Full TCP with normal timing and periodic progress:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T3 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-normal TARGET ``` **Faster timing on a stable path:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T4 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-faster TARGET ``` `-T3` is normal timing; `-T4` is more aggressive. Periodic progress changes display, not coverage. Recheck decisive results if loss or filtering makes observations uncertain. ##### TCP-only access through a SOCKS proxy Use ordinary connect calls when a previously established proxy is the only route. This is a bounded first view, not complete TCP coverage: ```bash proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/tcp-proxy-top100 TARGET ``` `proxychains` cannot turn SYN probes or UDP into proxied TCP connections. `-Pn` avoids discovery probes that may not traverse the proxy. Confirm the proxy route first, preserve the 100-port limit, and expand with another connect scan only when scope and path permit it.

methods.title: Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks
methods.clue: A listener has a port-based label or uncertain version
methods.conditions: A reachable selected port; scripts must match the application and permitted assessment behavior
methods.access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
methods.result: Application and version evidence sufficient to choose service enumeration or an exploit candidate
methods.mechanics: Port numbers and banners suggest a protocol; application responses and exact configuration constrain an exploit. NSE results remain candidates when the check cannot prove the vulnerable condition.
methods.checks:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sV -p PORTS TARGET -oA selected-services
nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME
```
methods.example: Observation: port 8443 is labelled HTTPS but the product is unknown. Test: version probes and a normal HTTP request. Illustrative output: a named management product and login route. Interpretation: map authentication and verify the build before exploit selection.
methods.verify: Preserve the responding product/version evidence and distinguish an inferred fingerprint from a confirmed vulnerable build.
methods.failure: A timeout, generic banner or scanner label leaves identity inconclusive; use native protocol clients or the unknown-port method.

recognition.where: Take the discovered open-port list and request protocol/version evidence rather than choosing attacks from conventional port numbers.
recognition.sample:
18080/tcp open http APPLICATION_SERVER
Service detection performed
recognition.spot: An HTTP response on a nonstandard port routes investigation to application mapping; a product string is still only fingerprint evidence.
recognition.confirm: Verify normal requests, hostname/TLS requirements and exact build/configuration before selecting an exploit.
recognition.enabled: Native protocol responses agree with the fingerprint: use that service's enumeration guide.
recognition.ruledout: A presumed SSH port instead speaks HTTP: discard the SSH-specific method for that endpoint.
recognition.unknown: Generic banners or timeouts do not identify a build; try protocol-aware/TLS discrimination.

methods.procedure:
> **Purpose:** Identify applications on discovered ports and choose only the probing needed for the next decision. ##### 4. Identify discovered applications ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services TARGET ``` > **Next:** choose service-specific enumeration from application evidence. A version match alone does not establish exploitability.
Variants — default scripts, named scripts and OS fingerprints ##### Identify applications on discovered ports **Version probing plus the default NSE script set:** use when those scripts answer relevant enumeration questions. ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -sC -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-default TARGET ``` Read the application evidence and script results. Default scripts add interactions; they do not complete service enumeration or prove exploitability. **Lighter version probing when time or fragile service behavior matters:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV --version-light -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-light TARGET ``` Light mode tries fewer uncommon probes and can miss an identity that the default intensity finds. Use the default first unless a concrete constraint justifies the tradeoff. ##### Select a named script **Inspect behavior locally:** ```bash nmap --script-help http-headers ``` **After identifying HTTP, inspect its relevant port(s):** ```bash nmap -sT -n -p PORTS --script http-headers -oA scans/http-headers TARGET ``` Returned headers are clues. Choose scripts for the question they answer and their behavior. ##### OS fingerprinting and bundled probing **Estimate OS from network-stack behavior:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O -oA scans/os TARGET ``` **Request more tentative OS guesses:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O --osscan-guess -oA scans/os-guesses TARGET ``` **Bundle OS/version detection, default scripts and traceroute:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -A -oA scans/combined-detail TARGET ``` OS guesses are hypotheses. These use default TCP coverage; `-A` does not mean all ports. Choose this bundle only when its additional probing is useful.

methods.title: Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence
methods.clue: TCP enumeration is incomplete for the objective or DNS/SNMP/RPC clues suggest UDP
methods.conditions: Raw-packet access and UDP reachability from the real source; bounded or full selection must be explicit
methods.access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
methods.result: UDP responders and documented open/filtered uncertainty
methods.mechanics: A UDP service may ignore an empty probe; ICMP errors and application responses distinguish states. Silence alone cannot distinguish open from filtered.
methods.checks:
```bash
sudo nmap -Pn -sU --top-ports 20 --reason TARGET -oA udp-initial
sudo nmap -Pn -sU -sV -p 53,161 TARGET -oA udp-focused
```
methods.example: Observation: UDP/161 is open|filtered. Test: a correctly formatted SNMP request with a justified community. Illustrative output: system OIDs return. Interpretation: SNMP is confirmed accessible; enumerate useful branches.
methods.verify: Use an application response for a confirmed service; document unresolved silence, coverage and ICMP rate-limit effects.
methods.failure: Do not translate UDP silence into a closed service. Retry a focused application-aware probe or a different permitted vantage point.

recognition.where: Inspect discovery results and DNS/SNMP/RPC clues, then probe a separate bounded UDP selection from the same source.
recognition.sample:
161/udp open|filtered snmp no-response
53/udp open domain udp-response
recognition.spot: A DNS response confirms a UDP application; open|filtered SNMP silence is a candidate requiring a correctly formatted request.
recognition.confirm: Check accepted service parameters, response identity and possible ICMP rate limiting.
recognition.enabled: A service-native request returns the expected OID/record: enumerate that application.
recognition.ruledout: An explicit port-unreachable response rules out that UDP endpoint for this source/time.
recognition.unknown: Silence can mean open or filtered; use a justified application-aware probe rather than declaring either.

methods.procedure:
> **Purpose:** Sample UDP separately, preserve ambiguous states, and expand only when the objective or evidence warrants it. ##### 5. Check UDP separately ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 20 -oA scans/udp-top20 TARGET ``` > **Limit:** this is a sample. `open|filtered` remains inconclusive; expand when evidence or the objective warrants it.
Variants — larger sample, selected ports, application probes and TCP + UDP ##### Common-port samples **Expand to 100 common ports when more coverage is warranted:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/udp-top100 TARGET ``` These are samples. `open|filtered` is inconclusive; TCP results cannot fill UDP gaps. ##### Selected ports **Check a relevant UDP port/list:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-selected TARGET ``` **Add application probes to resolve a useful candidate:** ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-detail TARGET ``` A reply can resolve ambiguity; no reply can leave it inconclusive. If discovery skips an assigned running host, add `-Pn` with the same limitations as TCP. ##### Full UDP coverage when the objective justifies the cost ```bash sudo nmap -sU -n -p- --stats-every 60s -oA scans/udp-all TARGET ``` This selects UDP ports 1-65535 and may take a long time because silence requires waiting and ICMP errors may be rate-limited. It is the coverage-expansion option, not a universal first command. Continue service work in parallel and preserve the result if the scan cannot finish. ##### Combined TCP/UDP selection **Example selection:** change the TCP (`T:`) and UDP (`U:`) lists for the actual question. ```bash sudo nmap -sS -sU -n -p T:22,80,445,U:53,123,161 -oA scans/tcp-udp TARGET ``` The port lists are examples, not complete coverage. UDP waiting can extend the combined scan.

methods.clue: Scanners disagree, a result is ambiguous, or a new identity changes accessible behavior
methods.conditions: A selected endpoint and a test that can resolve the decision-changing uncertainty
methods.access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
methods.result: An evidence-labelled queue of endpoints, access contexts and next tests
methods.mechanics: A TCP connection proves transport reachability, not successful protocol authentication or useful rights. Re-enumeration is required when identity or route changes.
methods.checks:
```bash
nc -nvz TARGET PORT
nmap -Pn -sT -p PORT --reason TARGET
```
methods.example: Observation: one scan calls a port filtered while Netcat connects. Test: repeat the focused scan and speak the application protocol. Illustrative output: a service banner returns. Interpretation: keep the application evidence and investigate timing/source differences.
methods.verify: Record which layer was demonstrated: transport, application, authentication, read/write or execution.
methods.failure: Connection success with no useful response needs a protocol-aware test; repeated identical failures without new evidence do not justify repeating the same path.

recognition.where: Compare saved scan results with one direct connection and a service-native request for the endpoint that changes your next decision.
recognition.commands:
```bash

nmap -Pn -sT -p PORT --reason TARGET
```
recognition.sample:
Connection to TARGET PORT succeeded
PORT/tcp open SERVICE syn-ack
recognition.spot: Independent TCP reachability supports an endpoint candidate, not credentials, read permission or execution.
recognition.confirm: Identify the application and validate the particular next-layer action.
recognition.enabled: The protocol answers and the intended access check succeeds: record that specific capability.
recognition.ruledout: The expected protocol is absent despite a listener: reject that protocol-specific hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: Conflicting source/time results need a controlled repeat and route comparison.

methods.procedure:
> **Purpose:** Resolve uncertainty that affects a decision, preserve coverage limits, and turn scan output into a service-enumeration queue. ##### 6. Resolve a result that changes your next action Keep source, destination, transport and port consistent when comparing results. Revisit relevant checks after a new route, foothold or identity changes access.
Variants — Netcat verification, response reasons and readable output ##### Netcat connection check **One TCP port:** replace PORTS with one number. ```bash nc -nv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS ``` **Short port range:** replace PORTS with a range such as `3388-3390`. ```bash nc -nvv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS ``` Success establishes TCP connection acceptance; refusal and timeout differ. The second form gives more verbose output. A three-second wait may be insufficient on a slow path. ##### Output and diagnostics **Readable text only, with verbose output and port-state reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -v --reason -p PORTS -oN scans/tcp-check.txt TARGET ``` Open saved `.nmap` or `.txt` output in a text editor. `-oA` writes `.nmap`, `.gnmap` and `.xml`; `-oN` writes only normal text. Use a different output prefix when retaining another run.
##### 7. Build the service queue Open the saved `.nmap` files in a text editor. For every useful endpoint, capture one line with this structure: ```text SOURCE -> TARGET | tcp/udp PORT | OBSERVED STATE | APPLICATION EVIDENCE | COVERAGE LIMIT | NEXT TEST ``` > **Next:** carry the complete endpoint tuple into [Stage 02 service enumeration](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/02-service-enumeration/README.md) and choose the cheapest protocol-aware test that can change your understanding or access. Keep an explicit return item for incomplete TCP, UDP or application coverage.
Interpretation cues — preserve what the scan actually established - `open` establishes a reachable endpoint from the scan source; it does not establish a vulnerability or usable authentication. - `closed` records an explicit rejection in that context. Move on unless later evidence changes the route, source or target state. - `filtered` leaves the listener state unresolved because filtering, loss or the path prevented classification. - `unfiltered` means the selected probe reached the port but could not determine whether it was open or closed; use a scan type that can answer the required question. - UDP `open|filtered` is inconclusive. A useful protocol probe may reduce uncertainty, but another silence can remain inconclusive. - `closed|filtered` is also an explicit ambiguity. Preserve it unless resolving the distinction changes the next action. - A port-based service label is a clue. Use application evidence before treating product, version, operating system or machine role as confirmed. - Record the exact target, transport, selected ports and source position. A successful narrow scan does not cover untested ports, the other transport or another network position.
##### 8. Prioritize and know when to rescan Rank candidates by the cheapest test likely to produce access, credentials, sensitive information or a decisive prerequisite. Prefer observed application behavior over conventional port numbers. Keep at least one return item for incomplete coverage so an attractive early service does not erase the rest of the map. Re-run network discovery after a new source host, route, tunnel or target restart. Re-enumerate a service after a new credential or identity. Inspect local listeners after a foothold. Recheck a previous result when the source, target state, port selection or network conditions changed—not simply because the first attack failed.

methods.title: Enumerate reachable endpoints from a Windows source
methods.clue: The useful vantage point is a Windows host without Nmap
methods.conditions: A permitted Windows shell, explicit target list and built-in networking support
methods.access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
methods.result: Selected TCP reachability from the Windows network position
methods.mechanics: A local TcpClient or Test-NetConnection uses the host's route and firewall context. Results from Kali do not substitute for reachability from this source.
methods.checks:
```powershell
Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4
Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port PORT
```
methods.example: Observation: Kali cannot reach an internal WinRM endpoint. Test: check TCP/5985 from the Windows foothold. Illustrative output: TcpTestSucceeded is True. Interpretation: a new route/source exists; choose a forward or run an authorized native client there.
methods.verify: Associate each result with the actual Windows source and selected port; do not claim UDP or full-port coverage.
methods.failure: A false result may be routing, filtering or service absence; use route and listener evidence before deciding the service is down.

recognition.where: From the Windows foothold inspect interfaces/routes, then check an assigned internal host's selected service ports.
recognition.sample:
InterfaceAlias   : ADAPTER
SourceAddress    : SOURCE_IP
RemotePort       : 445
TcpTestSucceeded : True
recognition.spot: The service is reachable from this Windows source; this can reveal a useful vantage point unavailable from Kali.
recognition.confirm: Confirm application/authentication and whether a forward or a native client can use that route.
recognition.enabled: A protocol request works from this source: choose an authorized service client or suitable tunnel.

methods.procedure:
> **Purpose:** Test TCP reachability from a Windows host when source position or available tooling matters. Test one TCP port from the Windows source host: ```powershell Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORTS ``` > **Read:** `TcpTestSucceeded`, source and destination addresses. Use one number for PORTS. Failure does not distinguish a closed port, filtering or a path problem.
Variants — scan ports 1-1024 or a selected port list ##### Scan a low-port range ```powershell 1..1024 | % {echo ((New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient).Connect("DC_IP", $_)) "TCP port $_ is open"} 2>$null ``` ##### Check a selected port list The example list can be changed to the endpoints of interest. ```powershell 22,80,443,445,3389 | % {echo ((New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient).Connect("TARGET", $_)) "TCP port $_ is open"} 2>$null ``` `$_` is the current port; errors are hidden. No printed result does not prove every port is closed. Results reflect the Windows host's access and the stated port selection.

methods.title: Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives
methods.clue: A nonstandard listener, slow TCP discovery or a scanner-specific candidate
methods.conditions: Explicit bounded scope; raw scanning alternatives need their required privileges and conservative rates
methods.access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
methods.result: A validated listener/protocol candidate rather than an unverified scanner finding
methods.mechanics: Fast discovery tools trade probing depth for speed. Recheck discovered ports with Nmap and a native client; a vulnerability-script label is not a complete exploit proof.
methods.checks:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET
nc -nv TARGET PORT
```
methods.example: Observation: fast discovery reports an unexpected high port. Test: a focused version probe and protocol request. Illustrative output: an HTTP response appears. Interpretation: treat it as a web application regardless of its port.
methods.verify: Confirm the endpoint through independent application behavior and preserve the rate/scope used for discovery.
methods.failure: No response may require TLS or a protocol-first request. Avoid treating speed-oriented results as complete, and keep prohibited mass vulnerability scanners outside the exam path.

recognition.where: Select an unexplained listener from the saved queue, compare native connection behavior, then use focused version/TLS probes.
recognition.commands:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET
nc -nv TARGET PORT
```
recognition.sample:
PORT/tcp open ssl/http APPLICATION
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://HOSTNAME/
recognition.spot: TLS and an HTTP redirect suggest a hostname-selected web application rather than an attack tied to the port number.
recognition.confirm: Reproduce the hostname/TLS request and confirm exact software/configuration.
recognition.enabled: A correctly addressed request produces the application: move to its normal behavior map.
recognition.ruledout: The banner disproves the originally assumed protocol: remove that service hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: No banner may mean a client-first protocol, TLS or filtering; use a discriminating normal request.

methods.procedure:
> **Use when:** Nmap remains the interpretation baseline, but a faster TCP discovery pass or a bounded web-server check is useful. These tools generate candidates; Nmap/manual protocol checks confirm them. ##### RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation > **Prerequisite:** RustScan and Nmap on Kali; direct TCP reachability. **Coverage:** only the explicit TCP range. **Decisive output:** a discovered port that Nmap can reproduce and identify. ```bash rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-followup ``` If the target or network becomes unstable, lower concurrency rather than trusting an empty result. RustScan does not replace UDP work and does not prove that closed/filtered ports were tested with the same semantics as Nmap.
Bounded first 1,000 TCP ports ```bash rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-1000 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-1000 ``` > Use only for a quick selection. It is not full TCP coverage and is not equivalent to Nmap's default top-1,000 selection.
##### Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation > **Prerequisite:** root/raw-packet access and a directly routed target. **Choose it:** for a large authorized address/port space where discovery speed matters. **Failure cue:** high loss or inconsistent results at the chosen rate. ```bash sudo masscan TARGET -p1-65535 --rate 500 -oL masscan-open.txt ``` Treat each hit as a candidate and recheck with Nmap: ```bash PORTS=$(awk '$1 == "open" && $2 == "tcp" {print $3}' masscan-open.txt \ | sort -nu | paste -sd,) test -n "$PORTS" && sudo nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p "$PORTS" TARGET -oA masscan-verified ``` Masscan's raw-packet model is not suitable through a TCP SOCKS proxy. A rate that overwhelms the path can create false negatives and disrupt the lab; record the rate with the result. ##### Unknown-port discrimination Start passively or with protocol-appropriate probes. Do not spray arbitrary strings at a stateful or destructive service. ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-version.txt nmap --script-help banner nmap -Pn --script=banner -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-banner.txt nc -nv TARGET PORT openssl s_client -connect TARGET:PORT -servername HOSTNAME curl -vk --max-time 10 https://TARGET:PORT/ ``` > **Next action:** route application evidence to the matching Stage 02 page. If TLS succeeds but HTTP does not, preserve the certificate names and protocol evidence instead of labelling it HTTPS. ##### NSE candidate checks Inspect a script before selecting it: ```bash nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME grep -i 'SCRIPT_NAME' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db ``` Run a named script against a confirmed service/port: ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script SCRIPT_NAME -p PORT TARGET -oN nse-SCRIPT_NAME.txt ``` The broad `vuln` category is candidate generation and can be intrusive or misleading. If its use is justified in the authorized lab, restrict it to identified ports and manually validate every result: ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script vuln -p PORTS TARGET -oN nse-vuln-candidates.txt ``` Avoid `*brute*` categories as a default; first establish exact service, known test identities, lockout/rate limits and explicit authorization. ##### Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation > **Prerequisite:** an identified HTTP(S) endpoint. **Choose it:** after manual baselining to identify common files, headers and server misconfiguration candidates. **Decisive output:** a finding manually reproduced with the same host, path and authentication context. ```bash nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -output nikto-TARGET-PORT.txt ```
HTTPS, host name and tuning variants ```bash nikto -h https://HOSTNAME:PORT -output nikto-HOSTNAME-PORT.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -vhost HOSTNAME -output nikto-vhost.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -Tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt ``` > Tuning codes are version-sensitive. Inspect `nikto -H` / local documentation before relying on a copied code set.
Nikto is explicitly listed as allowed by the current OffSec exam guide, but its findings remain scanner candidates. Recheck the guide before an exam and manually validate anything that affects an attack decision.

methods.title: Use anonymous or authenticated FTP file access
methods.clue: An FTP banner or accessible listing
methods.conditions: Anonymous login allowed or a valid FTP identity; data-channel connectivity and object-specific read/write rights
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: Retrieved files, configuration or a verified writable location
methods.mechanics: FTP authentication and directory listing do not guarantee downloads or uploads. Passive/active data channels can fail independently of the control connection; uploaded bytes need a separate execution consumer.
methods.example: Observation: anonymous login succeeds. Test: list and download one relevant readable configuration. Illustrative output: an application username is present. Interpretation: classify its credential context and test only a compatible service.
methods.verify: Retrieve recognizable bytes or independently verify an uploaded canary; distinguish listing, read and write rights.
methods.failure: Login succeeds but transfers hang: diagnose the data path. A writable upload directory alone does not establish command execution.

recognition.where: After identifying FTP, test the allowed anonymous context or one known credential and inspect its directory namespace.
recognition.sample:
230 Login successful
LIST: application.conf; backups/
RETR application.conf: 226 Transfer complete
recognition.spot: A listing identifies candidate artifacts; a completed RETR with recognizable bytes establishes read access.
recognition.confirm: Validate the account context, file contents, data-channel reachability and any separate write/consumer conditions.
recognition.enabled: The relevant file is readable and contains a current typed secret: follow credential classification.
recognition.ruledout: Anonymous login is denied: rule out anonymous access, retaining authenticated FTP as a separate possibility.
recognition.unknown: Login works but data transfer hangs: inspect active/passive data routing before concluding file access is denied.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognize:** FTP usually appears on TCP/21, but trust an FTP banner or protocol response on any port. **Goal:** determine authentication, listable/readable content and effective write locations. ##### Baseline: anonymous access ```bash ftp TARGET ``` At the prompts, try user `anonymous` and an email-like password. Then: ```text status pwd ls -la binary get FILE quit ``` If login succeeds but listing/transfer fails, use the client's `passive` command to toggle data-channel mode and retry once before changing credentials. > **Decisive output:** code `230` accepts the login; directory listings and successful `RETR` establish read access. Inspect downloaded backups, configuration, keys and source locally. Store target artifacts outside this public repository.
Variant — authenticated FTP ```bash ftp TARGET ``` Enter `USER` and the password when prompted. Enumerate from the authenticated root again; it may expose a different namespace than anonymous access.
Variant — curl listing, download and bounded write test ```bash curl --list-only ftp://TARGET/ curl -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER ftp://TARGET/ curl --user USER -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER --upload-file ./probe.txt ftp://TARGET/path/probe.txt ``` Omit `--user` for anonymous access. Let curl prompt for an authenticated password instead of placing it in shell history. Upload only a harmless uniquely named probe when write validation is necessary and authorized; remove it through the FTP client after the test.
Variant — focused Nmap helpers ```bash nmap -sV -p PORT --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst TARGET ``` `ftp-anon` checks anonymous login and may flag writable entries; `ftp-syst` asks for server/system information. Manually confirm useful access with a protocol client.
> **Failure cues:** `530` means that login was rejected, not that FTP has no other usable identity. A listing failure after `230` may be a data-channel/passive-mode or authorization problem. A successful upload proves write access only; it does not prove that a web server, scheduled task or privileged process consumes that file. > **Next action:** inspect recovered files; record exact read/write boundaries; validate any new credential once against its likely service; send a writable-consumer hypothesis to the appropriate web, execution or privilege-escalation block.

methods.title: Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access
methods.clue: An SSH service and a known password, private key or agent context
methods.conditions: Compatible authentication method, correct user, accepted key policy and the requested shell/subsystem permission
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: An authenticated shell, subsystem or forwarding capability with verified identity
methods.mechanics: SSH authentication can succeed while shell access is restricted. Key ownership, passphrase and server authorization matter independently; forwarding is a separately controlled feature.
methods.checks:
```bash
ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET
ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET
```
methods.example: Observation: a disclosed private key names a local user. Test: inspect the key and authenticate to that user. Illustrative output: a shell returns with a non-root UID. Interpretation: establish Linux state and inspect allowed forwarding.
methods.verify: Run hostname and id in the resulting context; retain whether a shell, SFTP or only forwarding was actually granted.
methods.failure: Permission denied may be username, key, passphrase, policy or method mismatch. A successful banner exchange proves none of these.

recognition.where: Find SSH in service discovery, then trace a candidate password/key back to its recorded user before a bounded authentication attempt.
recognition.commands:
```bash
ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET
ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET
```
recognition.sample:
Authenticated to TARGET using publickey
uid=USER_ID(USER) gid=GROUP_ID(GROUP)
recognition.spot: Accepted key authentication plus a verified shell identity establishes that specific login, not root or unrestricted forwarding.
recognition.confirm: Check actual account/shell/subsystem and separately inspect forwarding policy if a tunnel is needed.
recognition.enabled: The intended user can run commands: establish host/privilege/network state.
recognition.ruledout: The same valid key is not authorized for this user: rule out that username/key pairing.
recognition.unknown: A passphrase prompt or host policy rejection requires key/context diagnosis; it is not evidence that all SSH access is unavailable.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognize:** SSH commonly uses TCP/22. **Prerequisite for access:** an accepted authentication method plus a permitted account/session context. ##### Baseline: validate one known identity ```bash ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** the debug trace separates connection, host-key negotiation, offered authentication methods and account acceptance. A shell prompt establishes session access as that identity.
Variant — private key ```bash chmod 600 KEY ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` The key must correspond to an authorized public key for that account. `Permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user, wrong key, server policy or account restrictions.
Variant — discover methods for a known username ```bash nmap -p PORT --script ssh-auth-methods --script-args "ssh.user=USER" TARGET ``` This starts an authentication exchange and is logged; Nmap classifies it as intrusive. Use it only when the supported methods change the next decision.
Variant — non-interactive key check ```bash ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET 'id' ``` Batch mode will not prompt for passwords or key passphrases. It is useful only when the key is already usable non-interactively.
> **Failure cues:** timeout suggests route/filtering/service issues; refusal means no accepting listener in that context; host-key failure occurs before user authentication; `Permission denied` proves that the attempted method/context failed, not that every credential is invalid. A valid account may still have no shell or be restricted by server policy. > **Next action:** after a shell, verify `whoami`, groups, hostname and addresses, then re-enumerate locally. Password spraying and key-passphrase cracking belong to the credential-attack block, not this procedure.

methods.title: Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols
methods.clue: SMTP capabilities or mail-related account clues
methods.conditions: Reachable SMTP/POP3/IMAP service; enumeration or mailbox access must be enabled for the selected context
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: Validated mail capabilities, possible usernames or authenticated mailbox artifacts
methods.mechanics: VRFY/RCPT differences may disclose account existence but catch-all policy can invalidate inference. A valid recipient is not an authenticated mailbox or operating-system login.
methods.example: Observation: two recipient probes produce different replies. Test: compare known-invalid controls and repeated responses. Illustrative output: only one candidate is consistently accepted. Interpretation: retain a possible username and check account context before authentication testing.
methods.verify: Record response/control differences and separate inferred account existence from successful mailbox authentication.
methods.failure: Uniform replies, disabled VRFY or a catch-all make username enumeration inconclusive; investigate other identity sources.

recognition.commands:
```bash
nc -nv TARGET 25
```
Then enter the protocol dialogue:

```text
EHLO example.invalid
VRFY USER
VRFY INVALID_CONTROL
QUIT
```
recognition.sample:
220 HOSTNAME ESMTP
250-VRFY
VRFY USER -> 250 USER
VRFY INVALID_CONTROL -> 550 No such user
recognition.spot: A reproducible reply difference can expose a possible mailbox identity.
recognition.confirm: Check catch-all policy and account context; recipient acceptance does not prove mailbox credentials or OS access.
recognition.enabled: Controls support a real account and compatible credentials are available: validate its permitted mailbox/service access.
recognition.ruledout: All recipients are accepted by catch-all behavior: discard account-existence inference from this test.
recognition.unknown: Uniform policy replies leave usernames unknown; inspect another identity source.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognize:** SMTP commonly uses TCP/25, submission uses 587, and implicit TLS commonly uses 465. **Goal:** collect banner/capabilities, mail-domain clues and only defensible user evidence. ##### Baseline: banner and capabilities ```bash nc -nv TARGET PORT ``` Then enter: ```text EHLO example.invalid HELP VRFY USER EXPN postmaster QUIT ``` > **Decisive output:** `250-` capability lines reveal extensions such as STARTTLS or AUTH. `250` after `VRFY` may support a valid mailbox; `550` commonly rejects or denies it; `252` explicitly means the server will not verify and is not proof that the user exists.
Variant — STARTTLS or implicit TLS ```bash openssl s_client -connect TARGET:587 -starttls smtp -crlf -quiet openssl s_client -connect TARGET:465 -crlf -quiet ``` Run `EHLO example.invalid` after TLS negotiation. Certificate names and capabilities can yield host/domain clues; authentication still requires a supported identity and mechanism.
Variant — focused automated user checks ```bash smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT smtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT ``` `RCPT` testing requires an SMTP transaction and servers may deliberately normalize responses. Treat automation as candidate generation and manually compare decisive responses.
Variant — Windows source position ```powershell Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORT ``` This verifies TCP reachability only. Use an available Netcat/Ncat or OpenSSL client for protocol dialogue.
> **Failure cues:** multiline replies begin with `NNN-` and finish with `NNN `; read the final line. `503` often means the command sequence is wrong. Uniform `252` or `550` responses make enumeration inconclusive. A visible AUTH method does not mean anonymous relay or valid credentials. > **Next action:** add confirmed/candidate names and domains to the private evidence ledger; test new names only in the later credential block. Do not send real mail or run relay checks unless the objective requires it. ##### POP3 and IMAP handoff Mail-access services expose mailbox capabilities and, with legitimate credentials, stored messages that may contain workflow or reset links. ```bash openssl s_client -connect TARGET:995 -crlf -quiet # POP3S openssl s_client -connect TARGET:993 -crlf -quiet # IMAPS ``` POP3 dialogue: ```text CAPA USER USER PASS PASSWORD STAT LIST QUIT ``` IMAP dialogue: ```text a1 CAPABILITY a2 LOGIN USER PASSWORD a3 LIST "" "*" a4 LOGOUT ``` > Test one legitimately acquired credential. Capability output is not authentication; avoid brute-force NSE scripts until lockout/authorization is explicitly understood. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap mail blocks.

methods.title: Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers
methods.clue: A DNS server, domain name or host aliases
methods.conditions: Reachable DNS transport and relevant authoritative zone; AXFR requires an allowed TCP zone transfer
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: Hostnames, address relationships and possibly a zone inventory
methods.mechanics: A DNS answer belongs to a server and zone context. AXFR exposes zone records only when the server is authoritative and permits the transfer; names become discovery or virtual-host inputs.
methods.checks:
```bash
dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA
dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS
dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR
```
methods.example: Observation: the authoritative server permits AXFR. Test: inspect the returned A/CNAME records. Illustrative output: a previously unknown application hostname. Interpretation: confirm scope/address reachability and request that virtual host.
methods.verify: Identify responding server, record type, answer and zone authority; transfer refusal disproves only that transfer/context.
methods.failure: No answer may mean wrong server, recursion policy, transport or zone. Resolve authoritative context before retrying AXFR.

recognition.where: Use DNS-server evidence and discovered domain names to query authority and specific records before considering a transfer.
recognition.commands:
```bash
dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA
dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS
dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR
```
recognition.sample:
DOMAIN. SOA DC_HOST. HOSTMASTER.
HOSTNAME.DOMAIN. A TARGET
Transfer completed
recognition.spot: An authoritative zone and returned records can expose hostnames, aliases and applications needing separate enumeration.
recognition.confirm: Check each new name's scope/address and verify host/virtual-host behavior.
recognition.enabled: A permitted transfer returns a relevant new host: validate it through discovery.
recognition.ruledout: Transfer refused rules out AXFR on this server/zone/context; ordinary records may remain useful.
recognition.unknown: A timeout or non-authoritative response requires authority/transport checks before any zone conclusion.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognize:** DNS uses UDP/53 for most queries and TCP/53 for operations including conventional zone transfers and oversized responses. **Prerequisite:** a known or inferred domain for meaningful record and name enumeration. ##### Baseline: query the target DNS server directly ```bash dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS dig @TARGET DOMAIN A dig @TARGET DOMAIN MX dig @TARGET DOMAIN TXT ``` > **Decisive output:** `ANSWER` records disclose names, addresses, mail exchangers or text. The `aa` flag supports an authoritative answer. Record `status` separately from the answer count.
Variant — reverse lookup and zone transfer ```bash dig @TARGET -x IP dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR ``` A successful AXFR returns the zone records and closing SOA. `Transfer failed`, `REFUSED` or `NOTAUTH` only disproves an unauthenticated transfer from this source; continue ordinary queries.
Variant — name guessing after the domain is known ```bash dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -t std dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -D WORDLIST -t brt dnsenum --dnsserver TARGET DOMAIN ``` Check wildcard behavior before trusting large result sets. Every resolved in-scope name becomes a new discovery/service-enumeration input.
Variant — reverse sweep of an explicitly assigned range ```bash dnsrecon -r SUBNET -n TARGET ``` Use this only when the entire `SUBNET` is assigned. PTR names are clues; resolve/scan only in-scope results.
Variant — host and Windows nslookup ```bash host -t mx DOMAIN TARGET host -t txt DOMAIN TARGET ``` ```powershell nslookup HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=TXT HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=MX DOMAIN TARGET ```
> **Failure cues:** `NXDOMAIN` means that queried name does not exist in that view; `NOERROR` with no answer can mean the name exists but lacks that record type. Timeout can be filtering, loss or a silent/unreachable server. A recursive answer does not establish that the server is authoritative. > **Next action:** add new hostnames/IPs to the scoped queue, correlate naming roles with observed services, and repeat discovery/service identification for those in-scope endpoints.

methods.title: Inspect RPC/NFS exports and effective file identity
methods.clue: RPC/NFS listeners or export information
methods.conditions: Reachable RPC/NFS transports, permitted client address and an export whose UID/GID mapping grants relevant access
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: Readable files or a controlled write with established identity semantics
methods.mechanics: NFS authorization can depend on numeric IDs and export options. root_squash prevents remote UID 0 from automatically becoming server root; no_root_squash alone still needs a useful consumer or execution path.
methods.example: Observation: an export permits the assessment client. Test: inspect ownership and a scoped read. Illustrative output: a backup configuration is readable under a matching numeric UID. Interpretation: recover its secrets; assess writes separately.
methods.verify: Verify the export, mapped identity, actual bytes and any created file's server-side ownership.
methods.failure: An empty showmount response does not rule out NFSv4. Mount failure may be transport/export/client-policy rather than absence of files.

recognition.where: Follow RPC/NFS discovery with export inspection, then examine actual ownership/mapping on an allowed mount.
recognition.sample:
100003  3  tcp  NFS_PORT  nfs
Export list for TARGET:
/EXPORT CLIENT_SCOPE
recognition.spot: An export lists a filesystem candidate and client policy; it does not establish file access or trusted UID 0.
recognition.confirm: Use the owning procedure to verify NFS version, allowed client, numeric identity mapping, read/write and squash/mount policy.
recognition.enabled: The relevant mapped identity can read configuration: retrieve and classify its useful artifacts.
recognition.ruledout: The export permits a different client scope: rule out this source's mount route.
recognition.unknown: Empty showmount can miss NFSv4 context; confirm version/export behavior before declaring no NFS access.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognize:** rpcbind commonly appears on TCP/UDP 111 and NFS on TCP/UDP 2049, with additional dynamically assigned RPC ports. **Goal:** find exports, allowed client ranges and effective UID/GID-based permissions. ##### Baseline: list RPC services and exports ```bash rpcinfo -p TARGET showmount -e TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** `rpcinfo` maps RPC programs to versions/transports/ports. `showmount -e` returns exports and apparent allowed clients, but NFSv4-only servers may not expose the mount service and `showmount` completeness varies by implementation.
Variant — Nmap without mounting ```bash nmap -sV -p 111,2049 --script nfs-showmount,nfs-ls,nfs-statfs TARGET ``` The scripts can list exports, file attributes and access flags. Confirm access manually when a finding matters.
Variant — mount read-only first ```bash sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-audit sudo mount -t nfs -o ro,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -ls sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit ``` If version 3 fails and version 4 is advertised, retry with `-o ro,vers=4`. NFSv4 may present a pseudo-filesystem whose export path differs from `showmount` output.
Variant — inspect numeric ownership ```bash ls -lan /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -type f -readable -ls ``` NFS commonly authorizes Unix identities by numeric UID/GID. A matching local username is irrelevant if its number differs. `root_squash` usually maps remote UID 0 to an unprivileged identity; `no_root_squash` is dangerous but still requires a useful writable object and privileged consumption path.
Variant — bounded write verification ```bash sudo mount -t nfs -o rw,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit touch /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file ls -ln /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file rm /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit ``` Use a unique harmless name only when write validation is needed and authorized. Record the resulting numeric owner/group. Success proves write in that directory, not execution or privileged ownership.
> **Failure cues:** `showmount` failure does not rule out NFSv4. `access denied by server` can mean export client restrictions or wrong path/version. `permission denied` after mounting is file authorization, not network failure. Do not change local UIDs or write to an export during concept study. > **Next action:** inspect readable backups, home data, keys and configuration; record numeric ownership and actual write boundaries; send a writable/privileged-consumer hypothesis to the escalation block.

methods.title: Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities
methods.clue: SMB/RPC endpoints, domain clues or new credentials
methods.conditions: Reachable SMB/RPC; anonymous, guest, local or domain context must be explicit; share and filesystem ACLs both matter
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: Domain/user clues, readable files or object-specific writable access
methods.mechanics: Session establishment, share enumeration, filesystem rights and remote execution are separate authorization layers. A credential change can reveal entirely new shares and files.
methods.example: Observation: anonymous share listing is denied but a recovered domain credential works. Test: open one relevant share and retrieve a configuration. Illustrative output: a service account secret appears. Interpretation: record its identity and re-enter credential validation.
methods.verify: Prove the specific share/object action; a successful login or administrative indicator does not establish every remote-execution route.
methods.failure: Access denied after login usually means authorization/context. Test local/domain qualification and the exact object rather than repeating passwords.

recognition.where: Start from confirmed SMB and explicitly compare anonymous versus a known authenticated context, then open a relevant named share.
recognition.sample:
Sharename       Type
SHARE           Disk
NETLOGON        Disk
recognition.spot: A share name supplies a filesystem investigation target; listing it does not prove read, write or service creation.
recognition.confirm: Connect to the named share under the identity that listed it, then ls/get the exact object. Listing a share does not prove read or write. For a write candidate, verify the path operation and identify a separate execution consumer before treating it as access.
recognition.enabled: A relevant configuration can be retrieved: inspect its account/secret context.
recognition.ruledout: The authenticated account cannot read that object: discard the read path for this identity, not all SMB opportunities.
recognition.unknown: Login succeeds but listing fails: check a justified known share path and separate share/NTFS authorization.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognize:** direct-hosted SMB commonly uses TCP/445; NetBIOS session service commonly uses TCP/139; MS-RPC endpoint mapping commonly uses TCP/135. They are related Windows surfaces but not interchangeable. **Goal:** distinguish null, guest and authenticated contexts; enumerate shares, files, users, groups, domain/workgroup clues and actual permissions. ##### Baseline: list shares without credentials ```bash smbclient -N -L //TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** a share list proves that this access context can enumerate names. It does not prove access to share contents. `NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` means this context was denied; repeat after obtaining a legitimate credential.
Variant — authenticated share listing and connection ```bash smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'TARGET/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'guest%' ``` The first two forms use a domain identity, the third makes a local target account explicit, and the fourth tests a guest account with an empty password. Let the client prompt for non-empty passwords. Inside the share: ```text pwd ls allinfo FILE get FILE mkdir probe-dir rmdir probe-dir exit ``` Use a harmless uniquely named directory only when write permission must be verified. A successful create/remove establishes share-level write access, not code execution.
Variant — recursive retrieval ```bash smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' -c 'recurse ON;prompt OFF;mget *' ``` Run from a dedicated local evidence directory and review expected volume first. Search downloaded configuration, scripts, backups, keys and unattended-install files locally; never publish recovered data.
Variant — RPC null or authenticated session ```bash rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET rpcclient -U 'DOMAIN/USER' TARGET ``` Useful interactive queries: ```text srvinfo enumdomains enumdomusers enumdomgroups queryuser RID netshareenumall quit ``` Null-session denial is common on modern systems. Authenticated output must be labelled with the identity that produced it.
Variant — fast permission summary and consolidated candidates ```bash nxc smb TARGET -u USER -p PASSWORD --shares enum4linux-ng -A TARGET ``` NetExec (`nxc`) is the current command name on recent Kali releases; older material may use `crackmapexec`. These tools consolidate candidates. Confirm useful shares and files with `smbclient` or native access.
Variant — protocol, signing and time clues ```bash nmap -p 139,445 --script smb-protocols,smb2-security-mode,smb2-time TARGET ``` Signing and dialect results affect later relay/exploit decisions but are not vulnerabilities by themselves. The older `smb-os-discovery` script depends on SMBv1 behavior and may not identify modern hosts reliably.
Variant — Windows built-ins ```powershell net view \\TARGET /all Get-ChildItem \\TARGET\SHARE Get-Content \\TARGET\SHARE\FILE ``` These use the current Windows logon context unless alternate credentials or mappings are established. An existing connection to the same server under another identity can cause credential-conflict errors.
SMBMap — map rights, then read one useful file Use from Kali when SMB is reachable. Choose the same domain/local identity that worked with smbclient. Suppress write probes when inventorying reads; this means a writable label is not being tested here. ```bash # Known domain account: enumerate share access without creating a probe file smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --no-write-check # Inspect the selected share to a bounded depth smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -r 'SHARE' --depth 2 --no-write-check # Download the specific file found above smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --download 'SHARE\PATH\FILE' --no-write-check ``` > **Read:** a listed file must still be readable under this identity. A downloaded config/backup → classify its credential material, then test only the relevant account/service. A denied share → try another listed share or a newly obtained identity; do not infer a host-wide denial. [SMBMap upstream](https://github.com/ShawnDEvans/smbmap). For broader SMB/RPC collection, use the existing enum4linux-ng baseline; authenticate explicitly when credentials exist: ```bash # No credentials: anonymous RPC/SMB candidates enum4linux-ng -A TARGET # Known identity: domain objects visible to this account enum4linux-ng -A -w DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' TARGET ``` > **Next:** validate returned users/groups/shares with rpcclient or smbclient. A collector can return partial data despite a successful login.
> **Failure cues:** distinguish connection failure, authentication failure, share enumeration denial and file authorization denial. A share named `IPC$` is not a general file share. Guest acceptance may look like success while returning a restricted namespace. A share marked writable still needs a consumer/trigger before it becomes an execution path. > **Next action:** inspect readable content, record per-share rights, validate names/domain clues, and re-run authenticated enumeration whenever identity changes. Move file-consumer hypotheses to web/execution/escalation and signing/relay hypotheses to the later credential/AD blocks.

methods.title: Extract configuration and process information through SNMP
methods.clue: UDP/161 evidence or an exposed management plane
methods.conditions: An accepted read community or SNMPv3 identity/security level; transport and view permissions
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: Host, interface, software or process/configuration clues from permitted OID branches
methods.mechanics: An SNMP community acts as an access selector; views can expose only some trees. A successful system OID does not grant write access or all process data.
methods.example: Observation: a system OID responds. Test: inspect the relevant interface/process branch. Illustrative output: an internal subnet and application command line. Interpretation: return the subnet to scoped discovery and classify any exposed credential.
methods.verify: Preserve the OID, accepted security context and returned value; empty branches can reflect view restrictions.
methods.failure: Silence can mean UDP filtering, wrong community/version or denied view; change only the condition supported by evidence.

recognition.where: Take UDP/161 evidence and a justified management credential/community, then request a small known OID branch before a broad walk.
recognition.sample:
SNMPv2-MIB::sysDescr.0 = STRING: OS_AND_BUILD
SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0 = STRING: HOSTNAME
recognition.spot: A real OID response confirms the accepted read context and supplies software/name clues.
recognition.confirm: Determine which useful views/branches are actually readable; process data and write rights are separate.
recognition.enabled: A relevant interface/process branch returns useful data: follow the named subnet/application/credential.
recognition.ruledout: An explicit authorization failure rules out that security context/view.
recognition.unknown: UDP silence can be routing, version, community or view policy; a timeout cannot choose between them.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognize:** SNMP queries commonly use UDP/161. Versions 1 and 2c authenticate with a community string sent without modern transport protection; version 3 can provide user-based authentication and privacy. **Goal:** turn a valid read context into host, interface, route, process, software, user and listener clues. ##### Baseline: find a read community, then walk ```bash onesixtyone -c COMMUNITY_FILE TARGET snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` Use `-v1` instead when version 1 is indicated. Start with the standard system tree before a huge full walk. > **Decisive output:** returned OID/value pairs prove that the selected version/community can read those objects. Hostnames, interfaces, routes, users, processes and locally listening ports become new hypotheses to validate through the appropriate service or post-access path.
Variant — efficient v2c bulk walk ```bash snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` Bulk requests reduce round trips but require SNMPv2c or later. If the agent rejects them, fall back to `snmpwalk` with the verified version.
Variant — high-value Windows OIDs ```bash snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3 ``` These target user names, running process names, installed software and TCP listener ports. Availability depends on the agent and exposed MIB view.
Variant — SNMPv3 authenticated and private walk ```bash snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u USER -a SHA -A AUTH_PASSWORD -x AES -X PRIV_PASSWORD TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` The security level, authentication algorithm, privacy algorithm and credentials must match the configured SNMPv3 user. `authNoPriv` authenticates without encryption; `noAuthNoPriv` supplies neither and should be used only when that exact configuration is observed.
Variant — focused UDP verification ```bash sudo nmap -sU -sV -p 161 --script snmp-info TARGET ``` `snmp-info` extracts basic SNMPv3 engine information without proving a usable v1/v2c community.
> **Failure cues:** UDP silence can remain `open|filtered`; it does not prove that the community is wrong. `Timeout: No Response` can be version mismatch, wrong community, filtering, loss or an unavailable OID view. `No Such Object` means the queried OID is absent/not exposed, not that the whole service failed. Do not use a discovered write community to change configuration during enumeration. > **Next action:** translate output into exact host/service/user hypotheses, scan newly disclosed in-scope addresses/listeners from the proper source position, and keep configuration-changing SNMP actions outside this stage.
